sessions.t2: A childhood friend you remember well
p1: Are you a student or do you work?

I am a full-time student at the moment, so studying {takes up|koʻp vaqtimni oladi} most of my week. I am in my second year, and {alongside|bilan bir qatorda} my classes I do a bit of private tutoring at weekends, mainly to {put my knowledge into practice|bilimimni amalda qoʻllash}.
What are you studying?

I am studying economics, which {covers everything from|dan tortib hammasini qamrab oladi} basic microeconomics to statistics and public finance. The part I enjoy most is data analysis, because it forces you to {back up your arguments with|dalillar bilan asoslash} hard numbers rather than opinions.
Why did you choose this subject?

Honestly, it was a {deliberate choice|ongli tanlov} rather than an accident. I had always been curious about why some countries {thrive|gullab-yashnaydi} while others struggle, and economics seemed like the one subject that could give me a {systematic explanation|tizimli izoh} of that.
Do you enjoy studying it?

Most of the time, yes. Some modules are quite {demanding|talabchan, qiyin} and involve a lot of maths, but there is a real {sense of satisfaction|qoniqish hissi} when a complicated model finally clicks. I would say the difficulty is exactly what {keeps me engaged|qiziqishimni saqlab turadi}.
Do you often use headphones?

Almost every day, to be honest. They have become {an essential part of|ajralmas qismi} my routine, especially on the bus, and I would feel a bit {lost|yoʻqolgandek} without them. I only take them off when I am at home with my family.
What do you usually use headphones for?

Mainly for music and podcasts, but I also use them to {block out|toʻsib qoʻymoq} background noise when I am revising in the library. Occasionally I listen to IELTS listening tests with them, because you {pick up|ilgʻab olmoq} far more detail than through a speaker.
When did you first start using headphones?

I think I was around eleven or twelve, when my parents bought me a cheap {pair of earphones|quloqchinlar} for a school trip. They were nothing special and they {broke within a month|bir oyda sinib qoldi}, but I remember being genuinely excited about them.
Do you prefer using headphones or speakers?

It really depends on the situation. Headphones give you {far better sound quality|ancha yaxshi ovoz sifati} and privacy, so I use them on my own, but if friends come over, speakers are better because music becomes something {shared|birgalikda boʻlishiladigan} rather than personal.
Did you have a favourite teacher at school?

Yes, my literature teacher in year nine. She was the first person who made me feel that my opinion actually {carried weight|ahamiyatga ega edi}, and she had a way of explaining things that {brought the text to life|matnni jonlantirardi}.
What made this teacher special?

She never simply {spoon-fed us|tayyor javob bermoq} answers. Instead, she would ask a question and then wait, sometimes uncomfortably long, until somebody {took the plunge|jur'at qilib boshladi}. That patience taught us to think independently, which is a {rare quality|kamdan-kam uchraydigan fazilat} in a teacher.
Do you think teachers are important?

Enormously. A good teacher can {shape a child's entire attitude to|bolaning butun munosabatini shakllantirmoq} learning, while a poor one can {put them off|qiziqishini soʻndirmoq} a subject for life. Knowledge is available everywhere now, but motivation still comes from people, and that is what teachers provide.
Would you like to be a teacher in the future?

Possibly, but not immediately. I would want to gain some {real-world experience|amaliy tajriba} first, because I think students respect a teacher far more when they can draw on examples from outside the classroom. So teaching is more of a {long-term ambition|uzoq muddatli maqsad} for me.

p2.task: Describe a childhood friend you remember well.
bullets: what you used to do together
and explain why you still remember this person well
p2.ans:
The friend I would like to talk about is a boy called Aziz, who lived three houses away from us and was, for about six years, {practically inseparable from me|mendan deyarli ajralmas edi}.

We met in the most ordinary way possible. My family moved into the neighbourhood when I was around seven, and on the very first afternoon he simply appeared at our gate with a football under his arm and asked whether I wanted to play. That was it. There was none of the {awkwardness|noqulaylik} adults go through when they meet someone new; children seem to {skip that stage entirely|bu bosqichni umuman oʻtkazib yuboradi}.

After that, we spent almost every free hour together. We played football in the street until it got dark, cycled to the canal, and in winter we built what we proudly called a fortress out of snow, although it {collapsed within hours|bir necha soatda qulab tushdi}. What I remember most vividly, though, is not the games themselves but the conversations. We used to sit on his roof and talk about what we would be when we grew up, and both of us were absolutely convinced we would {make it big|katta muvaffaqiyatga erishmoq} somehow.

The reason he has {stuck in my memory|xotiramda muhrlanib qolgan} is partly that he moved away when we were thirteen, so the friendship ended abruptly rather than {fading out gradually|asta-sekin soʻnib bormoq}. But it is also because he taught me something I still value. He was completely unafraid of looking silly, and being around him made me much more {outgoing|kirishimli} than I naturally am. In a sense, a part of my personality was {shaped by|shakllantirilgan} that friendship, which is probably why, fifteen years later, I can still picture him standing at our gate with that football.

p3: Where do young people usually make friends?

School and university are still the {main breeding ground|asosiy muhit} for friendships, simply because you see the same people every day and shared routine {builds trust|ishonch hosil qiladi} naturally. Beyond that, sports clubs and part-time jobs play a big role, and of course a huge number of friendships now start online, through gaming or shared interests, and only later {move offline|real hayotga koʻchadi}.
Do you think children can make friends at family gatherings?

They certainly can, although those friendships tend to be {situational|vaziyatga bogʻliq}. Cousins who only meet twice a year can get on brilliantly for an afternoon, but without regular contact the bond rarely {deepens|chuqurlashadi}. That said, family gatherings are valuable because children are forced to interact with people they did not choose, which is good {social training|ijtimoiy mashq}.
Is it easier for children to make friends than adults?

Far easier, in my view. Children have no {social baggage|ijtimoiy yuk} - they do not worry about status, background or whether they will be rejected. Adults, on the other hand, tend to be {guarded|ehtiyotkor} and their time is limited, so friendships have to compete with work and family. Proximity does most of the work for children; adults have to make a {conscious effort|ongli harakat}.
Do you think friends are more important than family?

I would not rank one above the other, because they meet {entirely different needs|butunlay boshqa ehtiyojlar}. Family gives you {unconditional support|shartsiz qoʻllab-quvvatlash} and a sense of belonging, whereas friends give you understanding, because they are usually going through the same stage of life. Ideally the two {complement each other|bir-birini toʻldiradi} rather than compete.
Why do some people become closer to their friends than to their family members?

Usually because friendship is {chosen rather than inherited|tanlangan, meros emas}. You pick friends who share your values, so there is often more {common ground|umumiy nuqta} from the start. There can also be generational differences at home that make young people feel {misunderstood|notoʻgʻri tushunilgan}, and friends of the same age simply {relate to|tushunadi, his qiladi} their situation more easily.

sessions.t2: An interview with a famous person you watched
p1: Where do you live?

I live in Urgench, in a fairly quiet {residential area|turar joy massivi} about ten minutes from the centre. It is not the liveliest part of town, but it is {within easy reach of|yaqin joylashgan} everything I need, which suits me perfectly.
What do you like most about your home?

Probably the light. Our living room faces south, so from the morning onwards it is {flooded with sunlight|quyosh nuriga toʻlgan}, and that makes the whole place feel {welcoming|yoqimli, mehmondoʻst}. Small things like that make a surprising difference to your mood.
Is there anything you would like to change about your home?

If I am honest, the kitchen. It is {cramped|tor, siqiq} and very badly designed, so whenever more than two people are cooking we {get in each other's way|bir-birimizga xalaqit beramiz}. I would knock down one wall and open it up to the living room.
Why would you like to change it?

Mainly because the kitchen is where my family actually {spends time together|birga vaqt oʻtkazadi}. At the moment its size {puts people off|odamlarni bezdiradi} staying there, so everyone drifts to their own room. A more open space would naturally {bring us together|bizni birlashtiradi}.
When do you usually feel tired?

Late afternoon is my {low point|eng past nuqta}, roughly between four and six. My concentration {drops sharply|keskin pasayadi} then, and if I have been staring at a screen all day the tiredness is mental rather than physical.
What do you do when you feel tired?

I try not to {reach for|qoʻl uzatmoq, olmoq} coffee straight away, because it only postpones the problem. Instead I go for a short walk or do something completely unrelated for twenty minutes, and usually that is enough to {recharge my batteries|kuchimni tiklash}.

p2.task: Describe an interview with a famous person that you watched or listened to.
bullets: where you watched or listened to it
and explain why it was memorable for you
p2.ans:
I would like to describe an interview I watched roughly a year ago with a well-known Uzbek film director, which was posted on YouTube by a local media channel and ran for almost an hour.

I came across it {by chance|tasodifan} late one evening when I was scrolling through videos, and I genuinely only intended to watch the first few minutes. In the end I watched the whole thing without {so much as glancing at|hatto bir qarab ham qoʻymay} my phone.

The interview was not the usual {promotional exercise|reklama tadbiri} where a celebrity simply talks about their latest project. The interviewer asked him about failure, which is something famous people are rarely willing to {open up about|ochilib gapirmoq}. He talked about two films that had {flopped badly|katta muvaffaqiyatsizlikka uchradi}, about the years when he could not find funding, and about seriously considering giving up the industry altogether. What struck me was how {candid|samimiy, ochiq} he was; there was none of the polished, rehearsed quality you normally get.

There was one moment in particular that has {stayed with me|esimda qolgan}. He said that talent is enormously overrated and that what actually separates people is the willingness to keep working when nobody is watching and nobody is paying. He put it very bluntly, and coming from someone who had clearly {paid his dues|qiyinchiliklarni boshidan kechirgan}, it did not sound like an empty motivational slogan.

The reason it was memorable is that it completely {changed my perception of|men haqimdagi tasavvurimni oʻzgartirdi} success. Before that I tended to see accomplished people as somehow {a different breed|boshqa toifadagi odamlar}. That interview made it obvious that they simply {persevere|sabr bilan davom etadi} for longer than everyone else, and I found that far more encouraging than any success story.

p3: Why do you think interviews are popular among young people?

Because they offer something that a polished article cannot: {unfiltered|filtrlanmagan} personality. Young people are, I think, quite {sceptical of|shubha bilan qaraydigan} official images, and an interview lets them judge someone by how they react in real time. There is also the {sheer convenience|qulaylik} of it - you can listen while commuting or exercising.
What about older people? Do they enjoy watching interviews?

They do, but often for different reasons. Older viewers tend to be drawn to interviews with politicians, historians or public figures whose careers they have {followed for decades|oʻnlab yillar davomida kuzatgan}, so there is an element of {nostalgia|nostalji} involved. Younger audiences are usually more interested in entertainers and entrepreneurs.
Do you think people's interest in interviews depends on their age?

To a degree, yes, although I would say the {subject matter|mavzu} matters more than the format. Age shapes who you find interesting rather than whether you enjoy interviews as such. A well-conducted interview with a {compelling|qiziqarli, oʻziga tortadigan} guest will hold almost anyone's attention regardless of generation.
What is the difference between interviews with famous people and ordinary people?

With celebrities there is usually a {media-trained|media boʻyicha oʻqitilgan} layer to get past; they know how to give an answer without really answering. Ordinary people are generally more {forthcoming|ochiq, gapdon}, and their stories can be surprisingly {relatable|yaqin, tushunarli}, because listeners see themselves in them rather than admiring from a distance.
What kinds of questions are usually asked when interviewing young people?

Typically about ambitions, technology, education and {peer pressure|tengdoshlar bosimi} - essentially, about the future. Interviewers tend to ask them what they hope to achieve and how their generation differs from the previous one, which is a question young people are always {keen to|xohishli} answer.
How might these questions be different when interviewing older people?

The focus shifts from the future to {hindsight|orqaga nazar}. Older interviewees are asked what they would do differently, how society has changed and what advice they would pass on. In other words, they are treated as a source of {accumulated wisdom|toʻplangan donolik} rather than potential.
Do you think interviews will become more popular in the future?

Almost certainly, largely because {the barrier to entry|kirish uchun toʻsiq} has disappeared. Anyone with a microphone can now run a podcast, so the number of interviews has {multiplied|koʻpaydi}. The challenge will be quality rather than quantity - audiences will {gravitate towards|tomon intiladi} interviewers who genuinely prepare.

sessions.t2: A time you had to listen to someone but were not interested
p1: What do you usually do when you feel tired?

It depends how tired I am. If it is just {mental fatigue|aqliy charchoq} I go for a walk or make tea, but if I am genuinely {worn out|holdan toygan} I will take a twenty-minute nap, which honestly does more for me than an hour of pretending to study.
What kinds of things make you feel tired?

Long hours in front of a screen, mostly. Oddly, I find that doing nothing is more {draining|kuch oladigan} than being busy, because boredom {saps your energy|energiyangizni soʻrib oladi}. Crowded, noisy places also leave me exhausted even if I have barely moved.
Would you meet your friends when you are feeling tired?

Usually yes, and I often {end up|oxir-oqibat} feeling better for it. Seeing people I am comfortable with tends to {lift my mood|kayfiyatimni koʻtaradi}. The only exception is if I have an early start the next day - then I would rather {take a rain check|keyingi safarga qoldirmoq}.
Do you often feel tired after a busy day?

Quite often, but it is usually a {pleasant kind of tiredness|yoqimli charchoq} - the sort you get when you have actually achieved something. What really exhausts me is a day full of small interruptions where nothing {gets finished|tugallanadi}.
Do you like advertisements?

I have {mixed feelings|ikki xil his} about them. A clever advert with a good story can be genuinely entertaining, and I will happily watch it twice. What I cannot stand is the {intrusive|xalaqit beradigan} kind that interrupts a video every two minutes.
What kind of advertisements do you usually notice?

The ones that make me laugh or tell a short story rather than simply {listing features|xususiyatlarni sanab oʻtish}. I also notice outdoor advertising with very simple, {striking|koʻzga tashlanadigan} images, because you only have a couple of seconds to take a billboard in.
Are there many advertisements where you live?

Yes, particularly along the main roads, where billboards are {springing up|paydo boʻlmoqda} constantly. Personally I find the amount of visual advertising a little {overwhelming|haddan tashqari koʻp}, because it ends up cluttering what are otherwise quite attractive streets.

p2.task: Describe a time when you had to listen to someone, but you were not interested.
bullets: and explain how you felt about it
p2.ans:
The occasion that comes to mind is a three-hour seminar on insurance law that I attended last winter, given by a visiting lecturer at my university.

Attendance was compulsory, so about a hundred of us were {packed into|tiqilib oʻtirgan} a lecture hall on a Friday afternoon, which is probably the worst possible time to ask students to concentrate on anything. The lecturer was clearly an expert - nobody doubted his {command of the subject|mavzuni chuqur bilishi} - but he read almost the entire session directly from slides, in a completely {monotonous|bir xil, zerikarli} voice, without a single example.

I was not interested for two reasons. The first is simply that insurance law has no {bearing on|aloqasi bor} what I want to do, so I could not see the point of it. The second, and more important, is that he made no attempt to {engage the audience|auditoriyani jalb qilish}. He never asked a question, never paused, and never explained why any of it mattered. Within twenty minutes the room had {switched off|diqqatini yoʻqotdi} almost entirely, and people were quietly scrolling on their phones.

Interestingly, what I felt was not really boredom but {frustration|umidsizlik, asabiylashish}. I kept thinking that with a couple of real cases the same material could have been fascinating, and it seemed like a {wasted opportunity|boy berilgan imkoniyat}. I also felt slightly guilty for not paying attention, so I forced myself to take notes just to {stay awake|uygʻoq qolish}.

Looking back, though, it taught me something useful. It made me realise that being knowledgeable and being able to communicate are {two entirely separate skills|butunlay ikki xil koʻnikma}, and that if you cannot hold people's attention, even brilliant content will {fall on deaf ears|quloqqa kirmaydi}.

p3: Why are some people interested in talking to older people?

Mainly because older people offer {first-hand accounts|bevosita guvohlik} of things the rest of us only read about. There is also a difference in perspective: they tend to judge events over decades rather than weeks, which can be {refreshing|yangilik bagʻishlaydigan}. And many of them are simply excellent storytellers, since they grew up before screens {took over|egallab oldi} conversation.
What kinds of information do young people usually share with each other?

A great deal of it is about entertainment and technology - what to watch, what app to use, which course is worth taking. They also exchange a lot of {practical advice|amaliy maslahat} about studying and job opportunities. What they rarely share openly is anything that makes them look {vulnerable|zaif}, at least not outside a close circle.
How can people know whether someone is listening to them?

Mostly through {body language|tana tili} - eye contact, nodding, an open posture. But the clearest evidence is in the response: if someone asks a follow-up question or refers back to something you said earlier, they were genuinely listening. Anyone can nod while {miles away|xayoli boshqa joyda}.
Why is it important to listen carefully when someone is talking?

Because most misunderstandings come from half-listening rather than from disagreement. Careful listening also signals respect, and it {defuses|yumshatadi} conflict surprisingly quickly - people become far less {defensive|himoyalanuvchi} once they feel heard. Professionally, it also saves an enormous amount of time that would otherwise be spent correcting mistakes.
What would you do if someone did not listen to you?

I would not {take it personally|shaxsiy xafagarchilik sifatida qabul qilmoq} straight away, because they may simply be preoccupied. Usually I would stop, ask a direct question, or suggest continuing later. If it became a pattern, I would say so honestly, since {bottling it up|ichida saqlash} only breeds resentment.
Do you think young people are good listeners?

They can be, but I think {sustained|uzluksiz} attention is genuinely harder for my generation. We are used to content that changes every few seconds, so sitting through a long, slow explanation feels unnatural. Where young people do listen extremely well is with their peers, so it is a question of {motivation rather than ability|qobiliyat emas, motivatsiya masalasi}.

sessions.t2: A person who loves to grow plants
p1: Where is your hometown?

My hometown is Namangan, which is in the Fergana Valley, in the eastern part of the country. It is one of the largest cities in Uzbekistan, although it still {retains|saqlab qolgan} quite a traditional feel.
Could you describe your hometown a little?

It is a busy, green city with {tree-lined streets|daraxtzor koʻchalar} and a very large central bazaar that has been there for generations. The valley is extremely {fertile|unumdor}, so the region is known for its fruit and, more than anything, its flowers.
Do you like your hometown?

Very much. What I appreciate most is the {sense of community|jamoaviylik hissi} - neighbours genuinely know each other, which is something you {lose|yoʻqotasiz} in bigger cities. It is also small enough that you are never far from friends or family.
Would you say it is a big city or a small place?

By Uzbek standards it is definitely a big city, with several hundred thousand people. That said, it does not feel {overwhelming|bosim oʻtkazadigan} in the way Tashkent can, so it {strikes a nice balance|yaxshi muvozanatni topgan} between being lively and being manageable.
Do you like shopping?

I like it in small doses. Buying something I have actually planned for is enjoyable, but {wandering around|aylanib yurish} shops with no purpose {wears me out|meni charchatadi} very quickly. I am very much a targeted shopper.
How often do you go shopping?

For groceries, two or three times a week, usually at the local market. For clothes or anything more expensive, perhaps once every couple of months, and normally only when something {wears out|eskiradi} and genuinely needs replacing.
Do you usually compare prices when you go shopping?

Almost always, especially for anything that is not urgent. I will check two or three shops or {browse online|internetda koʻrib chiqmoq} first, because the difference can be considerable. For everyday items, though, I do not bother - the time is worth more than the saving.
Do you find it difficult to choose what to buy?

Sometimes, yes. When there are twenty {near-identical|deyarli bir xil} options I can end up {second-guessing myself|oʻzimdan shubhalanmoq} and buying nothing. I have learned to decide in advance what I need, which makes the whole process far less stressful.

p2.task: Describe a person who loves to grow plants.
bullets: what kinds of plants they grow
and explain why you think they enjoy it so much
p2.ans:
The person I want to describe is my grandmother, who has spent most of her life gardening and who is, without exaggeration, the most {devoted|sadoqatli} plant lover I know.

She lives in a small house on the edge of the city with a courtyard that she has turned into something close to a {miniature nursery|kichkina koʻchatxona}. She grows an enormous variety of things: grapes trained over a wooden frame, apricot and cherry trees, tomatoes and herbs in the summer, and along the whole length of one wall, roses, which are what she is really known for. Neighbours actually come to ask her advice, which she gives {at considerable length|ancha batafsil}.

The care she puts in is remarkable. She is out there at six in the morning before it gets hot, watering, {pruning|butamoq} and checking the leaves for disease. She makes her own compost from kitchen waste and is very {sceptical of|shubha bilan qaraydigan} chemical fertilisers, insisting that if you {look after the soil|tuproqni parvarish qilsang}, the plants take care of themselves. She also keeps everything in her head - what was planted where and when - without ever writing anything down.

As for why she enjoys it so much, I think there are several reasons. Gardening gives her a clear routine and a reason to be outside, which matters a great deal now that she is retired. There is also the obvious {satisfaction of seeing results|natijani koʻrish qoniqishi}: you plant something, you wait, and eventually it produces. But more than anything, I think it is her way of {passing something on|biror narsani meros qilib qoldirmoq}. Half of what grows in that courtyard came from cuttings her own mother gave her, so for her the garden is really a {living record|tirik yilnoma} of her family, and that is not something you can buy.

p3: Do many people in your country enjoy growing plants?

Yes, it is extremely common, partly for cultural reasons and partly because the climate is {favourable|qulay}. Almost every house with a courtyard will have grapevines or fruit trees, and even people in flats keep pots on their balconies. Growing at least some of your own food is still seen as {perfectly normal|butunlay odatiy}, not as a hobby.
What are the advantages of growing plants?

There are practical benefits - fresh produce, lower shopping bills, better air quality - but the psychological ones are just as important. Gardening is a well-known {stress reliever|stressni kamaytiruvchi}, it gets people outdoors, and it teaches patience, because nothing about it can be {rushed|shoshirilgan}. It also gives older people a valued role.
What kinds of plants are popular in your country?

Grapes are probably the most iconic, along with apricots, pomegranates and melons. In terms of ornamental plants, roses are very popular, and Namangan in particular is famous for flower growing. Indoors, people tend to keep {low-maintenance|parvarishi oson} plants like aloe and geraniums.
Do you think more people will grow plants in the future?

In cities I expect interest to grow, especially in indoor plants and balcony gardening, because people are increasingly aware of how much time they spend {cooped up indoors|uy ichida qamalib}. On the other hand, {plot sizes|yer maydonlari} are shrinking as flats replace houses, so people may grow more plants but on a far smaller scale.

sessions.t2: An interesting place you visited on holiday
p1: Where is your hometown?

I am from Namangan, a city in the eastern part of Uzbekistan, right in the middle of the Fergana Valley. My family has lived there for {several generations|bir necha avlod}, so I have very {deep roots|chuqur ildizlar} in the place.
Could you describe your hometown a little?

It is quite densely populated but surprisingly green, with wide avenues and a huge bazaar at its heart. The surrounding land is extremely {productive|hosildor}, so you see orchards as soon as you leave the city, and the whole region is renowned for flowers.
Do you like your hometown?

I do, though I can see its {shortcomings|kamchiliklar}. The traffic is getting worse and there are fewer career opportunities than in Tashkent. But it is affordable, it is safe, and people are genuinely {warm|samimiy}, which for me {outweighs|ustun keladi} the drawbacks.
Would you say it is a big city or a small place?

It is officially one of the biggest cities in the country, but in daily life it feels like a {collection of neighbourhoods|mahallalar toʻplami} rather than a metropolis. You constantly {bump into|duch kelmoq} people you know, which is something you would never experience in a really large city.
Do you like shopping?

Not particularly, if I am honest. I see it as a {necessary chore|zarur yumush} rather than a pastime. The one exception is bookshops, where I can happily lose an hour, which rather {undermines|puchga chiqaradi} my claim that I dislike shopping.
How often do you go shopping?

Food shopping happens {on a weekly basis|har hafta}, usually on Sunday morning at the market when everything is freshest. Other than that, I only go when there is a specific reason, so I might not set foot in a clothes shop for months.
Do you usually compare prices when you go shopping?

For big purchases, definitely. I will read reviews and compare a few sellers, because paying more for the {exact same item|aynan oʻsha mahsulot} is annoying. For small things I just buy whatever is closest - {haggling over|talashib oʻtirmoq} a few thousand soums is not worth the effort.
Do you find it difficult to choose what to buy?

Occasionally, especially with electronics, where the specifications all {blur together|bir-biriga qoʻshilib ketadi}. I have learned to set a budget and a couple of {non-negotiable requirements|majburiy talablar} before I start looking; otherwise I can spend a whole evening comparing and still not decide.

p2.task: Describe an interesting place you visited during a holiday or vacation.
bullets: and explain why you found it interesting
p2.ans:
The place I would like to talk about is Samarkand, which I visited with my family during a week-long holiday about two years ago.

We travelled there in early autumn, deliberately avoiding the summer, when the heat can be {unbearable|chidab boʻlmas}. We took the fast train from Tashkent, which took a little over two hours, and stayed in a small guesthouse in the old part of the city, only a short walk from Registan Square.

We spent most of our time simply exploring on foot. We visited Registan itself, the Bibi-Khanym Mosque and Shah-i-Zinda, which is a narrow street of {tiled|koshinli} tombs and is easily the most beautiful thing I have ever seen in my own country. We also wandered through the bazaar, tried far too much bread and halva, and in the evening went back to Registan when it was {lit up|yoritilgan}, which is a completely different experience.

What made it interesting was not only the architecture, striking though it is. It was the realisation that these buildings were {at the cutting edge of|eng ilgʻor darajada} science and design six hundred years ago. Standing in front of Ulugh Beg's observatory, where a ruler measured the length of the year to within a minute, {put things in perspective|narsalarga boshqacha qarashga majbur qildi} for me.

The other reason it {stands out|ajralib turadi} is more personal. I had studied all of this at school and, at the time, found it {utterly dull|juda zerikarli}. Seeing it in person turned a list of dates into something real. I came home with a much stronger sense of where I come from, and I think that is what the best kind of travel does - it {makes the familiar strange again|tanish narsani yangidan koʻrsatadi}.

p3: Why do people like visiting interesting places?

Partly out of pure {curiosity|qiziquvchanlik}, but also because travel {breaks the monotony|bir xillikni buzadi} of daily life. Seeing somewhere new forces you to pay attention in a way you simply do not at home. And of course there is a social dimension - people enjoy having experiences worth {sharing|boʻlishish} with others.
What kinds of places do people usually visit during holidays?

It splits roughly into three: beaches and mountains for people who want to {unwind|dam olmoq}, historical cities for those who want culture, and big capitals for shopping and nightlife. Increasingly I also notice people choosing {off-the-beaten-track|kam borilgan} destinations, precisely because they are not crowded.
Do you think people travel more now than in the past?

Considerably more. Flights are {relatively affordable|nisbatan arzon}, visa requirements have been {relaxed|yumshatilgan} in many places, and booking a trip takes minutes rather than days. On top of that, remote work means some people can travel without even taking leave, which was {unthinkable|tasavvur qilib boʻlmas} twenty years ago.
What are the advantages of visiting new places?

The obvious one is {broadening your horizons|dunyoqarashni kengaytirish}, but I would emphasise independence. Navigating an unfamiliar city, dealing with a language you do not speak, solving problems on the spot - all of that builds {self-reliance|mustaqillik}. Travel also tends to make people less {judgemental|hukm qiladigan}, because you see that there are many reasonable ways to live.
How can tourism affect local communities?

It {cuts both ways|ikki tomonlama ta'sir qiladi}. On the positive side it creates employment, funds the restoration of monuments and gives people a reason to keep traditional crafts alive. The downside is that popular areas can become {overrun|bosib ketilgan}, prices rise for residents, and culture can be reduced to a {performance for visitors|sayyohlar uchun tomosha}.
Do you think people will travel more or less in the future?

More, on balance, especially as middle classes expand in large countries. The one thing that might {hold it back|toʻxtatib turmoq} is environmental concern, since aviation is a major source of emissions. My guess is that people will still travel, but there will be growing pressure to travel {closer to home|uyga yaqinroq} and less frequently.

sessions.t2: A friend you enjoy talking to
p1: Where do you live?

I live in Tashkent, in a {high-rise block|koʻp qavatli bino} in the Yunusabad district. I have been there for about four years now, and although it is not the most characterful area, it is extremely {convenient|qulay} for the metro.
Which is your favourite room in your house?

Definitely my bedroom, mainly because I have {carved out|ajratib olgan} a small study corner by the window. That is where I do all my work, and having a space that is completely mine makes it much easier to {switch into|oʻtish, kirishmoq} a working frame of mind.
Do you read books?

Yes, although I read far less than I would like to. I usually manage a chapter before bed, and I tend to {alternate between|navbat bilan} fiction and non-fiction so that I do not {get stuck in a rut|bir xillikka tushib qolmoq}.
How often do you buy books?

Perhaps one a month, and most of them second-hand. I have a slightly embarrassing habit of buying faster than I read, so there is a {growing pile|ortib borayotgan uyum} on my desk of books I fully intend to get to.
Do you read more books now or did you read more in your childhood?

As a child, without question. Back then reading was my main form of entertainment and I would {devour|yutib yubormoq} a book in a weekend. Now it {competes with|raqobatlashadi} my phone and my studies, so although what I read is more serious, the quantity has definitely fallen.

p2.task: Describe a friend you enjoy talking to.
bullets: how long you have known them
and explain why you enjoy talking to this person
p2.ans:
The friend I would like to describe is Dilnoza, whom I met at university in our first week and have been close to ever since, so roughly four years now.

We were put in the same seminar group completely {at random|tasodifiy}, and I remember thinking at first that we had very little in common. She is studying law, I am not, and our tastes in almost everything are different. What we discovered, though, was that we {argue extremely well together|juda yaxshi bahslashamiz} - not aggressively, but in a way where neither of us takes offence.

Our conversations range enormously. Sometimes it is completely {trivial|arzimas} - complaining about lecturers, deciding where to eat - but the conversations I value are the longer ones, usually late at night, about what we actually want out of our careers, whether staying in the country is the right decision, and what we would change if we could {start over|qaytadan boshlash}. She also happens to be one of the very few people I can talk to about failure without feeling I have to {put a brave face on it|oʻzimni tetik koʻrsatmoq}.

The reason I enjoy talking to her so much comes down to two things. First, she is an exceptionally good listener - she does not simply wait for her turn to speak, and she will often {pick up on|ilgʻab olmoq} something I mentioned weeks earlier. Second, she is completely honest. If she thinks I am making a mistake she will {say so to my face|yuzimga aytadi}, which is rarer than people think, because most friends prefer to be agreeable.

Talking to her genuinely {clarifies my thinking|fikrlarimni tiniqlashtiradi}. I often go into a conversation confused and come out knowing what I actually believe, and I think that is the highest {compliment|maqtov} you can pay a friend.

p3: Where do you usually prefer to meet your friends?

Somewhere quiet enough to actually hear each other - a small cafe, or simply someone's home. I find that loud venues force you into {small talk|yuzaki suhbat}, whereas a calm setting lets the conversation {develop naturally|tabiiy rivojlanadi}. In good weather we often just walk, which is free and surprisingly {conducive to|qulay sharoit yaratadi} honest conversation.
Do you meet your friends in the same places now as you did when you were younger?

Not at all. As children we met outdoors, in the yard or at school, because we had {no money and no schedules|na pul, na jadval}. Now meeting requires planning and usually involves paying for something. That shift is convenient, but it does mean friendships take more {deliberate effort|ongli harakat} to maintain.
Is it important for leaders to communicate internationally?

It is essential. Most of the serious problems we face - climate, trade, security - {transcend borders|chegaralardan oshib ketadi}, and no country can address them alone. Beyond the practical side, regular contact between leaders {builds trust|ishonch hosil qiladi} and makes misunderstandings less likely to {escalate|keskinlashmoq} into something worse.
Do people always understand each other when they use a translator?

Rarely {in full|toʻliq}. A good translator can convey the meaning accurately, but humour, tone and cultural references often {get lost in translation|tarjimada yoʻqoladi}. There is also a delay that changes the rhythm of a conversation, so it tends to feel more formal and less {spontaneous|erkin, tabiiy} than speaking a shared language.
Why can't people solve some problems through talking?

Because talking only works when both sides genuinely want a solution. If the disagreement is about {fundamental values|asosiy qadriyatlar} rather than facts, no amount of discussion will close the gap. There are also cases where one party is negotiating {in bad faith|nosamimiy}, simply {playing for time|vaqtdan yutmoq}, and then dialogue becomes a tactic rather than a solution.
What are the common situations when people need to talk to strangers?

Everyday transactions, obviously - shops, taxis, asking for directions. But also job interviews, medical appointments and any kind of emergency, where you may have to {rely on|tayanmoq} a complete stranger. Networking events are another case, and in my experience those are the ones people find most {daunting|qoʻrqinchli}, because there is no clear script to follow.

sessions.t2: An enjoyable event
p1: Have you ever made something out of paper?

Yes, quite often as a child. I went through a phase of making paper aeroplanes and trying to work out which design {stayed in the air|havoda ushlanib turadi} longest. More recently I have made simple paper decorations for family celebrations, though I would not call myself {skilful|mohir}.
Did you make things from paper when you were a child?

Constantly. We had art lessons at school where we made {cut-out|qirqib olingan} animals and greeting cards, and at home I used to fold boats and float them in puddles. It was cheap entertainment, which mattered because we did not have many {store-bought|doʻkondan olingan} toys.
Do you like writing on paper?

I do, particularly for planning. There is something about writing by hand that {slows your thinking down|fikrlashni sekinlashtiradi} in a useful way, and I remember things far better when I have written them out rather than typed them.
Have you ever written a letter on paper?

Only a handful of times. I wrote to my grandmother when I was younger, and I have written thank-you notes for weddings. It feels like a {dying art|yoʻqolib borayotgan san'at}, which is a shame, because receiving a handwritten letter is far more {meaningful|ma'noli} than a message.
Do you prefer writing on paper or using a computer?

It depends entirely on the task. For anything long or that needs editing, a computer wins easily because you can {rearrange|qayta joylashtirmoq} everything instantly. But for brainstorming and note-taking, paper is far better - there are no notifications to {distract you|chalgʻitmoq}.

p2.task: Describe an enjoyable event.
bullets: where and when it took place
and explain why you enjoyed it so much
p2.ans:
The event I would like to describe is my cousin's wedding, which took place in Andijan last summer and was easily the most enjoyable day I have had in years.

It was held in late June, in a large hall on the outskirts of the city, and about three hundred people attended, which by Uzbek standards is fairly {modest|kamtarona}. Almost the entire extended family was there, including relatives I had not seen since I was a child, and that alone made the day special.

The celebration ran from the morning right through to nearly midnight. There was a long formal section with speeches and traditional ceremonies, followed by dinner, and then the music started and everything became far more {relaxed|erkin}. My uncles, who are normally very {reserved|kamgap, tortinchoq} men, got up to dance, and watching that was genuinely one of the funniest things I have ever seen. I also spent about two hours sitting with my grandmother while she {pointed out|koʻrsatib berdi} who everybody was and told stories about them, most of which I had never heard before.

What made it so enjoyable was not the food or the venue, although both were excellent. It was the fact that everyone {let their guard down|oʻzini erkin tutmoq}. In ordinary life people are busy and conversations are short, but at a wedding there is nowhere else to be, so you get whole afternoons with people you normally only greet {in passing|oʻtib ketayotib}.

Looking back, what I remember is not any single moment but the {atmosphere|muhit} - that particular feeling when several generations are in one room and everyone is genuinely happy at the same time. That does not happen often, and it made me realise how much I {take my family for granted|oilamni qadriga yetmayman} the rest of the year.

p3: What kinds of places do adults usually like to go to?

Adults tend to prefer places where they can {socialise and relax|muloqot qilib, dam olish} at the same time - restaurants, cafes, parks and, for some, the theatre or concerts. There is also a strong preference for quieter settings, because after a working week most people are looking to {unwind|dam olmoq} rather than be stimulated.
What is the difference between the places adults and children like to visit?

Children want places where they can be {physically active|jismonan faol} and where the rules are relaxed - playgrounds, amusement parks, zoos. Adults generally prioritise comfort and conversation. Put simply, children go somewhere to {do something|biror ish qilish uchun}, whereas adults go somewhere to be with someone.
What do children usually talk about when they spend time with their parents?

A great deal of it is about their day at school, their friends and things they want. Younger children in particular ask an endless stream of {why questions|nega degan savollar}. As they get older, conversations tend to narrow to practical matters, and children become noticeably more {selective about|tanlab} what they share.
Why is it important for parents to spend time with their children?

Because time is the {foundation of trust|ishonch poydevori}. Children who talk to their parents regularly are far more likely to come to them when something serious goes wrong. It also shapes behaviour - children {pick up|oʻzlashtiradi} attitudes to work, money and conflict mainly by observation rather than instruction.
Do you think children and adults enjoy the same activities?

Some overlap - sport, travel, films - but the reasons differ. A child enjoys a hike because it is an adventure; an adult enjoys the same hike because it is {a break from|dan tanaffus} routine. Where they genuinely align is anything competitive, because {the appeal of winning|gʻalaba qozonish jozibasi} does not really change with age.
How have people's choices of entertainment changed over time?

They have shifted from {communal|jamoaviy} to individual. Entertainment used to mean gathering - a cinema, a wedding, a football match - whereas now a great deal of it happens alone on a screen. It has also become {on demand|talab boʻyicha}: people no longer organise their evening around a broadcast, which is convenient but has arguably made entertainment less of a {shared experience|birgalikdagi tajriba}.

sessions.t2: A person who is good at making things
p1: What do you like about your flat or apartment?

The best feature is the balcony, which looks out over a small park. It is not large, but I have put a chair and some plants out there, and it has become the place where I {wind down|dam olaman} in the evening.
Would you like to change anything about your apartment?

The storage, mostly. There are no {built-in cupboards|devorga oʻrnatilgan shkaflar}, so everything ends up in boxes and the place looks {cluttered|tartibsiz} however much I tidy. I would also replace the windows, because the insulation is poor in winter.
How long have you been living there?

About three years now. I moved in when I started my course, and although I originally saw it as {a temporary arrangement|vaqtinchalik yechim}, I have {grown attached to|koʻnikib qolganman} the area and I am in no hurry to leave.
Do you like shopping?

Reasonably, though I would not call it a hobby. I enjoy markets far more than shopping centres, because there is some {interaction|muloqot} involved and you can often {bargain|savdolashmoq}. Malls I find rather impersonal.
How often do you go shopping?

Small amounts frequently - I pick up fresh food every two or three days rather than doing one enormous weekly shop. For anything else, I go {as and when|zarurat boʻlganda} I need it, which is not very often.
What kind of things do you usually buy?

Mainly {everyday essentials|kundalik ehtiyoj mollari}: food, household items, occasionally books. If I make a larger purchase it is usually something related to studying, like a laptop accessory, because I would rather spend on things that {earn their keep|foydasini beradigan}.
Do you prefer shopping alone or with someone else?

Alone, for efficiency - I know what I want and I can be out in ten minutes. With friends, shopping turns into a {social occasion|ijtimoiy tadbir}, which is enjoyable but takes three times as long. The only time I want company is when I need a {second opinion|boshqa birovning fikri} on clothes.

p2.task: Describe a person you know who is good at making things.
bullets: what kinds of things they make
how they learned to do it
and explain why you admire their skill
p2.ans:
I would like to talk about my neighbour Rustam, who is a carpenter by trade and who can, as far as I can tell, make almost anything out of wood.

He is in his fifties and has a workshop attached to his house, which is always full of {sawdust|arra kukuni} and half-finished projects. Officially he makes furniture - tables, doors, wardrobes - but what he really enjoys are the more intricate pieces: carved panels, wooden boxes, and traditional {latticework|panjara} screens of the kind you see in old houses. He made a chest for my mother about ten years ago that is still one of the nicest things in our home.

He learned the trade the traditional way, as an {apprentice|shogird}. He left school at sixteen and spent almost eight years working for an older master craftsman in the region, doing nothing but sanding and sweeping for the first year. He says that period taught him patience more than technique, and that most young people today want to {skip the boring part|zerikarli qismini oʻtkazib yuborish} and go straight to the interesting work, which is why so few of them {stick with it|oxirigacha davom etadi}.

What I admire is partly the skill itself - he works almost entirely by eye and rarely measures anything twice - but more than that, it is his attitude. He is completely {uncompromising|murosasiz} about quality. I once watched him break apart a door he had spent two days on because of a flaw nobody else would ever have noticed.

I think that matters because we live in an age of things designed to be {thrown away|tashlab yuboriladigan}. Rustam makes objects intended to last longer than he will, and there is something quietly impressive about that kind of {craftsmanship|hunarmandchilik}.

p3: Do you think children should learn arts and crafts at school?

Absolutely, and not simply as a break from academic subjects. Crafts develop {fine motor skills|mayda motorika}, spatial awareness and patience, and they give children who struggle academically a chance to {excel at something|biror narsada zoʻr boʻlish}. They also connect children to traditional skills that would otherwise {die out|yoʻqolib ketmoq}.
What can children learn from making things by hand?

They learn that good results take time and that mistakes are part of the process, which is difficult to teach through a textbook. Making something physical also gives {immediate feedback|bevosita natija} - if it is badly built, it falls apart - so children develop a realistic sense of {cause and effect|sabab va oqibat}.
Do you think creativity is something people are born with?

I think a certain amount of {natural inclination|tabiiy moyillik} exists, but it is greatly overstated. Most creative people I know are simply people who have practised a great deal and are not afraid of producing bad work. Environment matters far more than genetics - a child who is encouraged to experiment will almost always end up more creative than one who is {discouraged from|qaytarilgan} it.
Can people become more creative through practice?

Definitely. Creativity is largely about having enough {raw material|xom ashyo} in your head to combine in new ways, and that only comes from doing the work. Professional designers and writers rarely wait for inspiration; they have {systematic methods|tizimli usullar} for generating ideas, which is proof that creativity can be trained.
Why is creativity important for children?

Because it teaches flexible thinking. A child who is used to finding several solutions to a problem will {cope far better with|ancha yaxshi bardosh beradi} situations where there is no obvious answer. It also builds confidence, since making something from nothing gives children a real sense of {ownership|egalik hissi} over their own ideas.
Are creative skills useful in the workplace?

Increasingly so. Routine tasks are being {automated|avtomatlashtirilmoqda} at speed, so what remains valuable is exactly what machines do badly - original thinking, problem-solving and design. Even in conservative fields like accounting or law, the people who {get ahead|oldinga chiqadi} tend to be the ones who can rethink a process rather than simply follow it.

sessions.t2: An advertisement that you remember
p1: Do you work or are you a student?

I am a student, although I also work part-time, so I am really {juggling the two|ikkalasini birga olib boryapman}. Most of my week is taken up by classes, and I work {on the side|qoʻshimcha ravishda} at weekends.
What do you do?

I study international relations at university, and my part-time job is in a small translation agency, where I mostly proofread documents. It is not glamorous, but it {pays reasonably well|yaxshigina toʻlaydi} and it is directly relevant to what I want to do later.
What do you like about your work or studies?

The variety, above all. No two documents are the same, so I am constantly {picking up|oʻrganib boryapman} new terminology. At university, what I enjoy most is the discussion element - you are expected to {defend a position|fikrni himoya qilish} rather than simply memorise facts.
Is there anything you dislike about it?

The deadlines can be {punishing|ogʻir, qiynoqli}, especially when a university assignment and a work project {fall in the same week|bir haftaga toʻgʻri keladi}. I also find proofreading mentally tiring, because you have to concentrate on detail for hours at a stretch.
Do you like shopping?

Honestly, not very much. I would rather spend money on experiences than objects, so I tend to be quite {frugal|tejamkor}. When I do shop, I go in with a list and stick to it, which removes most of the enjoyment but also most of the {impulse purchases|oʻylamasdan qilingan xaridlar}.
How often do you go shopping?

Weekly for food, and perhaps four or five times a year for anything else. I have become more deliberate about it recently, partly because I moved into a small flat and quickly realised that {clutter builds up|narsalar yigʻilib qoladi} very fast.
What do you usually buy when you go shopping?

Mostly food and household basics. Beyond that, books and the occasional item of clothing, and I always try to buy something of decent quality that will last rather than {replacing things constantly|doimiy almashtirish}, which works out cheaper {in the long run|uzoq muddatda}.
Do you prefer shopping online or in physical stores?

Online for anything standardised - electronics, books - because the choice is far wider and you can compare reviews. For clothes and food I much prefer shops, since {sizing is unpredictable|oʻlchamlar noaniq} and I like to see fresh produce before I buy it.

p2.task: Describe an advertisement that you remember.
bullets: where and when you saw it
and explain why you still remember it
p2.ans:
The advertisement I remember most clearly is a short film made for a national bank, which I first saw on television about three years ago and have since seen several times online.

It ran for roughly two minutes, which is unusually long for a commercial, and it {dispensed with|voz kechgan} almost everything you would expect from a bank advert. There were no interest rates, no smiling staff and no logo until the very last frame.

The story followed an elderly man in a village who was saving money in an old tin box. Every few weeks he added a small amount, and the camera simply showed him counting it at the kitchen table. Gradually you realised, from photographs on the wall, that he was saving for his granddaughter's education. Towards the end, she was shown arriving at a university in the city, and the final shot was of him sitting alone at the same table with the empty box, looking completely {content|mamnun}. Only then did the bank's name appear, with a single line about helping families {plan for the future|kelajakni rejalashtirish}.

There was no dialogue at all, and I think that is precisely why it worked. It {let the images do the talking|tasvirlarga gapirishga imkon berdi}, and it trusted the audience to understand.

The reason it has {stuck with me|esimda qolgan} is that it managed to be moving without being {manipulative|manipulyativ}, which is a very fine line in advertising. Most commercials {shout at you|baqiradi} about features and discounts and are forgotten within seconds. This one sold an idea rather than a product, and I think that is far more effective. I could not tell you a single thing about that bank's services, but I remember the company, and presumably that was the whole point.

p3: Do advertisements actually increase a company's sales?

In most cases, yes, though the effect is easier to see with new products than with {established brands|tanilgan brendlar}. Advertising is particularly powerful at {raising awareness|xabardorlikni oshirish} - people cannot buy what they do not know exists. For mature brands it works more as {reinforcement|mustahkamlash}, keeping the name in people's minds so that it is the default choice.
What types of advertisements are most effective nowadays?

{Targeted|maqsadli} digital advertising, without question, because it reaches people who have already shown an interest. Alongside that, influencer marketing has become extremely effective, since a recommendation from a person feels more {trustworthy|ishonchli} than a corporate message. Traditional television advertising still works for {mass-market|ommaviy bozor} products, but its influence is clearly {waning|susaymoqda}.
Why do some successful or premium brands choose not to use mainstream advertising?

Because {exclusivity|eksklyuzivlik} is part of what they are selling. If a luxury brand advertises everywhere, it starts to feel ordinary, and that {undermines|zaiflashtiradi} the whole proposition. Such brands rely instead on {word of mouth|ogʻzaki tarqalish}, careful placement and scarcity, which creates the impression that the product is sought after rather than being pushed.
Should advertising aimed specifically at children be restricted?

I believe so. Young children cannot reliably distinguish between entertainment and {persuasion|ishontirish}, so advertising to them is not a fair exchange. Several countries have already {imposed restrictions|cheklovlar joriy qilgan} on advertising food and toys during children's programming, and the evidence suggests it reduces {pester power|bolalarning qistovi} without harming legitimate business.
Should there be strict regulations on advertising harmful products such as alcohol and tobacco?

Definitely, because the cost of those products falls on the whole society through healthcare. Most countries already {ban outright|butunlay taqiqlaydi} tobacco advertising, and I would extend similar rules to alcohol, particularly anything that {glamorises|jozibali koʻrsatadi} drinking to young audiences. Regulation is not about denying adults choice; it is about not actively encouraging harm.
To what extent are advertisements nowadays truthful and reliable?

They are rarely dishonest in a way that would be {actionable|sudga beriladigan}, since advertising standards do exist, but they are highly selective. Companies present the most flattering interpretation of the facts and {bury the qualifications|shartlarni yashiradi} in small print. So I would say most advertising is technically accurate and {deeply misleading|chuqur chalgʻituvchi} at the same time.
Should advertisements mainly provide information about the product?

Ideally they would, but I recognise that is {unrealistic|real emas}. Purely informational advertising is easily ignored, and in categories where products are almost identical, emotion is the only real differentiator. My view is that advertising should be free to be creative, provided the factual claims it makes can be {substantiated|asoslangan}.

sessions.t2: A quiet place that you always visit
p1: What are you studying?

I am studying computer science, which is broader than people assume - it ranges from programming to databases and a fair amount of mathematics. My particular interest is in {data processing|ma'lumotlarni qayta ishlash}.
Why did you choose this subject?

Partly for {pragmatic|amaliy, hisob-kitobli} reasons, since the job market is strong, but mainly because I like problems that have a definite answer. There is a {logic to it|mantiqi bor} that appeals to me, and you get instant feedback - your code either works or it does not.
What do you enjoy most about your studies?

The moment when something that has been failing for hours suddenly runs correctly. It sounds trivial, but that {sense of breakthrough|yorilish hissi} is genuinely addictive, and it makes all the frustration beforehand feel {worthwhile|arzigulik}.
What do you usually do in the evening?

On a normal weekday I study for an hour or two, then have dinner with my family and {wind down|dam olaman} with something undemanding - a series or a book. I try to keep the last half hour {screen-free|ekransiz}, though I do not always manage it.
Do you prefer spending your evenings at home or outside?

At home, generally. By the evening I have had enough {stimulation|qoʻzgʻatuvchi ta'sir} for one day and I value the quiet. That said, once or twice a week I will go out with friends, otherwise home starts to feel a little {confining|siqiq}.
Did you do the same things in the evening when you were a child?

Not really. As a child, evenings were spent playing outside until it got dark, and then the whole family would watch television together, because there was only one set. Now everyone {retreats to|chekinadi} their own room and their own screen, which I think is a genuine {loss|yoʻqotish}.
Do you usually go out in the evening?

Not on weekdays, no. At weekends I do, usually to meet friends for dinner or to walk around the centre when it is cooler. I would not describe myself as {a night owl|kechalari faol odam} - I am far more productive in the morning.

p2.task: Describe a quiet place that you always visit.
bullets: and explain why you like this quiet place
p2.ans:
The quiet place I want to describe is the reading room on the top floor of my university library, which has become something of a {refuge|panohgoh} for me over the past two years.

It is a long room with high windows along one side, old wooden desks and, crucially, a rule of complete silence that is {strictly enforced|qat'iy amal qilinadi}. Most students prefer the ground floor, where you can talk, so the top floor is almost always half empty - I would guess there are rarely more than fifteen people in a room built for eighty.

I go there four or five times a week, usually in the middle of the morning, and I tend to stay for three or four hours. I do my most difficult work there: anything that requires {sustained concentration|uzluksiz diqqat}, like writing essays or working through problem sets. I have noticed that I get more done in two hours in that room than in an entire evening at home, where I am constantly {interrupted|xalaqit berilgan}.

The reason I like it so much goes beyond the silence. Part of it is the effect of being surrounded by people who are all working; it creates a kind of {quiet pressure|jimgina bosim} that makes it embarrassing to open your phone. Part of it is the physical space itself - the high ceilings and natural light make it feel {calm rather than oppressive|bosiq emas, xotirjam}.

But honestly, the main reason is that it is one of the very few places where nobody can reach me. In a city where you are permanently {contactable|bogʻlanish mumkin boʻlgan}, having a few hours where no one expects an answer is genuinely valuable. I always leave feeling {clear-headed|boshim tiniq}, which is not something I can say about many places.

p3: Why do some people prefer quiet places?

Because noise is {mentally taxing|aqlan charchatadi} even when we are not consciously aware of it. Some people are simply more {sensitive to stimulation|ta'sirchan} and find that constant background sound makes it impossible to think clearly. For introverts in particular, quiet is how they {recover their energy|energiyasini tiklaydi}.
What kinds of places are usually quiet?

Libraries, museums, places of worship and cemeteries, where silence is {socially expected|ijtimoiy me'yor}. Beyond that, natural places - forests, mountains, the countryside at night. What those have in common is either a rule enforcing quiet or simply an {absence of machinery|texnika yoʻqligi}, which is the real source of most urban noise.
Why are quiet places important in cities?

Because urban noise is {relentless|tinimsiz} and has measurable effects on health - sleep quality, stress levels, even blood pressure. Quiet spaces act as a kind of {safety valve|xavfsizlik klapani}, giving people somewhere to recover. They are also important for equality: wealthier residents can afford quiet housing, so public quiet spaces are often the only option for everyone else.
Why is it difficult to find quiet places nowadays?

Mainly {urban density|shaharlarning zichligi} and traffic. As cities grow, construction is constant and roads run closer to homes. There is also a cultural element - background music is now played in almost every shop and cafe, so silence has become something you have to {actively seek out|ataylab izlamoq} rather than the default.
Do young people like quiet places?

Less than older people, on the whole, but I think that is often {misread|notoʻgʻri talqin qilinadi}. Young people are perfectly happy in libraries and parks; what they dislike is {enforced silence with nothing to do|majburiy jimlik}. Interestingly, there is a growing interest among students in silent study spaces, precisely because concentration has become so difficult.
Should governments create more quiet public spaces?

Yes, and I would argue it is a {public health measure|jamoat salomatligi chorasi} rather than a luxury. Practical steps would include pedestrianising streets, planting trees, which absorb sound remarkably well, and designating quiet zones in parks. It is relatively {inexpensive|arzon} compared with most infrastructure and the benefits reach everyone.
What are the benefits of spending time in a quiet place?

Better concentration is the obvious one, but there are also documented {psychological benefits|psixologik foyda} - lower stress, improved mood and better sleep. Quiet also allows for reflection, which is almost impossible when your attention is constantly being {pulled in different directions|har tomonga tortiladi}.
Do you think there will be more or fewer quiet places in the future?

Fewer in absolute terms, as cities expand, but I suspect they will become more {deliberately designed|ataylab loyihalangan}. Quiet is increasingly treated as a resource worth protecting, and I would not be surprised if it becomes {a selling point|sotuv ustunligi} for housing and even for cafes, in the way clean air already is.

sessions.t2: Your least favourite food
p1: Where is your hometown?

My hometown is Tashkent, the capital, where I was born and have lived my whole life. It is by far the largest city in Central Asia, and it has changed almost {beyond recognition|tanib boʻlmas darajada} in the last decade.
What is your hometown famous for?

Several things. Historically, it is known for the Chorsu bazaar and the old town, and more recently for its metro, which has some genuinely {ornate|bezakli} stations. It is also known as a very green city - there are trees along most major roads, which makes the summers {bearable|chidasa boʻladigan}.
What is your daily routine like?

Fairly {structured|tartibli}, on weekdays at least. I get up at around seven, have breakfast, and I am at university by nine. Classes run until the afternoon, then I study, and I try to do some exercise before dinner. I am usually in bed by eleven.
What do you usually do during the day?

Most of my day is spent either in lectures or in the library. I also work part-time two afternoons a week, so on those days everything else {has to be squeezed in|siqib joylashtirish kerak} around it. In between, I try to {make time for|vaqt ajratmoq} at least one proper break outdoors.
Do you have the same routine every day?

Not exactly - my timetable varies, so some days start at eight and others at eleven. But the {broad shape|umumiy koʻrinishi} of the day is consistent, which I find helpful. Having a rough routine means I do not waste energy deciding what to do next.
Is there anything you would like to change about your daily routine?

I would like to get up earlier and use the first hour for myself rather than {rushing out of the house|uydan shoshib chiqish}. I would also like to be more disciplined about my phone, because I lose an embarrassing amount of time to it {without noticing|sezmasdan}.

p2.task: Describe your least favourite food.
bullets: and explain how you react when you are offered it
p2.ans:
The food I like least, without any real competition, is boiled liver, and my dislike of it is strong enough that I can recognise the smell from another room.

I first tried it when I was probably six or seven. My grandmother cooked it regularly because she was absolutely convinced it was good for {building up your strength|kuch toʻplash}, particularly for children, and in fairness she may well have been right - liver is famously {rich in iron|temirga boy}. Unfortunately, nutritional value was not high on my list of priorities at that age.

There are two things I object to. The first is the texture, which I find {grainy and dry|donador va quruq} no matter how it is prepared. It seems to {absorb all the moisture|butun namlikni yutib yuboradi} in your mouth. The second is the aftertaste, which is metallic and very persistent; you can still taste it twenty minutes later, which is not something I would say about any other food.

I have tried it several times since, cooked in different ways, partly because people keep insisting that I simply have not had it prepared properly. Fried with onions it is marginally better, but I have never {come round to it|koʻnikib qolmoq}.

As for how I react, it depends entirely on the situation. At home I will simply say no, and nobody {takes offence|xafa boʻlmaydi}. If I am a guest, however, refusing food is considered fairly rude in our culture, so I will take a small portion and {work my way through it|asta-sekin yeb chiqish} politely. I have become quite skilled at eating it with a lot of bread. It is a small price to pay for not {offending the host|mezbonni xafa qilish}, and I doubt anyone has ever noticed.

p3: Why do some people dislike certain types of food?

A great deal of it is {genetic|irsiy} - some people are far more sensitive to bitter compounds, for instance, which explains why certain vegetables divide opinion so sharply. Beyond biology, early experiences matter enormously. If a food is associated with being forced to eat it or with feeling ill, that {aversion|nafrat, yoqtirmaslik} can last a lifetime.
Why do people's food preferences change as they get older?

Partly physiology: our sense of taste {dulls|kuchsizlanadi} with age, so strong flavours that overwhelmed us as children become pleasant. But exposure matters even more - the more often you encounter a food, the more likely you are to accept it. Adults also eat for reasons beyond pleasure, such as health, which {broadens their diet|ratsionni kengaytiradi}.
Do you think children should be encouraged to try food they dislike?

Encouraged, yes; forced, no. Research suggests a child may need to try something ten or more times before accepting it, so {repeated gentle exposure|takroriy, yumshoq taklif} works. Pressure, on the other hand, tends to {backfire|teskari natija beradi} and create a lasting dislike. The sensible approach is to keep offering without making it a battle.
Why do some people prefer traditional food to international food?

Familiarity and {emotional association|hissiy bogʻliqlik}, mostly. Traditional dishes are tied to family and celebration, so eating them is partly about identity rather than taste. There is also trust involved - people know exactly what is in a dish they grew up with, whereas unfamiliar cuisine carries a small element of {risk|xavf}.
How have people's eating habits changed in recent years?

They have become faster and more {globalised|globallashgan}. People eat out and order in far more, portions have grown, and meals are increasingly eaten alone or in front of a screen. At the same time there is a {counter-trend|qarama-qarshi tendensiya} among the more educated towards home cooking and local produce, so habits are moving in two directions at once.
Do you think people eat more unhealthy food nowadays than in the past?

On the whole, yes. Processed food is cheaper, more available and {engineered to be hard to stop eating|toʻxtamaslik uchun ishlab chiqilgan}. Combined with more sedentary lifestyles, that has driven a clear rise in obesity. The one qualification I would add is that people are also far better informed than they used to be, so the knowledge is there even if the {behaviour lags behind|xatti-harakat orqada qoladi}.

sessions.t2: A place you have been to that was boring
p1: What do you study?

I study architecture, which is a rather {demanding|talabchan} course - it combines design, engineering and a surprising amount of history. We spend most of our time in the studio rather than in lectures.
Why did you choose this subject?

Because it sits {at the intersection of|kesishmasida} art and science, and I could never decide between the two. I also like the idea that the work is permanent; a building you design might still be standing in a hundred years, which is quite a {sobering thought|jiddiy oʻylantiradigan fikr}.
Do you enjoy your studies?

Very much, although it is {relentless|tinimsiz}. The workload is heavier than almost any other course and deadlines often mean working through the night. But the studio atmosphere is excellent, and you genuinely {learn from your classmates|kursdoshlaringizdan oʻrganasiz} as much as from the tutors.
What part of your studies do you find most interesting?

The early stage of a project, when nothing is fixed yet and you are just {sketching out|chizib koʻrmoq} possibilities. Once the technical drawings begin it becomes much more {laborious|mashaqqatli}. I also enjoy studying historical buildings and working out why they were built the way they were.
Do you usually wear a watch?

I do, most days. It started as a practical habit, because I did not want to take my phone out during lectures, but now it feels {odd|gʻalati} without one. I would say it has become part of how I dress rather than purely functional.
What kind of watches do you like?

Simple, {understated|kamtarona} ones - a plain face, a leather strap, nothing flashy. I am not particularly interested in smartwatches, because I already have quite enough devices {competing for my attention|e'tiborim uchun kurashayotgan}.
Did you wear a watch when you were a child?

Yes, I was given a cheap digital one when I was about eight and I was extremely proud of it. It had an alarm and a stopwatch, and I remember {timing everything|hamma narsani oʻlchash} for weeks - how long it took to walk to school, how long I could hold my breath.
Are you interested in space?

Reasonably, though I would call myself a {casual observer|oddiy qiziquvchi} rather than an enthusiast. I follow major missions in the news and I find images from telescopes genuinely {awe-inspiring|hayratlanarli}, but I have never studied it seriously.
Did you learn anything about space at school?

We covered the basics in physics and geography - the solar system, phases of the moon, that sort of thing. It was taught rather {dryly|quruq}, mostly as facts to memorise, which is a shame because it is a subject that {lends itself to|juda mos keladi} wonder.
Would you like to travel into space one day?

In principle it sounds extraordinary, but in practice I think I would {give it a miss|voz kechardim}. The risk is considerable and the conditions are uncomfortable. I would happily watch it from the ground and leave the actual journey to people who are far braver than I am.

p2.task: Describe a place you have been to that was boring.
bullets: and explain why you found it boring
p2.ans:
The place I want to describe is a small regional museum I visited on a school trip when I was about fifteen, in a town a couple of hours outside the city.

We went because it was the last week of the school year and the trip had presumably been organised months earlier by someone who had never actually been there. Around forty of us were {bussed in|avtobusda olib borildi} on a very hot morning, and we were told we would be there for three hours, which turned out to be roughly two hours and forty minutes too long.

The museum consisted of four rooms. The exhibits themselves were not the problem - there were old tools, some coins and a reconstruction of a traditional house, which could all have been interesting. The problem was how it was presented. Everything was in {glass cases|shisha vitrinalar} with tiny typed labels giving a date and nothing else. There was nothing to touch, nothing to try, no explanation of why any of it {mattered|ahamiyatli edi}. Our guide read from a prepared text in a completely {flat|jonsiz} voice and did not once ask us a question.

Within twenty minutes almost everyone had {lost interest|qiziqishini yoʻqotdi}. People were sitting on windowsills, and the teachers spent more energy keeping us quiet than the guide spent explaining anything.

Looking back, I think it was boring not because the subject was dull but because it had been arranged for objects rather than for visitors. Nobody had asked what a fifteen-year-old might actually want to know. It taught me that almost anything can be made {engaging|qiziqarli} with the right presentation, and equally that almost anything can be made {excruciatingly dull|nihoyatda zerikarli} without it.

p3: Why do some people get bored more easily than others?

Differences in temperament play a part - some people have a higher need for {novelty and stimulation|yangilik va qoʻzgʻatuvchi ta'sir} and become restless quickly. Habit matters too: anyone accustomed to constant fast-changing content will find slower activities harder to tolerate. And people with strong internal interests are rarely bored, because they can {entertain themselves|oʻzini band qila oladi}.
What do people usually do when they feel bored?

The default now is to {reach for a phone|telefonga qoʻl uzatmoq}, which provides instant distraction but rarely satisfaction. Others will call someone, eat, or start a task simply to fill the time. Interestingly, boredom is also a well-known trigger for {impulsive behaviour|oʻylamasdan qilingan xatti-harakat}, from unnecessary shopping to snacking.
Do you think people today get bored less often than in the past?

They experience fewer {empty moments|boʻsh daqiqalar}, certainly, because any gap can be filled with a screen. But I am not convinced they are less bored - a lot of scrolling is itself a form of boredom. What has changed is that boredom is now {suppressed rather than resolved|hal qilinmay, bosiladi}.
Why do children sometimes feel bored even when they have many things to do?

Often because the choice itself is {overwhelming|dovdiratadigan}, and because toys that do everything leave nothing for the child to add. Children also lose interest quickly when an activity is chosen for them. And sometimes what looks like boredom is really a request for {attention|e'tibor} rather than for entertainment.
Is it important for people to experience boredom sometimes?

I think it is genuinely valuable. Boredom is uncomfortable, and that discomfort is what {prompts|turtki beradi} people to invent, create or simply think. Children who are never bored rarely develop the ability to {amuse themselves|oʻzini ovuntirish}, and adults who fill every gap lose the reflective time where most good ideas actually appear.
What can parents do to help children deal with boredom?
