The most useful thing is often to do nothing - to {resist the urge|istakni jilovlash} to solve it immediately. Providing {open-ended|ochiq, cheklanmagan} materials such as paper, blocks or simply outdoor space works better than another screen. Modelling matters too: children who see their parents reading or making things learn that quiet time can be filled productively.
Do you think technology has made people less able to deal with boredom?

I would say yes, in the sense that it has lowered our {tolerance|chidamlilik} for it. When distraction is available within a second, the muscle that lets you sit with an unstimulating moment {weakens|zaiflashadi}. The evidence is fairly visible - people find it difficult to queue, or even to wait at traffic lights, without checking a phone.

sessions.t2: An important decision that turned out well
p1: Where is your hometown?

I am from Fergana, a mid-sized city in the east of the country, surrounded by mountains on three sides. It is quite a {planned|rejalashtirilgan} city by Uzbek standards, with wide straight streets, which makes it easy to get around.
What do you like most about your hometown?

The pace of life, above all. Everything is {within walking distance|piyoda yurish masofasida} and nobody seems to be in a hurry, which after a few days in Tashkent feels enormously relaxing. The parks are also unusually good for a city of that size.
Is your hometown a good place for young people?

It is a pleasant place to grow up, but I would not say it is ideal for young adults. There is a {limited range of|cheklangan doirada} career opportunities and not a great deal to do in the evenings, so a lot of my friends have {moved away|koʻchib ketgan} to the capital.
Would you like to continue living there in the future?

Possibly later in life. At the moment I want to be somewhere with more opportunities, but I can easily imagine {settling down|joylashib qolmoq} there once I have established a career, because it would be a far better place to raise a family.
Do you enjoy shopping?

Up to a point. I enjoy it when I have a clear purpose, but shopping for its own sake {leaves me cold|menga qiziq emas}. My friends can spend an entire day at a shopping centre, which to me sounds more like an {endurance test|chidamlilik sinovi}.
What kind of things do you usually buy?

Everyday necessities and, occasionally, something for my hobbies - mainly books and stationery. I am quite {selective|tanlovchan} about clothes and tend to buy a few good items rather than a lot of cheap ones.
Do you prefer shopping online or in shops?

Online, mostly, because it saves time and the selection is {vastly wider|ancha keng}. The one drawback is that you cannot inspect what you are buying, so for anything where quality matters - shoes, for instance - I still prefer to go in person.
How often do you go shopping?

Very frequently for food, because I like to cook with fresh ingredients, so two or three times a week. For anything else, maybe once a month, and even then it is usually because something has {worn out|eskirgan} rather than because I want something new.
Did you enjoy shopping when you were a child?

I loved it, but only because it usually {ended with|bilan tugardi} sweets or a toy. What I actually enjoyed was the bazaar itself - the noise, the colours and the sellers calling out. As a shopping experience it was far more {entertaining|qiziqarli} than a modern supermarket.

p2.task: Describe an important decision you made that turned out to be a good decision.
bullets: and explain why it turned out to be a good decision
p2.ans:
The decision I want to talk about is my choice to turn down a place at a university in another city and stay where I was, which I made about three years ago.

I had applied to a well-regarded institution in Tashkent and, somewhat to my surprise, I was accepted. Everyone around me assumed it was {a foregone conclusion|oldindan hal boʻlgan masala} that I would go - it was the more prestigious option and it was what my friends were doing. But when I looked at it carefully, the course content was actually weaker in the area I cared about, and the cost of living would have meant working long hours and studying part-time.

It was a genuinely difficult decision for two reasons. The first was {social pressure|ijtimoiy bosim}: refusing the more famous university looked, from the outside, like a lack of ambition, and I had to explain myself to a lot of relatives. The second was that I could not be sure I was not simply {taking the easy way out|oson yoʻlni tanlamoq} and staying close to home out of fear. I spent about two weeks {going back and forth|ikkilanib yurdim} before I committed.

In the end it {proved to be the right call|toʻgʻri qaror boʻlib chiqdi}, and for reasons I could not have predicted. Because I was not working to pay rent, I had time to take on research projects, and one of my lecturers eventually offered me a position as her assistant. That opened far more doors than the name of a university ever would have. I also stayed close to my family during a period when, as it happened, my father was unwell and needed support.

What I {took away from|olib chiqdim} the whole experience is that the most impressive option and the best option are frequently not the same thing, and that it is worth {thinking for yourself|mustaqil fikrlash} even when everyone around you is certain.

p3: Why do some people find it difficult to make decisions?

Often it is {fear of regret|afsuslanishdan qoʻrqish} rather than a lack of information - people worry more about choosing wrongly than they value choosing at all. Having too many options also {paralyses|falaj qiladi} us, because every choice means giving something up. And some people have simply never been allowed to decide for themselves, so they lack practice.
Do you think young people can make good decisions on their own?

In many areas, yes. Young people are often better informed than their parents about technology and careers, and decision-making is a skill that only develops through {being allowed to make mistakes|xato qilishga ruxsat berish}. Where they are at a disadvantage is anything requiring {long-term perspective|uzoq muddatli qarash}, simply because they have less experience to draw on.
What kinds of decisions should parents make for their children?

Anything involving {safety and health|xavfsizlik va salomatlik}, clearly, and major financial commitments. Beyond that, I think parents should gradually {hand over|topshirmoq} control - letting a child choose their clothes, then their hobbies, then their subjects. A child who reaches eighteen having never made a real decision is poorly prepared for adulthood.
Is it better to make decisions quickly or take a long time to think?

It depends on the {stakes|xavf darajasi}. For reversible, low-cost decisions, speed is better - deliberating over what to eat is a waste of energy. For major, irreversible choices, taking time is clearly wise. The mistake most people make is {agonising over|azoblanib oʻylash} trivial decisions and rushing the important ones.
What factors should people consider before making an important decision?

The realistic {downside|salbiy tomoni} rather than only the best outcome, whether the decision can be {reversed|orqaga qaytarish} if it goes wrong, and what it will cost in time as well as money. I would also add a personal test: whether you would still be comfortable with the choice if nobody else ever found out about it.
Do people usually ask others for advice before making important decisions?

Most do, though I suspect a great deal of it is {seeking reassurance|dalda izlash} rather than genuine advice - people often decide first and then look for agreement. Advice is most valuable from someone who has actually {been in your position|shu holatda boʻlgan}, and least valuable from people who will not live with the consequences.
Who has more influence on people's decisions, friends or family?

It shifts with age. In adolescence, {peer influence|tengdoshlar ta'siri} is strongest, because belonging matters enormously at that stage. As people get older, family regains influence, particularly for decisions about marriage, money and career. Family tends to shape {long-term values|uzoq muddatli qadriyatlar}, while friends affect day-to-day choices.

sessions.t2: A natural place you enjoy visiting
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student at the moment - I am in the third year of a four-year degree, so studying is very much my {full-time occupation|asosiy mashgʻulot}.
What do you study?

I study environmental science. It is quite an {interdisciplinary|fanlararo} subject, combining biology, chemistry and a fair amount of policy, which means you are never doing the same thing for very long.
Why did you choose this subject?

Partly because of where I grew up. The Aral Sea disaster is something every child here learns about, and seeing the {consequences of|oqibatlari} poor environmental management so close to home made the subject feel {urgent|dolzarb} rather than theoretical.
What do you like most about your studies?

The fieldwork, without question. Spending a week taking water samples teaches you more than a month of lectures, and it is enormously satisfying to {see the theory play out|nazariyani amalda koʻrish} in a real landscape.
Is there anything you don't like about your studies?

The amount of statistics, if I am honest. I understand why it is necessary, but processing data can be extremely {tedious|zerikarli}, and it is a long way from the reason most of us chose the subject.
What would you like to do after you finish your studies?

Ideally I would like to work for an organisation dealing with water management, either governmental or an NGO. If that {falls through|amalga oshmasa}, I would consider a master's degree abroad, because the research facilities here are still fairly {limited|cheklangan}.
What do you remember about your first day at secondary school?

Mostly the feeling of being {utterly lost|butunlay adashgan}. The building seemed enormous compared with primary school, and we had a different teacher for every subject, which was completely new. I remember spending the first break trying to work out where my next class was.
How did you feel on your first day?

A mixture of excitement and {apprehension|xavotir}. I was proud of being considered old enough to move up, but I was also very aware that I no longer knew everybody, and at that age that is quite {unsettling|bezovta qiladigan}.
Did you make any new friends at secondary school?

Yes, and quite quickly. Two of the people I met in my first week are still close friends now. I think shared uncertainty {breaks the ice|muzni yorib beradi} very effectively - everyone was equally nervous, so people were unusually open.
What did you enjoy most about your school?

The extracurricular side. We had a debating club that I joined in my second year, and that did more for my confidence and my English than any lesson. It also gave me a {sense of belonging|tegishlilik hissi} that I did not get from classes alone.
Is there anything you would like to change about your secondary school?

I would have liked far more emphasis on {practical skills|amaliy koʻnikmalar}. We were extremely well drilled in memorising information but poorly prepared for things like public speaking, managing money or working in a team - all of which turn out to matter enormously afterwards.

p2.task: Describe a natural place you enjoy visiting.
bullets: what you do when you are there
and explain why you enjoy visiting it
p2.ans:
The natural place I would like to describe is a stretch of the Amu Darya about forty minutes outside Urgench, where the bank opens out into a wide area of sand and low scrub.

Getting there is straightforward but not glamorous. We drive out along the main road and then turn onto a dirt track for the last couple of kilometres, which in a small car is a rather {bumpy|notekis} experience. There is no car park, no signs and no facilities of any kind, which is precisely why it is usually empty.

I go with my family or a few friends, normally two or three times a year, and almost always in the early evening, because during the day the heat is {oppressive|ezuvchi}. We usually take a picnic and stay until the sun goes down. Sometimes we swim, although the current is strong enough that you have to be {sensible|ehtiyotkor} about where you go in. Mostly, though, we simply sit and talk, and I have taken to bringing a camera because the light in the last hour before sunset is extraordinary.

What I enjoy about it is partly the {sheer scale|kengligi} of the landscape. The river is very wide at that point and there is nothing on the horizon, which makes you feel pleasantly {insignificant|ahamiyatsiz}. There is also almost no noise beyond the water and the wind, and after a week in the city that silence is genuinely restorative.

But there is something more specific too. This is a river that has been {under enormous pressure|katta bosim ostida} for decades because of irrigation, and standing next to it, you cannot help thinking about how {fragile|nozik, mo'rt} it is. So the place is beautiful and slightly {sobering|oʻylantiradigan} at the same time, and that combination is what keeps drawing me back.

p3: Do you think natural parks should be restricted in order to protect them?

In sensitive areas, yes. Where a habitat is genuinely {fragile|nozik}, limiting visitor numbers, restricting access to marked paths or closing sites during breeding seasons is entirely justified. The risk of blanket restriction, though, is that people stop feeling any {connection to|bogʻliqlik} nature, and public support for conservation depends on that connection. The best approach is {managed access|boshqariladigan kirish} rather than exclusion.
Do advances in science and technology have a negative effect on the natural environment?

Historically the answer is clearly yes - industrialisation, intensive agriculture and transport have all {taken a heavy toll|ogʻir zarar yetkazgan}. But it would be one-sided to stop there. Technology also gives us satellite monitoring, renewable energy and far more efficient irrigation. The technology itself is {neutral|betaraf}; the outcome depends on whether it is deployed with environmental cost in mind or purely for short-term profit.
Which is more important: protecting nature or developing the economy?

I would question the assumption that they are {in opposition|qarama-qarshi}. In the short term there is often a genuine conflict, but in the long run an economy that destroys its own resource base is not viable - the Aral Sea is the clearest example imaginable. So I would say environmental protection is not an alternative to development but a {precondition for|shart} sustainable development. Where a poor country genuinely has to choose, wealthier nations that already industrialised should {bear a share of|ulushini koʻtarish} the cost.

sessions.t2: A trip you often take but dislike
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student, currently in my final year, so most of my time at the moment is {consumed by|band qilgan} my dissertation.
What is your major?
My major is marketing, which sits within the business school. It covers consumer behaviour, market research and branding, so it is a mixture of {psychology and commerce|psixologiya va savdo}.
What is exciting about your major?

What I find genuinely fascinating is how {irrational|mantiqsiz} consumer behaviour turns out to be. We like to think we make careful decisions, but studies show that packaging, order and even music in a shop {sway our choices|tanlovimizga ta'sir qiladi} far more than price does.
What is one thing you do not like about your major?

There is a certain amount of {repetition|takrorlanish} between modules - the same theories come up in three different courses. I also sometimes feel uneasy about the {ethical side|axloqiy jihat}, because a lot of what we study is essentially how to persuade people to buy things they do not need.
Did you go to parks when you were younger?

Constantly. There was a park about ten minutes from our house and my mother took us there almost every afternoon in summer. It was {the default activity|asosiy mashgʻulot} for children then, because there was very little else to do.
How popular is it for people to go to parks?

Extremely popular here, especially in the evening once the heat {subsides|pasayadi}. You will see whole families out walking, children playing and older people sitting together. Parks are essentially {free public entertainment|bepul ommaviy dam olish joyi}, which matters a great deal.
Do you enjoy going to parks?

I do, though I go for different reasons now. As a child it was about playing; now it is somewhere to walk, clear my head or meet a friend without {spending money|pul sarflash}. I particularly like going early in the morning, when they are almost {deserted|boʻm-boʻsh}.

p2.task: Describe a trip that you often take but dislike.
bullets: how often you make this trip
and explain why you dislike it
p2.ans:
The trip I would like to describe is the journey I make between Tashkent and my family's home in Samarkand, which I do roughly once a month during term time.

I usually travel by shared taxi rather than by train, and that is really the {root of the problem|muammoning ildizi}. The train is comfortable but it sells out days in advance, and my plans are rarely fixed that far ahead, so I end up going to the taxi stand and taking whatever is leaving.

The journey itself takes around four hours, sometimes five. You sit in a car with three strangers, and the driver will not leave until every seat is filled, so you can easily wait forty minutes before you even {set off|yoʻlga chiqmoq}. The car is almost always too hot or too cold, the driver's music is not negotiable, and there is no realistic way to work or sleep. On one occasion we broke down outside Jizzakh and waited two hours by the roadside in the middle of the afternoon.

What I dislike most, though, is not the discomfort so much as the {unpredictability|noaniqlik}. I can never tell anyone when I will arrive, which makes the whole day difficult to plan. There is also a genuine {safety concern|xavfsizlik masalasi}, because drivers are paid per trip and some of them {drive far too fast|haddan tashqari tez haydashadi} on roads that do not really allow for it.

The reason I keep making the journey is obvious - my family is at the other end, and four uncomfortable hours is a small price for a weekend at home. But it is the one part of the month I {actively dread|jiddiy qoʻrqaman}, and if I could afford to book the train every time, I would {do so without hesitation|ikkilanmasdan shunday qilardim}.

p3: Why do some people dislike travelling?

For a variety of reasons. Some find the {logistics|tashkiliy jihat} genuinely stressful - packing, documents, connections. Others dislike being away from a familiar routine, or suffer physically from motion sickness and disturbed sleep. And for some, travelling means {a loss of control|nazoratni yoʻqotish}, because delays and problems are largely out of your hands.
What kinds of trips do people usually find boring or tiring?

Long journeys with nothing to look at - motorway driving, or overnight flights where you cannot properly sleep. {Routine commutes|kundalik qatnov} are probably the worst, because there is no novelty at all. Business trips can also be surprisingly draining, since you see airports and meeting rooms and almost nothing of the place itself.
Why do people continue taking trips they do not enjoy?

Usually because the {destination justifies|manzil oqlaydi} the journey. Visiting family, attending a wedding or keeping a job may all require travel that nobody would choose for its own sake. It is essentially a {trade-off|murosa}: people tolerate several unpleasant hours for something they value at the end.
Do you think travelling is more stressful now than it was in the past?

It is faster and safer but arguably more stressful in certain respects. {Security procedures|xavfsizlik tekshiruvlari}, crowded airports and tight connections create anxiety that did not exist before. On the other hand, travel used to be genuinely dangerous and unpredictable, so I think the stress has simply {changed in character|xarakteri oʻzgargan} rather than increased overall.
What can people do to make a long journey more enjoyable?

Preparation makes an enormous difference - downloading something to watch or listen to, taking food, and choosing a seat sensibly. I would also say {managing expectations|kutilmalarni boshqarish} helps: if you accept in advance that it will be long, delays feel less infuriating. Breaking the journey with a stop, where possible, {transforms|butunlay oʻzgartiradi} the experience.
Why do some people prefer travelling alone while others prefer travelling with friends or family?

Travelling alone gives you {complete freedom|toʻliq erkinlik} over the schedule and forces you to interact with people you would otherwise never meet. Travelling in a group is more secure, cheaper in some respects, and gives you {shared memories|umumiy xotiralar} afterwards. It really comes down to whether someone values independence or company more.
How might travelling change in the future?

I expect it to become both easier and more {restricted|cheklangan}. High-speed rail and better digital systems will remove a lot of the friction, but environmental pressure may make short flights more expensive or socially unacceptable. There is also the possibility that improved virtual technology will {reduce the need for|ehtiyojni kamaytiradi} business travel considerably, leaving leisure travel as the main reason to go anywhere.

sessions.t2: An important river or lake
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I work full-time now - I finished my degree two years ago and went straight into employment, so my student days are {behind me|ortda qoldi}.
What do you do?
I work as a junior analyst for a logistics company. My job mainly involves tracking shipments, identifying {bottlenecks|toʻsiqlar} in the supply chain and preparing reports for management.
Do you like your work or studies?

On the whole, yes. The company is small enough that I have real responsibility, which would not happen in a large corporation at my level. The hours can be long, but I feel I am {learning at a fast rate|tez sur'atda oʻrganyapman}.
What do you like most about your work or studies?

Solving problems that have a visible result. When I find a route that saves two days on a delivery, that is a {tangible|aniq, sezilarli} improvement, and it is much more satisfying than work where you never see the outcome.
Do you think you will continue doing the same work in the future?

Probably in the same industry, though not necessarily the same role. I would like to move towards {strategy|strategiya} rather than day-to-day operations. That said, I am only two years in, so I am {keeping my options open|imkoniyatlarni ochiq qoldiryapman}.
Do you often see advertisements?

Constantly, although I would say I only {consciously register|ongli ravishda sezaman} a small fraction of them. Between billboards, social media and video platforms, I would estimate I am exposed to dozens every day without really noticing.
What kind of advertisements do you usually notice?

Ones with humour or a genuine story. I also notice advertising that is {unusually well designed|gʻoyat chiroyli ishlangan} - a striking image on a billboard will make me look even if I have no interest in the product.
Do you like advertisements?

I appreciate the creative ones and resent the rest. What bothers me is the {sheer volume|hajmining koʻpligi} and the way online advertising follows you around after a single search, which feels {invasive|shaxsiy hayotga aralashish}.
Have you ever bought something because of an advertisement?

Yes, more often than I would like to admit. Most recently a pair of running shoes, after seeing the same advert repeatedly. To be fair, the product was good, but I am fairly sure the advertising {planted the idea|gʻoyani miyamga soldi} rather than responding to a need I already had.
Do you think advertisements are useful?

They serve a real purpose - without advertising, small businesses would have almost no way of {reaching customers|mijozlarga yetib borish}, and a lot of free online content would not exist. The problem is not advertising itself but the {lack of restraint|cheklovning yoʻqligi} with which it is used.

p2.task: Describe an important river or lake.
bullets: and explain why you think it is important
p2.ans:
The body of water I would like to talk about is the Aral Sea, which lies on the border between Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan and which, until fairly recently, was one of the four largest lakes in the world.

I first learned about it at school, where it is taught in some detail, and later studied it more seriously at university. I have also seen photographs and documentaries showing the {abandoned|tashlab ketilgan} fishing boats sitting on dry sand, sometimes fifty or sixty kilometres from the nearest water. Those images are difficult to forget.

Historically, the lake supported a substantial fishing industry - tens of thousands of people made their living from it - and the surrounding climate was {moderated|yumshatilgan} by the water, with milder winters and cooler summers. From the 1960s onwards, however, the two rivers feeding it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, were {diverted|burib yuborilgan} on a massive scale to irrigate cotton fields. Within a few decades the lake had lost the overwhelming majority of its volume.

I consider it important for two very different reasons. The first is what it once was: a lake that {sustained|ta'minlab turgan} an entire regional economy and ecosystem. The second, and frankly the more significant now, is what it has become - probably the clearest example anywhere in the world of how quickly human activity can {wipe out|yoʻq qilmoq} something that seemed permanent. The exposed seabed is full of salt and agricultural chemicals, which the wind carries for hundreds of kilometres, and the health consequences for local people have been severe.

There has been some success in the northern section, where a dam has allowed the water to {partially recover|qisman tiklanmoq}, and that matters because it shows the damage is not entirely {irreversible|qaytarib boʻlmas}. But for me the Aral Sea is important above all as a warning.

p3: Why are rivers and lakes important to people?

Most obviously as a source of drinking water and irrigation - civilisations have historically formed along them for exactly that reason. They also provide food, transport and, increasingly, {hydroelectric power|gidroelektr energiya}. Beyond the practical, they have enormous cultural value; many communities define themselves by the river they live beside.
What are the main differences between rivers and lakes?

The essential difference is movement. A river is a {flowing|oqar} system, which means it renews itself relatively quickly and can carry pollution downstream. A lake is largely {still|turgʻun}, so anything that enters it tends to accumulate, which makes lakes far more vulnerable to long-term contamination. Rivers also connect regions, whereas lakes are usually a {focal point|markaziy nuqta} for a single area.
How do rivers and lakes benefit the environment?

They support an extraordinary concentration of {biodiversity|biologik xilma-xillik} - freshwater habitats hold a share of the world's species out of all proportion to their size. They also regulate local climate, recharge groundwater and act as {natural drainage|tabiiy suv oqimi} during heavy rainfall, which reduces flooding.
What problems can pollution cause to rivers and lakes?

Agricultural runoff causes {algal blooms|suvoʻtlarning koʻpayishi} that strip the water of oxygen and kill fish. Industrial waste introduces heavy metals that {accumulate in the food chain|oziq zanjirida toʻplanadi} and eventually reach people. Plastic and untreated sewage make water unusable for drinking, and the cost of cleaning a contaminated lake is enormous compared with preventing the damage.
Why do some people choose to live near rivers or lakes?

Traditionally because of the water itself - fertile land, fishing and transport. Today it is more often about {quality of life|hayot sifati}: views, cooler air in summer, and opportunities for recreation. There is also good evidence that being near water has a {calming psychological effect|tinchlantiruvchi psixologik ta'sir}, which is presumably why waterside property is so expensive.
Should governments spend more money protecting rivers and lakes?

I think they should, and I would argue it is economically sensible rather than merely idealistic. Restoring a damaged water system costs far more than protecting it - the Aral Sea being the obvious illustration. Since rivers cross borders, this also requires {international cooperation|xalqaro hamkorlik}, which is difficult but unavoidable.
What can individuals do to keep rivers and lakes clean?

The direct actions are simple enough - not dumping waste, disposing of chemicals and medicines properly, and reducing plastic use. Less obviously, household choices matter: {phosphate-free|fosfatsiz} detergents and careful use of garden chemicals reduce what ends up in the water. And collectively, people can {put pressure on|bosim oʻtkazmoq} local authorities, which is probably more effective than any individual action.
Do you think rivers and lakes will be more or less important in the future?

Considerably more important. Fresh water is becoming {scarce|tanqis} in many regions, populations are growing and climate change is making rainfall less predictable. Water is already described as a potential source of conflict between states. So I would expect rivers and lakes to be treated far more as {strategic assets|strategik resurslar} than they have been.

sessions.t2: Someone who had difficulties but was successful
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am studying accounting - although I also help out in my family's business at weekends, so I get a small {taste of|ta'mini tatib koʻrish} the working world alongside my course.
What do you like about the area where you live?

It is quiet and very {well served|yaxshi ta'minlangan} for everyday needs - there is a market, a clinic and a school all within a few minutes' walk. The neighbours have lived there for decades, so there is a real {sense of community|jamoaviylik hissi}.
What do you dislike about the area where you live?

The traffic, mainly. The main road has become much busier over the last few years and parking is a {constant headache|doimiy bosh ogʻrigʻi}. There is also a shortage of green space - the nearest proper park is a fifteen-minute drive.
Is the area where you live usually tidy?

Generally, yes. The residents {take pride in|faxrlanadi} keeping the street clean and there is a communal clean-up a couple of times a year. The one problem is around the market, where rubbish {piles up|toʻplanib qoladi} by the end of the day.
Do you like keeping your room tidy?

I like the result far more than the process. Left to myself I will let things {accumulate|toʻplanib bormoq} for a week and then tidy everything at once. I have noticed that I concentrate considerably better when my desk is clear, so it is worth the effort.
Do you often use headphones?
Almost daily. They are {indispensable|ajralmas} on public transport, and I also use them when I am studying, because instrumental music helps me {tune out|e'tibor bermaslik} background noise.
When do you usually use headphones?

Mostly while commuting and while working. I avoid using them when I am walking near roads, though - I had a {near miss|arang qutulgan holat} a couple of years ago and since then I have been much more careful about {staying aware of|hushyor boʻlish} my surroundings.
What kind of headphones do you prefer?

Over-ear ones, because the sound is fuller and they are more comfortable for long periods. I do own wireless earbuds for convenience, but they {run out of battery|batareyasi tugaydi} at the worst possible moments, so I still carry a wired pair as a backup.

p2.task: Describe someone who had difficulties but was successful.
bullets: and explain why you find their story inspiring
p2.ans:
The person I would like to describe is a woman called Nodira, who runs a small chain of bakeries in my city and who started with almost nothing about twelve years ago.

I know her because my mother has been buying bread from her since the very first shop opened, and over the years the story has {come out in pieces|bo'lak-bo'lak ayon boʻlgan} during conversations at the counter.

Her difficulties were considerable. Her husband died when she was in her early thirties, leaving her with two young children, no qualifications beyond secondary school and no savings to speak of. She had worked at home her whole adult life, so she had no professional experience whatsoever. She started by baking at home and selling to neighbours, which brought in very little, and she was {turned down|rad etilgan} for a bank loan twice on the grounds that she had no {collateral|garov} and no credit history. Eventually she borrowed a small amount from relatives, which she has said was far harder than borrowing from a bank, because failing would have meant {letting down|umidini oqlamaslik} people she saw every week.

What she achieved from that starting point is genuinely impressive. She now has four shops, employs around twenty people - mostly women in similar situations to her own - and supplies several restaurants. Both of her children have finished university.

The reason her story is inspiring to me is not the commercial success as such. It is that she succeeded without any of the advantages we usually assume are necessary: no education in business, no capital, no connections. What she had instead was an {extraordinary work ethic|gʻoyat mehnatsevarlik} and a refusal to see her situation as {final|oxirgi, qaytarib boʻlmas}. She once said that the first two years were simply about {not stopping|toʻxtamaslik}, and I have thought about that remark many times since.

p3: What does it mean to be successful in life?

It is highly {subjective|sub'ektiv}. Conventionally it means wealth, status and recognition, but I would define it as having built something worthwhile and being at peace with the choices you made. By that measure a respected teacher on a modest salary may be far more successful than a wealthy person who {sacrificed everything else|qolgan hammasini qurbon qilgan} to get there.
What makes a person successful in business?

A combination of things, but I would put {resilience|bardoshlilik} first, because most businesses fail at least once. Beyond that: understanding customers rather than assuming you know what they want, {managing cash carefully|pul oqimini ehtiyotkorlik bilan boshqarish}, and being willing to change direction when the evidence says you should. Connections and timing also play a larger role than most successful people {care to admit|tan olishni xohlaydi}.
Is it more difficult to become successful in business nowadays?

It is different rather than uniformly harder. Starting a business has never been easier - you can reach customers online with minimal capital. But competition is {global|global} rather than local, and markets change faster, so surviving is harder than starting. I would say the {barrier to entry|kirish toʻsigʻi} has fallen while the barrier to lasting success has risen.
What qualities are important for success in business?

Persistence, obviously, but also {adaptability|moslashuvchanlik} and a certain tolerance for risk. Good judgement about people matters enormously, because most serious business problems are ultimately about hiring or partnership. And I would add honesty, which is not simply an ethical point - a reputation for {reliability|ishonchlilik} is the cheapest form of marketing there is.
Do you think money is the most important measure of success?

It is the easiest to measure, which is why it dominates, but it is a poor measure on its own. It tells you nothing about health, relationships or whether the work was worth doing. That said, I would not {dismiss it|e'tiborsiz qoldirmoq} either - financial security removes a great deal of stress, and it is easy to underrate that if you have never been without it.
Why do some people become successful while others do not?

Partly effort and judgement, but I think we systematically {underestimate|kam baholaymiz} the role of circumstances - where someone was born, what education they had access to, whether they had a safety net that allowed them to take risks. Two equally capable people can end up in very different places, so I am cautious about explanations that are purely about {individual merit|shaxsiy fazilat}.
Is success more dependent on hard work or luck?

Both are necessary and neither is sufficient. Luck creates opportunities, but hard work is what {puts you in a position|sizni holatga keltiradi} to notice and use them. My view is that hard work {raises the probability|ehtimolni oshiradi} of a lucky break rather than replacing it, and the people who deny luck entirely are usually the ones who have had it.
What can young people do to become successful in the future?

Develop skills that are genuinely hard to replicate, rather than chasing whatever is currently fashionable. Beyond that, I would say {build a reputation early|obroʻni erta shakllantirish} - being someone who finishes what they start is noticed far more than people expect. And learn to be comfortable with failure, because anyone who avoids it entirely has almost certainly not {attempted anything ambitious|ulkan ishga qoʻl urmagan}.

sessions.t2: A person who would like to work in the medical field
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my second year of a bachelor's degree, so I am {fully occupied|butunlay band} with my studies at the moment.
What do you study?
I study biology, with a particular focus on {human physiology|inson fiziologiyasi}. It is quite a heavy course with a lot of laboratory work, but it is exactly what I hoped it would be.
Do you enjoy your studies?

I do, genuinely. Some of the memorisation is {gruelling|charchatadigan} - anatomy in particular - but the practical sessions are excellent, and there is something very satisfying about understanding how your own body actually works.
What do you like most about your studies?

The laboratory work. Reading about a process is one thing, but {observing it under a microscope|mikroskop ostida kuzatish} makes it real. I also like that biology is constantly {being revised|qayta koʻrib chiqilmoqda} - things we were taught two years ago have already been updated.
Do you like singing?

I enjoy it, though I would not claim to be any good. I sing constantly when I am alone - in the shower, cooking, walking - and it genuinely {lifts my mood|kayfiyatimni koʻtaradi}. In front of other people, however, I am extremely {self-conscious|uyatchan}.
How often do you sing?

Almost every day in some form, even if it is only {humming along to|ohangini xirgoyi qilish} something on the radio. Properly singing, with the intention of sounding good, is rarer - perhaps at family gatherings a few times a year.
When do you usually sing?

Usually when I am doing something else that occupies my hands - washing dishes, tidying, walking home. It seems to happen {automatically|oʻz-oʻzidan} when my mind is not fully engaged, which I suspect is true for most people.
Have you ever taken part in a singing competition?

Only once, at school, and it was not a success. I was about twelve, I {forgot the words|soʻzlarni unutdim} halfway through, and I have avoided stages ever since. Looking back it was a useful lesson in {preparation|tayyorgarlik}, even if it was painful at the time.
If you had the chance, would you like to join a singing course?

I think I would, actually. Not with any ambition to perform, but because I am curious about how much of singing is {trainable|oʻrganish mumkin} rather than natural. From what I understand, breathing and technique account for a great deal more than people assume.

p2.task: Describe a person who would like to work in the medical field, such as a doctor or nurse.
bullets: and explain whether you think they will be successful
p2.ans:
The person I would like to talk about is my cousin Malika, who is currently in her fourth year at medical university in Tashkent and intends to become a paediatrician.

She is three years older than me and we grew up spending most of our summers together, so I have watched this ambition develop {from the very beginning|boshidanoq}. Even as a child she was the one who {took charge|mas'uliyatni oʻz zimmasiga olardi} when someone fell over, and she was strangely unbothered by things that made the rest of us squeamish.

Her choice of specialisation was not accidental. Her younger brother was seriously ill for several months when she was about fourteen, and she spent a great deal of that time in hospital with him. She has said that what struck her was not the treatment itself but the difference the staff made - one doctor in particular took the time to explain everything to her parents in plain language, and she has described that as the moment she decided. So her motivation has always been quite {specific|aniq} rather than a vague wish to help people.

Medical training here is long and {notoriously demanding|juda mashaqqatli ekani ma'lum}. She studies far harder than anyone else I know, and she has already begun volunteering at a clinic to {gain practical exposure|amaliy tajriba orttirish} before she is formally required to.

As for whether she will succeed, I am fairly confident she will, and not primarily because she is academically capable, although she is. It is because she has the temperament for it: she stays calm, she listens properly, and she is very good at explaining complicated things simply - which, in paediatrics, matters as much as clinical knowledge, since you are effectively treating the parents as well as the child. If anything, my concern is that she will {work herself into the ground|oʻzini charchatib qoʻyish}, because she finds it almost impossible to say no.

p3: In your country, do children like biology?

Many do, particularly the practical side - dissection, plants, anything involving animals. Where interest {tails off|pasayadi} is when the syllabus becomes heavy on terminology and diagrams to memorise. So I would say children like biology as a subject but not always as it is taught, which is a {common complaint|keng tarqalgan e'tiroz} about science education generally.
Why is being a doctor a hard job?

The training alone takes the best part of a decade. Beyond that, the hours are long, the {emotional burden|hissiy yuk} is considerable, and mistakes carry consequences that most professions never face. Doctors also have to keep learning throughout their careers, because treatments change constantly, and they deal with people at their most {distressed|iztirobdagi}, which is exhausting in a way that is easy to underestimate.
Why do young children want to become doctors?

Partly because it is one of the few professions children actually {encounter|duch keladi} - they meet doctors, so the job is visible in a way that, say, an auditor's is not. It also carries obvious {prestige|obroʻ} and is strongly encouraged by parents. And children respond to the simple idea of making sick people better, which is far more {compelling|jozibador} than most job descriptions.
What qualities does a good doctor need?

Clinical competence is the baseline, but beyond that I would say {empathy|hamdardlik} and communication skills. A doctor who cannot explain a diagnosis clearly leaves patients frightened and less likely to follow treatment. They also need {composure under pressure|bosim ostida xotirjamlik}, honesty about uncertainty, and the humility to ask a colleague when they do not know.
Is working as a doctor more difficult than other jobs?

It is difficult in a particular way rather than simply harder. Plenty of jobs involve long hours and stress. What distinguishes medicine is the combination of {high stakes|katta mas'uliyat}, emotional exposure and the length of training. I would hesitate to rank professions, though - a nurse or a teacher would have a fair claim to being just as demanding for far less {recognition|e'tirof}.
Why do some people choose medical careers?

Motives vary. For some it is genuine {vocation|kasbiy da'vat} - often after a personal experience with illness. For others it is job security and social standing, which are both considerable. Family expectation plays a significant role here as well. I think the ones who {last|chidaydi} are usually those with an intrinsic interest in the work itself.
How can schools encourage children to learn more about biology?

By making it {hands-on|amaliy}. Growing plants, keeping a class aquarium, simple experiments - anything where children observe rather than memorise. Bringing in visitors from medical or veterinary professions also helps, because it {connects the subject to|fanni bogʻlaydi} real careers. And field trips to natural areas do more for interest in ecology than any textbook chapter.
Do you think the medical profession will change in the future?

Substantially. {Diagnostic tools|tashxis vositalari} using artificial intelligence are already outperforming humans in some areas such as reading scans, and remote consultation is expanding rapidly. My expectation is that technology will {take over|oʻz zimmasiga oladi} much of the pattern-recognition work, which should free doctors to focus on judgement and the human side of care - the part that is hardest to {replicate|takrorlash}.

sessions.t2: An interesting video you have watched
p1: Do you have many friends?

Not a large number, but a solid few. I would say I have three or four genuinely close friends and then a wider circle of people I get on with. I have always preferred {depth over breadth|miqdordan koʻra sifat} in friendships.
What do you usually do with your friends?

Fairly ordinary things - eat out, walk, occasionally play football. A lot of our time together is just {sitting and talking|oʻtirib suhbatlashish}, honestly. We do not need an activity to justify meeting.
How often do you meet your friends?
Perhaps once a week as a group, though I speak to at least one of them most days. It was easier at university when we {crossed paths|duch kelardik} naturally; now it takes actual planning.
Do you prefer spending time with one friend or a group of friends?

One-to-one, in most cases. Conversations in a group tend to stay on the {surface|yuzaki}, whereas with one person you can talk about something properly. Groups are more fun, but individual meetings are more {meaningful|ma'noli}.
What qualities do you look for in a friend?

Reliability above all - someone who {follows through|va'dasini bajaradi} on what they say. Beyond that, honesty, and a sense of humour. I also value people who are genuinely pleased when things go well for you, because that is rarer than it sounds.
Have your friendships changed as you have grown older?

Considerably. As a child friendship was about {proximity|yaqinlik} - whoever lived nearby. Now it is about shared values, and I have far fewer friends but know them much better. I have also become more {comfortable with|koʻnikkanman} the fact that some friendships simply fade, which used to bother me.
Do you like looking at the stars?

I do, though the opportunity is rare in the city. Whenever I am somewhere genuinely dark I find it {mesmerising|maftun etadigan}, and it always surprises me how many stars are actually there once the {light pollution|yorugʻlik ifloslanishi} is gone.
Did you learn about stars when you were a child?

A little, at school and from my grandfather, who could identify several constellations. He taught me to find the Plough, which is honestly the {full extent|toʻliq hajmi} of my knowledge, but I still look for it whenever I am outside at night.
When was the last time you looked at the stars?

About two months ago, when I stayed overnight in the mountains. The sky was completely clear and we {lay on our backs|chalqancha yotdik} for nearly an hour. It was the first time in years that I had seen the Milky Way properly.
Can you see many stars where you live?
Very few, unfortunately. Street lighting and {haze|tutunli havo} from traffic mean you might see a dozen on a good night. It is one of the things I miss most about being outside the city.
Would you like to learn more about stars?

I would, particularly the practical side - being able to {orient myself|yoʻnalishni topish} by the sky rather than simply admiring it. I have downloaded apps for this a few times but never {stuck with|davom ettirmadim} them, which is probably a lack of discipline rather than interest.
Are you interested in space?

Moderately. I follow the major missions and I find the {sheer scale|ulkanligi} of it fascinating, but I would not describe it as a passion. It is more that occasionally I read something about it and spend an evening {going down a rabbit hole|chuqur berilib ketmoq}.
Did you enjoy learning about space at school?

Yes, it was one of the few parts of physics I looked forward to. Unfortunately it was covered very briefly, and mostly as facts to be {reproduced in an exam|imtihonda takrorlash}, which rather {dampened|soʻndirdi} the enthusiasm.
Would you like to travel into space?
Honestly, no. I admire the people who do, but the risk and the physical demands do not appeal to me at all. I would happily accept a {virtual experience|virtual tajriba} of it instead.
Do you often watch videos or documentaries about space?

Occasionally - perhaps a few times a year, usually when a new set of telescope images is released. I prefer documentaries that explain the {underlying science|asosiy ilmiy jihat} rather than ones that simply show impressive visuals.
What would you like to know about space?

The obvious question: whether there is life elsewhere. Beyond that, I am curious about what is happening at the {edge of the observable universe|kuzatiladigan olamning chekkasi}, because the idea that there is a limit to what can ever be seen is genuinely {unsettling|bezovta qiladigan}.

p2.task: Describe an interesting video you have watched.
bullets: and explain why you found it interesting
p2.ans:
The video I would like to describe is a documentary I watched on YouTube about how the modern shipping container transformed global trade, which sounds {unpromising|qiziqarsizdek} but turned out to be genuinely fascinating.

I watched it at home, alone, late one evening. It came up in my recommendations and I clicked on it more or less {out of idleness|zerikkanimdan}, expecting to watch two minutes. It ran for about forty and I watched all of it.

The film explained that before the 1950s, loading a ship was done by hand, sack by sack, and it could take a week in port. An American businessman called Malcom McLean had the apparently obvious idea of putting goods into standard steel boxes that could go straight from a lorry onto a ship without being {unpacked|ochilmagan}. The documentary then traced what followed: the cost of shipping {collapsed|keskin tushdi} by something like ninety per cent, which made it economically sensible to manufacture goods on the other side of the world. Entire industries moved, port cities that could not handle containers {went into decline|tanazzulga yuz tutdi}, and new ones grew in their place.

What made it interesting to me was the realisation that something so {mundane|oddiy} - a metal box - could reshape the world economy more profoundly than most inventions we celebrate. The documentary made the point that we tend to credit dramatic technologies while overlooking {unglamorous|jozibasiz} ones that turn out to matter far more.

It also {changed how I look at|qanday qarashimni oʻzgartirdi} ordinary objects. Since watching it I have found myself wondering about the {supply chain|ta'minot zanjiri} behind everyday things, which is not something that had ever occurred to me before. Any video that leaves you noticing things you had previously ignored has, I think, done its job.

p3: Why do people enjoy watching videos online?

Convenience is the main reason - content is available instantly, at any length, on any subject. Video is also {undemanding|talab qilmaydigan} compared with reading; you can absorb it while doing something else. And the algorithms are extremely effective at {serving up|taklif qilish} material that matches your interests, which makes it easy to keep watching.
What types of videos are popular among young people in your country?

Short entertainment clips dominate, along with music videos and gaming content. There is also substantial interest in {educational content|ta'limiy kontent} - language learning, exam preparation and tutorials. And vlogs remain popular, I think because young people are drawn to the sense of knowing someone {personally|shaxsan}, even if that intimacy is largely manufactured.
Do you think educational videos are useful for children?

Genuinely useful, provided they are {supplementary|qoʻshimcha} rather than a replacement. Video is excellent at demonstrating processes that are hard to describe in words - an experiment, a historical reconstruction. The limitation is that watching is {passive|passiv}, and children need to practise and be corrected before they have really learned anything.
Why do some videos become extremely popular?

Usually a combination of an {emotional hook|hissiy ilinj} - humour, outrage or surprise - and good timing. Content that people want to send to someone else spreads fastest, because sharing is what drives the numbers. Beyond that, there is a considerable element of {chance|tasodif}; algorithms amplify whatever gets early engagement, so small differences {snowball|qor toʻpiday oʻsadi}.
Do people spend too much time watching videos nowadays?

Many do, yes. The platforms are deliberately designed to {maximise watch time|koʻrish vaqtini koʻpaytirish}, with autoplay and endless feeds, so it takes conscious effort to stop. The concern for me is not the total hours so much as the {displacement|siqib chiqarish} - time that would otherwise go to sleep, exercise or face-to-face contact.
How has technology changed the way people learn?

It has made information {universally accessible|hamma uchun ochiq}, which is a genuine revolution - a student anywhere can watch lectures from leading universities. It has also allowed learning to happen {at your own pace|oʻz sur'atingizda}. The downside is that access is not the same as understanding, and technology has done little to help people with {motivation and persistence|motivatsiya va sabr}, which is where most learning actually fails.
Can videos replace traditional classroom learning?

Not entirely, in my view. Videos can deliver content extremely efficiently, but classrooms provide feedback, accountability and peer interaction. The {social pressure|ijtimoiy bosim} of a class is what keeps most students working. I think the realistic model is {blended|aralash} - video for content delivery, classroom time for discussion and correction.
Do you think the way people watch videos will change in the future?

I expect content to become shorter and more {personalised|shaxsiylashtirilgan}, with AI generating or editing material for individual viewers. Interactive and immersive formats will probably grow too. What I suspect will not change is the underlying appeal - people have always wanted stories delivered easily, and video is simply the current {vehicle|vosita} for that.
What are the advantages and disadvantages of short videos?

They are accessible, easy to share and can convey a single idea very effectively. The disadvantage is that complex subjects get {compressed to the point of distortion|buzib koʻrsatiladigan darajada siqiladi}, and constant short-form consumption appears to {erode|yemiradi} the ability to concentrate on anything longer. They are excellent for discovery and poor for depth.
Should parents control what kind of videos their children watch?

Yes, especially for younger children, because platforms' own safeguards are {far from reliable|ishonchli emas}. But control should mean guidance rather than pure restriction - watching together and discussing what they see teaches judgement, whereas blanket bans simply {push it out of sight|koʻzdan yashiradi}. As children get older, the aim should be to {hand over|topshirmoq} that judgement gradually.

sessions.t2: An occasion when you received good service
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am studying tourism management, which is a three-year programme, and I am about halfway through it.
What do you like most about your studies?

The fact that it is {outward-looking|tashqariga yoʻnaltirilgan}. We study other countries, cultures and how the industry works internationally, and there is a strong practical element - we have already done a placement at a local hotel, which taught me more than a term of lectures.
What do you dislike about your studies?

Some of the theory feels rather {removed from reality|hayotdan uzoq}. We spend a lot of time on models that, from what I saw during my placement, nobody in the industry actually uses. I would prefer more {case studies|amaliy misollar} of real businesses.
Do you think it is important to be polite?

Extremely. Politeness is essentially the {lubricant|moylovchi vosita} of daily life - it costs nothing and it prevents an enormous number of unnecessary conflicts. It also signals respect, which matters especially when you disagree with someone.
Who taught you to be polite when you were a child?

My parents, mainly, and my grandmother, who was very {particular about|talabchan edi} greetings and how you spoke to older people. A lot of it was taught by example rather than instruction - you {absorb|oʻzlashtirasiz} the way adults around you behave without noticing.
Did you wake up early when you were a child?
Yes, out of necessity, since school started at eight. At weekends, though, I would {sleep in|uzoq uxlash} as long as I possibly could, like most children.
Do you usually wake up early now?

I do, and by choice now rather than obligation. I get up at around six, and the first hour of the day, before anyone messages me, is easily my most {productive|samarali}. I have found that the earlier I start, the {less rushed|kamroq shoshiladigan} the whole day feels.

p2.task: Describe an occasion when you received good service in a shop or restaurant.
bullets: and explain why you thought the service was so good
p2.ans:
The occasion I would like to describe happened in a small electronics shop in Namangan about a year and a half ago, when I went in to buy a replacement laptop charger.

I had gone there fully expecting to spend a fair amount of money, because the original charger had failed and I assumed I would have to buy the manufacturer's own version, which is {notoriously overpriced|narxi juda qimmatligi bilan mashhur}. I explained the problem to the man behind the counter, who was probably in his forties and clearly {knew his stock inside out|mahsulotini juda yaxshi bilardi}.

Rather than immediately selling me something, he asked me to bring the old charger in. When I did, he spent about ten minutes testing it and established that the charger was actually fine - the problem was a damaged cable, which he then {repaired on the spot|joyida ta'mirladi} for a fraction of what a new unit would have cost. He also pointed out that I had been coiling the cable in a way that was {putting strain on|zoʻriqish berayotgan} the connector, and showed me how to avoid it.

What made this good service was not simply that he was friendly, although he was. It was that he acted {against his own immediate interest|oʻz manfaatiga qarshi}. He could very easily have sold me an expensive charger and I would never have known the difference. Instead he solved the actual problem and charged me almost nothing for it.

The result, of course, is that I have bought everything electronic from that shop since, and I have recommended it to at least a dozen people. So it was not even a {sacrifice|qurbonlik} commercially - it was simply a longer view of the same transaction. That experience convinced me that genuine service and good business are usually {one and the same|bir xil narsa}.

p3: What makes a good service?

Competence first - the person actually knowing what they are talking about. Then attentiveness without {hovering|boshida turib olish}, and honesty about what a product can and cannot do. What distinguishes excellent service from adequate service is usually {anticipation|oldindan sezish}: noticing what a customer needs before they have to ask.
Why is good customer service important for businesses?

Because it is what {generates repeat custom|qayta xarid qildiradi}, and keeping an existing customer is far cheaper than finding a new one. It is also the most credible form of advertising - people trust recommendations from friends far more than any campaign. In competitive markets where products are nearly identical, service is often the only real {point of difference|farqlovchi jihat}.
Do you think public services are good in your country?

They have improved considerably, particularly with digitalisation - many things that once required a whole day of queuing can now be done online. Healthcare and education, however, remain {uneven|notekis}: standards in the capital are far higher than in rural districts. So I would say the direction is positive but there is still a significant {gap|tafovut} to close.
What public services do people use most often?

Healthcare, education and transport, overwhelmingly. Beyond those, administrative services - registering documents, paying utilities - which people use less frequently but which shape their opinion of the state disproportionately, because those are the interactions people find most {frustrating|asabbuzar}.
How can governments improve public services?

Digitalisation is the obvious lever, since it removes both queuing and opportunities for {petty corruption|mayda korrupsiya}. Beyond that, training and paying staff properly, and collecting genuine feedback rather than {going through the motions|shunchaki koʻrinish uchun}. Accountability matters most - services improve when there is a real consequence for poor performance.
Should public services be free for everyone?

Essential services such as basic healthcare and school education should be, in my view, because access to them determines {life chances|hayotdagi imkoniyatlar} and no child should be excluded by income. For other services, a modest charge can reduce waste, provided there are {exemptions|imtiyozlar} for those who cannot pay. The principle should be that nobody is denied something essential for financial reasons.
Do you think technology can improve public services?

Substantially, and it already has. Online appointments, digital records and electronic payment systems save enormous amounts of time and reduce human error. The caution I would add is the risk of {excluding|chetlatib qoʻyish} elderly or rural users who lack devices or confidence, so digital systems should {run alongside|yonma-yon ishlashi} traditional ones rather than replacing them outright.

sessions.t2: A time when you saw children behaving badly
p1: Do you live in a house or an apartment?
I live in an apartment, on the seventh floor of a building in the north of the city. It is not large - two bedrooms - but it is {more than adequate|yetarlidan ham ortiq} for the three of us.
How long have you lived there?
About six years now. We moved when I was starting secondary school, and although it took me a while to {settle in|koʻnikmoq}, I would not want to move again now.
What do you like most about your accommodation?

The view, oddly enough. Being on the seventh floor means we look out over the rooftops rather than into someone else's window, and in the evening you can see the mountains on a clear day. It makes a small flat feel far less {enclosed|yopiq}.
Do you enjoy cooking?

I do, though I came to it {late|kech}. I only started properly when I was about eighteen, and I found it surprisingly relaxing - it is one of the few activities where you cannot really think about anything else, which makes it a good way to {switch off|miyani dam oldirish}.
How often do you cook?

Three or four times a week. On busy days someone else in the family takes over, but I usually cook at weekends when there is time to make something more {elaborate|murakkab} than the usual weeknight meal.
Who usually cooks in your family?

Traditionally my mother, and she still does most of it, but we have gradually {shared it out|boʻlishib olganmiz} more evenly. My father cooks on Sundays, mainly plov, which he regards as {his speciality|uning ustunligi} and which nobody is allowed to interfere with.

p2.task: Describe a time when you saw children behaving badly.
bullets: and explain how you and others reacted
p2.ans:
The occasion I want to describe took place on a long-distance bus journey from Tashkent to Bukhara about two years ago, and it lasted rather a long time.

There were two boys, I would guess aged around seven and nine, travelling with their mother, who was sitting a few rows behind them. From about twenty minutes into the journey, they began running up and down the aisle, {shouting at the tops of their voices|baqirib} and pulling at the headrests of other passengers' seats. One of them repeatedly {kicked the back of|orqasiga tepdi} the seat in front, which happened to belong to an elderly man who was trying to sleep.

Their mother intervened occasionally, but never {followed through|oxiriga yetkazmadi}. She would tell them to sit down, they would sit for perhaps two minutes, and then it would start again. After a while she stopped saying anything at all and simply looked out of the window, which I suspect was {sheer exhaustion|toza charchash} rather than indifference.

The reaction of the other passengers was interesting. Nobody said anything directly, because in our culture correcting someone else's children is regarded as {overstepping|chegaradan chiqish}. Instead there was a lot of {pointed sighing|ma'noli xoʻrsinish} and exchanged glances. Eventually the driver stopped at a service station and spoke to the mother quietly, and after that the boys were considerably calmer.

My own reaction was more sympathetic than irritated, to be honest. Four hours on a bus is a great deal to ask of a seven-year-old, and nobody had given them anything to do. I did think, though, that the real issue was the {inconsistency|izchillikning yoʻqligi} - the children had clearly learned that instructions were not enforced, so there was no reason to take them seriously. It struck me that {following through|aytganini bajarish} matters far more than how strict a parent is.

p3: Why do some children behave badly?

There are several common reasons. Often it is simply {attention-seeking|e'tibor talab qilish} - negative attention is still attention. Boredom and tiredness account for a great deal, especially in situations children were never designed to sit through. And where rules are {applied inconsistently|izchil qoʻllanilmaydi}, children naturally test the boundaries, because they have learned that the boundaries move.
What can parents do when their children behave badly?

The most effective approach seems to be calm consistency - stating a clear consequence and then actually {carrying it out|amalga oshirish}. Removing the child from the situation works better than arguing in front of an audience. It also helps enormously to {pre-empt|oldini olish} the problem: making sure children are fed, rested and have something to occupy them prevents most incidents entirely.
Should parents punish children for bad behavior?

There should be consequences, certainly, but I would distinguish that from punishment in the traditional sense. Physical punishment is both {ineffective and harmful|samarasiz va zararli} according to almost all the research - it teaches fear rather than understanding. Proportionate consequences, explained clearly, work far better, and so does {praising good behaviour|yaxshi xatti-harakatni maqtash}, which parents tend to do far less often.
How can schools deal with children who behave badly?

Clear, consistently applied rules are the foundation, but schools also need to {look behind|ortidan qaramoq} the behaviour, since persistent disruption usually indicates something else - difficulties at home, learning problems, or bullying. Exclusion may be necessary occasionally, but it rarely {addresses the underlying cause|asosiy sababni hal qiladi}, and often makes matters worse.
Do you think children behave differently now compared with the past?

Differently, yes, though I would resist the idea that they are simply worse. Children today are less {deferential|hurmat bilan boʻysunadigan} towards adults, which reflects a broader cultural shift towards questioning authority - and that is not entirely a bad thing. What has genuinely changed is attention: constant screen use appears to make sitting quietly harder than it was for previous generations.
What role do teachers play in teaching children good behavior?

A very significant one, because children spend a large part of their waking life at school and teachers are the main model of how adults outside the family behave. Teachers also manage something parents rarely do: behaviour {within a group|guruh ichida}, where children must learn to take turns and resolve conflicts. Much of that learning is {implicit|bevosita aytilmagan} rather than taught directly.
Who should be mainly responsible for children's behavior, parents or teachers?

Parents, primarily - they have the child for far longer and they establish the {core values|asosiy qadriyatlar}. Schools should reinforce those rather than being expected to create them from nothing, which is an unrealistic burden frequently placed on teachers. That said, it is not really a {division of labour|ish taqsimoti}; where the two work in the same direction, results are dramatically better than when they {undermine|zaiflashtiradi} each other.

sessions.t2: A place in nature that you enjoy visiting
p1: Do you live in a flat or a house?

I live in a flat, in a five-storey block built in the Soviet period. It is not modern by any means, but the walls are thick and the rooms are a decent size, which you do not always get in {newer developments|yangi binolar}.
How long have you lived there?
My family has been there for almost twenty years, so effectively my whole life. Everyone in the building knows everyone else, which is becoming quite {rare|kamyob} in cities now.
Can you describe your flat?

It has three rooms plus a kitchen and a small balcony. The living room is the largest and doubles as a {dining room|ovqatlanish xonasi} when we have guests. It is decorated fairly simply - my parents are not people who {chase trends|modaga ergashadigan}.
What do you like most about your flat?

The kitchen, without a doubt. It is unusually large for a flat of that age, and it is where the family actually {congregates|toʻplanadi}. Most of the important conversations in our family have happened around that table.
Is there anything you dislike about it?

The lack of a lift is the main complaint, particularly for my grandmother. The plumbing is also {temperamental|injiq} - the hot water {gives out|toʻxtab qoladi} without warning every few months, usually in winter.
Did you enjoy trying new things when you were a child?

I was quite {cautious|ehtiyotkor}, actually. I would watch other children do something several times before attempting it myself. My parents tell me I was the child who refused to go on any ride at an amusement park until my younger sister had {tested it|sinab koʻrgan}.
What kind of new things did you like trying?

Anything that could be done alone rather than in front of people - new books, new recipes, drawing. I was much more willing to {take a risk|tavakkal qilish} when there was no audience, which I think is still true of me now.
Did your parents encourage you to try new things?

Yes, and quite {persistently|qat'iyat bilan}. They enrolled me in a swimming class I did not want to attend and a music school I resented at the time. In hindsight I am grateful, because both gave me skills I would never have {acquired|orttirgan} on my own initiative.
Is there anything new you would like to try in the future?

I would like to learn to drive properly, which I have been {putting off|kechiktirib yuryapman} for years. Beyond that, I would genuinely like to try public speaking in a formal setting, precisely because it is the thing I find most {intimidating|qoʻrqinchli}.

p2.task: Describe a place in nature that you enjoy visiting.
bullets: and explain why you enjoy being there
p2.ans:
The place I would like to describe is a stretch of the Chimgan mountains, roughly two hours' drive from Tashkent, where there is a valley with a stream running through it that my family has been visiting for years.

We usually go in late spring or early autumn. Summer is too crowded and the heat is {punishing|azob beradigan} even at altitude, whereas in May the slopes are still green and the water is high from the {snowmelt|qor suvi}. We normally go as a group of six or seven - my parents, my sister and a couple of family friends - and we make a whole day of it, leaving early and coming back after dark.

The valley itself is quite narrow, with steep sides covered in juniper, and the stream runs over rocks so the sound of water is constant. There are a few flat areas near the bottom where people spread out blankets. We usually walk for an hour or two first, following the stream upwards, and then come back down and cook, because my father insists that food tastes different {in the open air|ochiq havoda}, and he is probably right.

What I enjoy about it is partly physical. The air is noticeably cooler and cleaner than in the city, and after a few hours you feel {genuinely refreshed|chinakamiga tetiklashgan} in a way that a day indoors never achieves. There is also no phone signal for most of the valley, which at first felt inconvenient and which I now consider the best thing about it.

But the real reason is that it has become a kind of {family ritual|oilaviy an'ana}. I have been going since I was small, and the place is now {bound up with|bogʻlanib ketgan} memories of different stages of my life. Going back is as much about that continuity as it is about the scenery.

p3: How is nature important to people?

At the most basic level it provides everything we depend on - air, water, food. Beyond that, the psychological benefits are now {well documented|yaxshi hujjatlashtirilgan}: even short periods outdoors lower stress and improve concentration. And there is a cultural dimension, since landscapes are central to how communities {define themselves|oʻzini anglaydi}.
What natural places do people usually visit?

Mountains and rivers, primarily, because those are what we have. Coastal countries would say beaches, obviously. In cities, parks and botanical gardens do much of the same work on a smaller scale - they are the {accessible substitute|qulay muqobil} for people who cannot travel out at weekends.
Do you think people are spending more time in nature nowadays?

It is {contradictory|ziddiyatli}. In one sense clearly not - we live and work indoors more than any previous generation, and children in particular spend far less time outside. But there has been a visible rise in deliberate outdoor recreation - hiking, camping, cycling - among adults. So unstructured time outdoors has {declined|kamaygan} while organised outdoor activity has grown.
Why do some people prefer spending time in nature?

Because it is one of the few environments with no {demands|talablar} on your attention. In a city you are constantly being signalled at; in a forest nothing requires a response. Some people also find the {sense of scale|ulkanlik hissi} comforting - being somewhere that does not revolve around human concerns puts everyday anxieties in proportion.
What can people do to protect natural places?

The immediate things are obvious: taking rubbish home, staying on paths, not lighting fires carelessly. More significantly, people can {support|qoʻllab-quvvatlamoq} organisations doing conservation work and be careful about where they travel, since the most fragile places suffer most from visitor numbers. Collective pressure on authorities probably matters more than any individual habit.
Do children nowadays spend enough time outdoors?

Almost certainly not. Between screens, longer school hours and parents' entirely understandable {safety concerns|xavfsizlik xavotirlari}, unsupervised outdoor play has largely disappeared. That matters because outdoor play is how children develop physical confidence and learn to {assess risk|xavfni baholash} for themselves - skills that cannot really be taught indoors.
How can cities provide people with more opportunities to enjoy nature?

Small interventions {add up|yigʻilib katta natija beradi}: street trees, green roofs, pocket parks on unused land. More ambitiously, cities can {restore|tiklamoq} rivers that were built over and create green corridors linking parks so that wildlife can move. What matters most is distribution - a single large park is less useful than many small green spaces {within walking distance|piyoda yurish masofasida} of where people actually live.

sessions.examiner: Tall older man, grey hair and glasses
sessions.t2: A time when you were very busy
p1: Please describe your hometown a little.

I am from Tashkent, which is the capital and by some distance the largest city in Central Asia. It is a city of {sharp contrasts|keskin qarama-qarshiliklar} - Soviet apartment blocks next to glass towers, and an old town that has barely changed in decades.
What is your hometown well-known for?

Several things: the metro, which has unusually decorative stations; Chorsu bazaar; and the fact that it was largely rebuilt after the 1966 earthquake, which is why so much of it looks {uniform|bir xil}. It is also known for being remarkably green for a city in a desert region.
Do you like your hometown?

I do, though not {uncritically|tanqidsiz}. It has energy, opportunity and excellent food, but the traffic is worsening and a lot of older buildings are being {torn down|buzib tashlanmoqda} in a way I find regrettable. Overall, the advantages {outweigh|ustun keladi} the frustrations.
Is that a big city or a small place?

Very much a big city - around three million people, I believe. That said, it functions as a series of districts, and most residents rarely leave their own, so in daily life it can feel {surprisingly local|kutilmaganda mahalliy}.
How long have you been living there?
My whole life, so about twenty-two years. I have travelled, but I have never lived anywhere else, which means I probably {take a lot of it for granted|koʻp narsani oddiy deb bilaman}.
Would you like to live in the countryside in the future?

Possibly when I am older. The appeal is obvious - space, quiet, clean air - but I am realistic about the {trade-offs|murosalar}: fewer services, limited healthcare and a great deal of driving. I suspect the honest answer is that I romanticise it slightly.
Do you ever get bored?
