Rarely in the sense of having nothing to do; more often I get bored in the middle of a task, when something becomes {repetitive|takrorlanuvchi}. Genuine empty-time boredom has almost disappeared from my life, which I am not sure is entirely a good thing.
When would you feel bored?

Waiting - in queues, in transit, in meetings that could have been an email. Also during any activity where I have no {say in the outcome|natijaga ta'sir qila olmaslik}, because what makes something engaging for me is having to make decisions.
Do you think school is boring?

Parts of it inevitably are. Any system teaching thirty students at once has to move at an average pace, so some are {left behind|orqada qoladi} and others are {held back|ushlab turiladi}. The subjects themselves are rarely boring; the delivery frequently is.
Do you feel more bored now than when you were young?

Less, if anything, but I am also far less able to {tolerate|chidamoq} it. As a child I could stare out of a window for an hour quite happily. Now, if there is a thirty-second gap, I reach for my phone, which suggests my {threshold|chegaram} has dropped considerably.
What skills would you like to learn?

Practically, I would like to learn to drive and to improve my public speaking. Beyond that, I would love to learn a musical instrument properly - I attempted the guitar twice and {gave up|voz kechdim} both times, which I regard as {unfinished business|tugallanmagan ish}.

p2.task: Describe a time when you were very busy.
bullets: and explain how you felt about it
p2.ans:
The busiest period I can remember was about eight months ago, during a two-week stretch when my final university deadlines happened to coincide with an unusually demanding spell at my part-time job.

What made it difficult was not any single task but the {sheer accumulation|toʻplanib qolgani} of them. I had a ten-thousand-word dissertation due, two other assignments, and my employer had lost a member of staff, so I was asked to cover extra shifts at what was genuinely {short notice|qisqa muddat}. On top of that, my younger brother was preparing for his own exams and I had promised to help him, which I was not willing to {go back on|qaytib olmoq}.

I managed it, more or less, by becoming far stricter about time than I usually am. I started {blocking out|ajratib qoʻyish} my day in advance - actual hours written down rather than a vague list - and I made myself do the hardest work first thing in the morning, when I am sharpest. I also made a decision that felt uncomfortable at the time: I deliberately {let some things slide|ba'zi narsalarni e'tibordan chetda qoldirdim}, including the gym and most of my social life, on the basis that two weeks of neglect would not do lasting damage.

Emotionally it was a mixture. For the first week I found it {oddly energising|gʻalati tarzda ruhlantiruvchi} - there was no time to hesitate, so I simply worked. By the second week the tiredness had {caught up with me|meni bosib olgan edi} and I was irritable and sleeping badly.

Looking back, though, I learned more about myself in that fortnight than in the whole year around it. I discovered that I am capable of a great deal more than I assume, but also that I cannot {sustain|davom ettirmoq} that pace, and that pretending otherwise is how people end up {burning out|tamomila charchash}.

p3: Why are some people busier than others?

Circumstances account for much of it - caring responsibilities, financial pressure, the nature of a job. But personality matters too: some people find it difficult to {turn things down|rad etish} and end up taking on more than they can handle. And a certain number are busy without being productive, because they have never learned to {prioritise|muhimini tanlash}.
Do you think people are busier nowadays than in the past?

They feel busier, certainly, though whether they actually work more hours is {debatable|bahsli}. What has changed is that work now follows people home through their phones, so there is no clear end to the day. There are also more {competing demands|raqobatlashuvchi talablar} - people are expected to work, exercise, socialise and keep up online simultaneously.
Is it good to be busy all the time?

Being occupied is generally positive - it gives structure and purpose. Being {permanently overloaded|doimiy ortiqcha yuklangan} is not, because it leaves no capacity for reflection or recovery, and that is where both creativity and good judgement come from. Constant busyness can also become a way of {avoiding|qochish} things people do not want to think about.
Why do some people enjoy having a busy lifestyle?

Partly because it provides a clear sense of {momentum|harakat, sur'at} and achievement - a full schedule feels like proof that you matter. Busyness has also acquired a certain {status|maqom} in modern culture; saying you are busy signals that you are in demand. And for some people, activity is genuinely their preferred state and idleness makes them restless.
How can people manage their time effectively?

The most useful habit is distinguishing between urgent and important, since most people spend their day on the urgent. Beyond that: doing the hardest task first, {batching|guruhlab bajarish} similar tasks, and above all being willing to say no. Realistic planning matters too - people consistently {underestimate|kam baholaydi} how long things take, sometimes by a factor of two.
Do you think students nowadays have too many things to do?

Many do. Alongside academic work there is enormous pressure to build a {portfolio|toʻplam} - volunteering, competitions, languages, internships - because admissions and employers expect it. A good number also work to support themselves. The result is that free time has become something students feel {guilty about|aybdor his qiladi}, which I think is genuinely unhealthy.
What are the disadvantages of being too busy?

Health is the first casualty - sleep, diet and exercise are the things people cut. Relationships suffer, since they require unhurried time. And the quality of work itself declines: when everything is rushed, mistakes {creep in|kirib qoladi}. There is also good evidence that chronic stress {impairs|zaiflashtiradi} exactly the kind of thinking that busy people most need.

sessions.t2: A place you would like to visit again
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student. I am in the third year of a degree in economics, so I still have a year and a half to go before I {enter the job market|ish bozoriga chiqaman}.
What do you study?

Economics, with a concentration in finance in the later years. It covers everything from {macroeconomic policy|makroiqtisodiy siyosat} to statistics, and there is far more mathematics involved than most people expect.
Why did you choose your field of study?

Because it explains things I had always been curious about - why prices rise, why some countries develop and others do not. It is also a very {transferable|koʻchma, keng qoʻllanadigan} degree; it opens doors in banking, government and consultancy rather than {tying you to|bogʻlab qoʻymoq} one career.
What do you like most about your studies?

The way it {reframes|qayta talqin qiladi} everyday decisions. Once you understand concepts like opportunity cost, you start noticing them everywhere - in how you spend your time, not just your money. That is genuinely useful beyond the exam hall.
Do you like taking pictures?

I do, though I am very much an {amateur|havaskor}. I like photography because it makes you look at ordinary things more carefully - once you start thinking about light and composition, you notice details you would otherwise {walk straight past|e'tibor bermay oʻtib ketmoq}.
How often do you take pictures?

Casually, most days - a photo of something on the way to university. More deliberately, perhaps once a fortnight, usually when I go somewhere new or the light is unusual. I probably take far more than I ever {look back at|qayta koʻrish}.
What do you usually take pictures of?

Architecture and street scenes, mainly. I am drawn to old buildings and to the contrast between them and the new ones going up around them. I take far fewer photographs of people, partly because I feel {awkward|noqulay} asking.
Do you prefer taking pictures with a phone or a camera?

A phone, for practical reasons - it is always with me, and the best camera is the one you actually have. A proper camera produces noticeably better results, particularly in low light, but I am not usually carrying one when something {worth photographing|suratga olishga arziydigan} happens.

p2.task: Describe a place you have been to and would like to visit again.
bullets: and explain why you would like to go back
p2.ans:
The place I would most like to return to is Bukhara, which I visited for the first and so far only time about four years ago, during a short trip with two friends.

We went in October, which turned out to be an excellent decision, because the summer crowds had gone and the weather was {mild|yumshoq}. We stayed for three nights in a guesthouse in the historic centre, in a building that was apparently around two hundred years old, with a courtyard in the middle.

We did the obvious things - the Ark fortress, the Kalyan minaret, the covered bazaars - but what I remember most is the walking. The old town is almost entirely {pedestrianised|piyodalar uchun}, and because it has never really been rebuilt, the streets still follow their original {layout|joylashuv}. We spent whole afternoons simply getting lost in it. In the evenings we sat by the Lyabi-Hauz pool, where locals and visitors all seem to {end up|toʻplanadi} at the same time of day.

The reason I want to go back is that I did not, in all honesty, appreciate it properly the first time. At nineteen I was largely interested in the photographs. Since then I have read a great deal more about the history of the region, and I now understand what I was actually looking at - that Bukhara was for centuries one of the major {centres of learning|ilm markazlari} in the Islamic world. I would like to see it again with that knowledge.

There is also a simpler reason. It is one of very few places where a whole city, rather than a single monument, has {survived largely intact|deyarli butunligicha saqlanib qolgan}, and walking through it genuinely felt like moving through a different century. That sensation is rare, and I would like to {experience it again|yana his qilish}.

p3: Why do people like visiting the same places again?

Familiarity removes the {stress of the unknown|noma'lumlik stressi} - you know where to eat and how to get around, so you can simply enjoy it. There is also a {nostalgic element|nostalgik jihat}: returning somewhere lets you measure how much you have changed. And a repeat visit reveals detail that a first visit, spent on the main sights, always misses.
What kinds of places do people usually want to visit more than once?

Places with a strong {emotional association|hissiy bogʻliqlik} - somewhere they spent a childhood holiday, or where something significant happened. Beyond that, cities with enough {depth|chuqurlik} that one visit cannot exhaust them, and natural places that change with the season, since a mountain in spring is effectively a different place in autumn.
Is it better to revisit a place or travel somewhere new?

It depends on what you want. Somewhere new gives you {novelty and perspective|yangilik va yangi qarash}; returning gives you depth and comfort. Personally I would say new places are more valuable when you are young and have the energy for them, and revisiting becomes more appealing as {time becomes scarcer|vaqt tanqis boʻlgani sari} and you would rather not gamble on a disappointment.
Why do some people prefer travelling to familiar places?

Partly {risk aversion|xavfdan qochish} - an unfamiliar destination might not live up to expectations, whereas a known one will not disappoint. Language and cultural barriers also put people off. And for families with young children, the {practicalities|amaliy jihatlar} matter enormously; a known destination is simply far less exhausting to manage.
How can tourism affect popular places?

Economically it is usually positive - it funds restoration and creates work. But when numbers pass a certain point, the effects turn negative: housing is converted to short-term rentals, prices rise beyond what residents can afford, and the local character is gradually replaced by shops selling souvenirs. Several European cities are now actively trying to {cap|cheklamoq} visitor numbers, which would have been unthinkable a generation ago.

sessions.t2: A problem you helped someone with
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student at the moment, in my second year, so studying takes up {the bulk of|katta qismini} my time.
What do you study?
I study pharmacy, which is a five-year programme here. It is largely chemistry and biology in the early years, and becomes far more {clinical|klinik} later on.
Why did you choose this subject?

I was drawn to healthcare but did not want the {unpredictable hours|noaniq ish vaqti} of being a doctor. Pharmacy seemed like a good compromise - you are still directly helping people, but the work is more {structured|tartibli}, and there is a clear career path afterwards.
Do you like eating vegetables?

Yes, genuinely - I would happily eat a meal that was entirely vegetables. I did not as a child, but my taste {broadened|kengaydi} considerably once I started cooking for myself and discovered they are only unpleasant when badly prepared.
What vegetables do you usually eat?

Tomatoes and cucumbers almost daily, since they are in every salad here. Beyond that, carrots, onions and peppers, because they {form the base of|asosini tashkil qiladi} most of the dishes I cook. In winter the choice narrows considerably and we {fall back on|qaytamiz} pumpkin and cabbage.
Did you eat vegetables when you were a child?

Not willingly. My mother used to {hide them in|yashirardi} soups and stews, which worked until I was old enough to identify them. Looking back, I think the problem was that they were always boiled, which is probably the least appealing way to serve anything.
Do you think it is important to be polite?

Very much so. Politeness is what allows people who disagree, or who do not know each other, to interact without friction. It also costs nothing, which makes rudeness particularly {unjustifiable|oqlab boʻlmaydigan} in my view.
Who taught you to be polite?

My family, above all my grandfather, who was extremely {strict about|qat'iy edi} manners - greetings, giving up your seat, addressing older people properly. Much of it was taught by {example|namuna} rather than instruction, which I think is the only way it really works.
Are people in your country generally polite?

On the whole, yes, particularly in the sense of hospitality, which is taken very seriously here. Politeness towards {strangers|notanish odamlar} in public - in traffic, or queuing - is perhaps less consistent, and you notice the contrast between how warmly a guest is treated and how people behave on the road.

p2.task: Describe a problem you helped someone with.
bullets: and explain how you felt about helping them
p2.ans:
The occasion I want to describe is when I helped a neighbour of ours, a woman in her late sixties, sort out a problem with an online banking application about a year ago.

She had been persuaded by her son to start receiving her pension electronically, and the bank had installed an app on her phone. Within a few weeks she was completely {locked out of|kira olmaydigan} it - she had changed her password, forgotten the new one, and after several attempts the account had been {frozen|bloklangan} for security reasons. She had no idea what to do, and because her son lives abroad, she had nobody to ask. When she mentioned it to my mother she was clearly quite {distressed|xavotirda}, because she genuinely believed her money had disappeared.

What I did was fairly simple in technical terms, though it took most of an afternoon. I first checked the account status by calling the bank's helpline with her, since they would only speak to the account holder. We then went to the branch in person, because the reset had to be done with identification. Once it was working again, I spent about an hour {walking her through|bosqichma-bosqich tushuntirish} the app - how to check her balance, how to get back in if she forgot the password - and I wrote the steps out on paper in large handwriting, which she said was more useful than anything else.

How I felt about it is slightly complicated. It was satisfying, obviously, but what {stayed with me|esimda qoldi} was how unnecessary the whole problem had been. A system designed without older users in mind had made someone feel foolish about something that was not her fault.

It also made me realise that the most valuable help is often not {expertise|mutaxassislik} but simply time and patience - I did nothing she could not have done herself if someone had sat with her at the beginning.

p3: Why do people help others with their problems?

A mixture of motives. Genuine {empathy|hamdardlik} accounts for a great deal - most people find it uncomfortable to watch someone struggle. There is also {reciprocity|oʻzaro yordam}: helping builds relationships you may need later. And in societies like ours there is a strong cultural expectation, particularly towards neighbours and relatives, so helping is partly a {social obligation|ijtimoiy majburiyat}.
What kinds of problems do people usually ask others for help with?

Practical ones, mainly - moving house, fixing something, filling in official forms. Technology has become a very common one, particularly across generations. People are far more {reluctant to|istamaydi} ask for help with financial or emotional difficulties, because those feel like admissions of failure, even though they are the ones where help matters most.
Do young people help others more than older people?

They help differently rather than more. Young people are quicker to offer practical or technological help and have more {physical energy|jismoniy kuch} for it. Older people tend to help through advice, experience and, often, financially. If anything, older generations are more likely to help {as a matter of course|oddiy hol sifatida}, whereas young people wait to be asked.
Should people always help others when they have problems?

Not unconditionally. There are cases where helping {removes the incentive|rag'batni yoʻqotadi} for someone to solve a problem themselves, and repeatedly rescuing an adult from the consequences of their own decisions rarely helps them. I would also say people need to {set limits|chegara qoʻyish}, because someone who helps everyone at their own expense eventually has nothing left to give.
How can helping others benefit the person who provides the help?

There is solid evidence that helping improves the helper's own wellbeing - it is sometimes called the {helper's high|yordam berishdan kelgan quvonch}. It builds relationships and reputation, which has obvious practical value. And teaching or explaining something to someone else is one of the most effective ways to {consolidate|mustahkamlash} your own understanding of it.
Do you think people are becoming less willing to help each other nowadays?

In cities, possibly - {anonymity|anonimlik} reduces the sense of obligation, and people are genuinely busier. But I would not overstate it. What has changed is the form: help is now often organised through online fundraising or volunteering platforms rather than informal neighbourly assistance. So the {impulse|turtki} remains; it has simply been {channelled|yoʻnaltirilgan} differently.

sessions.t2: A time you saved money to buy something
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I study law, and I am currently in my third year, which is generally considered {the heaviest|eng ogʻiri} of the four.
What do you like about your studies?

The {rigour|qat'iylik} of it. Law forces you to be precise about language in a way no other subject does, and I enjoy the argumentative side - building a case and anticipating how it will be {challenged|e'tiroz bildirilishi}.
What do you dislike about your studies?

The {sheer volume|hajmining koʻpligi} of reading. There are weeks when you are expected to get through several hundred pages of cases, and a fair amount of it is repetitive. I also find the older legal language unnecessarily {impenetrable|tushunib boʻlmas}.
When do you usually get tired?

Mid-afternoon, particularly after a heavy lunch, and again late in the evening if I have been reading for several hours. Mental fatigue {creeps up on me|sezdirmay keladi} more gradually than physical tiredness, and often I only notice when I realise I have read the same paragraph three times.
Do you ever go out when you are tired if your friends invite you?

Usually yes, and I almost always feel better for it. A change of {setting|muhit} seems to be more restorative than lying down. The exception is if I have something important the next morning - then I will decline, though I admit I feel slightly {guilty|aybdor} about it.

p2.task: Describe a time when you saved some money to buy something.
bullets: how long you saved for it
and explain how you felt when you bought it

followUp.q: Did you tell anyone that you were saving money?
followUp.a: Only my sister, and that was mainly by accident - she noticed I had stopped going out and asked why. I deliberately did not tell my parents, because I was fairly sure they would have offered to {make up the difference|farqini toʻlash}, and the whole point for me was to do it without help. Looking back, keeping it to myself also meant there was nobody to {let down|umidini puchga chiqarish} if I failed, which made it less stressful.

p2.ans:
The thing I saved for was a laptop, about three years ago, when I was starting university and my old one had reached the point where it {took ten minutes to start up|ishga tushishiga oʻn daqiqa ketardi}.

The model I wanted cost the equivalent of roughly four months of what I was earning, and I was determined to buy it without asking my parents, partly out of {pride|gʻurur} and partly because they were already covering my tuition.

It took me about five months in the end. I was working part-time at a language centre, teaching two evenings a week and on Saturdays, and I decided to {set aside|ajratib qoʻymoq} everything from the Saturday shifts and live on the rest. To make that work I had to be quite {disciplined|intizomli}: I stopped eating out, which was where most of my money had been {quietly disappearing|bilinmay ketardi}, and I started taking the bus rather than a taxi. I also kept a note of every expense in my phone for the first month, which was genuinely {eye-opening|koʻzni ochadigan} - I had no idea how much small purchases were adding up to.

There were two points where I nearly {gave in|taslim boʻldim}. Once there was a sale and I came very close to buying a cheaper model, and once my phone broke and I had to {dip into|olib ishlatmoq} the savings, which set me back three weeks.

When I finally bought it, the feeling was not quite what I expected. There was satisfaction, obviously, but it was much more about the saving than the laptop. I had proved to myself that I could {see something through|boshlagan ishni oxiriga yetkazish} over months rather than days, and honestly, that turned out to be worth more than the machine. I have been much more careful with money ever since.

p3: What do people usually save money for?

The largest categories are housing and education, which for most families are the two big {life goals|hayotiy maqsadlar}. Beyond those, weddings - which here can be extremely expensive - cars, and travel. A smaller number save without a specific target, simply as a {safety net|xavfsizlik yostigʻi}, and I would argue that is the most sensible form of saving.
What do you think people should save money for?

An emergency fund, before anything else. Most financial difficulty comes not from bad planning but from an {unexpected shock|kutilmagan zarba} - illness, job loss, a major repair - and having a few months of expenses set aside prevents a problem from becoming a crisis. After that, I would prioritise education, since it {pays for itself|oʻzini oqlaydi} over a lifetime, over consumer goods that {depreciate|qadrsizlanadi} immediately.
Do more people save money for gadgets nowadays?

Certainly among young people. Phones and laptops have become {status symbols|maqom belgisi} as much as tools, and there is considerable social pressure to have a current model. I would add that instalment plans and credit have changed the picture - many people no longer save for gadgets at all, they simply buy now and pay later, which is {a different habit entirely|butunlay boshqa odat}.
Should children be taught about money at school?

Definitely, and I find it strange that it is not universal. Children will all handle money for the rest of their lives, yet the subject is left {entirely to chance|butunlay tasodifga} and to what their parents happen to know. Basic financial literacy - budgeting, how interest works, the real cost of borrowing - would prevent a great many of the problems adults {run into|duch keladi}.
How can schools teach children about money?

Practically rather than theoretically. Running a small school enterprise, managing a class budget for a trip, or simulating a monthly household budget teaches far more than a lecture. For older students, teaching how {compound interest|murakkab foiz} works on both savings and debt is probably the single most valuable lesson, because it is genuinely {counter-intuitive|kutilganidan boshqacha}.
Do children know more about money now compared to previous generations?

They are more {exposed to|duch keladi} it - they see prices online and many have digital payment access from an early age. But exposure is not understanding, and I would argue they may understand it less well, because money has become {abstract|mavhum}. A child who never sees cash has no physical sense of a sum being spent, and that arguably makes restraint harder rather than easier.

sessions.t2: An interesting video you watched
p1: What kinds of websites do you usually visit?

Mostly a small number that I use repeatedly - news sites, one or two academic databases for my coursework, and video platforms. I also spend more time than I should on forums, where people discuss things {in depth|chuqur} rather than in short posts.
What are the most popular websites in your country?

Social media and messaging platforms dominate, Telegram above all - it is used here for almost everything, including news and shopping. Beyond that, video platforms and local {classified advertising|e'lonlar} sites where people buy and sell.
Did the website you visited change since you last went on it?

Yes, one of the news sites I use {redesigned|qayta ishladi} its layout a few months ago. The look is more modern, but they have {buried|koʻmib tashlagan} the search function, which is what I actually used most. It is a common pattern - redesigns often prioritise appearance over {usability|qulaylik}.
Have there been any changes to the websites you often visit?

Constantly, though most are {incremental|bosqichma-bosqich} and you barely notice. The most obvious trend is that sites have become far more aggressive about {pop-ups|qalqib chiquvchi oynalar} and subscription prompts, and a lot of content that was once free now sits behind a {paywall|toʻlov devori}.
Do you live in a noisy or a quiet area?

Fairly quiet, fortunately. We are a few streets back from the main road, so traffic noise is {muffled|boʻgʻiq}. The main disturbance is construction, which in recent years has become {a fact of life|hayotning bir qismi} in almost every neighbourhood here.
Is the area where you live crowded with people and cars?

During the day it is busy, particularly near the school, and parking has become a genuine problem because car ownership has risen much faster than the streets were designed for. In the evening it {quietens down|jimib qoladi} considerably.
Do you know any of your neighbours?

Yes, most of them - we live in a mahalla, and that system means neighbours are involved in each other's lives to a degree that people from other countries find {surprising|hayratlanarli}. Everyone contributes to weddings and funerals, so you inevitably know each other well.
Do you often talk with your neighbours?

Regularly, though usually briefly - greetings in the street, a short conversation about something practical. Proper conversations tend to happen at {communal events|jamoaviy tadbirlar}. I would say we are on good terms without being close friends, which is probably the {ideal arrangement|eng maqbul holat}.

p2.task: Describe an interesting video you watched.
bullets: what kind of video it was
and explain why it was interesting to you
p2.ans:
The video I would like to describe is a short documentary about how traditional silk paper is still made by hand in Samarkand, which I came across on a travel channel on YouTube about six months ago.

I found it more or less {by accident|tasodifan}. I had been searching for something completely unrelated and it appeared in the sidebar; the thumbnail showed a man beating mulberry bark with a wooden mallet, which was unusual enough to make me click on it.

The video followed the entire process from beginning to end. It began with cutting branches from mulberry trees, then showed the bark being {stripped|shilingan}, boiled for hours, and pounded until the fibres {separated|ajraladi}. The pulp was then spread on a mesh frame, dried, and finally {polished|silliqlangan} with a smooth stone until the surface became almost glossy. The whole thing takes several days and is done entirely by hand, using a technique that had essentially {died out|yoʻqolib ketgan} and was revived about thirty years ago by one family working from historical descriptions.

What I found interesting was partly the craft itself, which is {extraordinarily labour-intensive|nihoyatda mehnat talab qiladigan}. But more than that, it was the historical point the film made almost in passing: that Samarkand was one of the first places outside China where paper was produced, and that this technology spread westwards from there. I had learned that fact at school as a single sentence, and seeing it {brought to life|jonlantirilgan} as an actual physical process made it real in a way a textbook never had.

I also liked that the video did not {romanticise|romantiklashtirmoq} it. The craftsman was quite open about the fact that it is barely commercially viable and that his children are unlikely to continue it, which gave the whole thing a slightly {melancholy|gʻamgin} quality that I thought was honest.

p3: Do you think videos can teach people new things effectively?

Very effectively for certain kinds of learning. Anything involving a visible process - a technique, a repair, an experiment - is far better shown than described, and video allows you to {pause and repeat|toʻxtatib, qayta koʻrish} at your own pace. Where video is weaker is with abstract material that requires you to work through problems yourself, because watching is {inherently passive|tabiatan passiv}.
Can people learn all skills just by watching videos?

No, and I think this is a common {misconception|notoʻgʻri tasavvur}. Video can convey knowledge but not judgement, and it cannot give you {feedback|fikr-mulohaza}. You can watch a hundred videos on swimming and still drown, because the skill lives in the body rather than in the information. Anything requiring physical practice or professional responsibility needs supervised practice as well.
Should governments regulate video content online?

To some extent, yes - there is a clear case for regulating content involving children, incitement to violence and deliberate {disinformation|dezinformatsiya}, particularly on health. The difficulty is that regulation easily {slides into|oʻtib ketadi} censorship, and governments are not neutral parties when the content concerns them. My preference would be for enforced transparency about how content is promoted, rather than direct control over what may be said.
What can people learn from videos, and what can they not?

Videos are excellent for {procedural knowledge|amaliy bilim} - how something is done - and for exposure to ideas and places you would otherwise never encounter. What they cannot provide is the {sustained struggle|uzoq mashaqqat} that genuine expertise requires: practice, correction, and the experience of getting things wrong. They also cannot teach the {tacit|aytilmagan} parts of a skill, the judgements that experienced people make without being able to explain them.

sessions.examiner: British older man, very friendly and funny
sessions.t2: A time you went to a noisy place
p1: Are you working or are you a student?
I am a student. I study engineering, and I am {midway through|oʻrtasidaman} the course, so I have another two years to go.
What do you like or find interesting about your studies?

What I find most interesting is that engineering is about working {within constraints|cheklovlar doirasida} - cost, materials, time. There is never a perfect solution, only the best available one, and I find that far more interesting than problems with a single correct answer.
Do you like buying shoes?

Not especially. I find it one of the more {frustrating|asabbuzar} things to shop for, because sizing varies so much between brands that you cannot rely on your usual size. When I find a pair that fits well I tend to {stick with|sodiq qolmoq} that brand for years.
Have you ever bought shoes online?

I have, twice, and one of those was a mistake - they were a full size too small and returning them was {more trouble than it was worth|arzimasdi}. Now I only buy online if it is an exact repeat of something I already own.
Which do you prefer, fashionable shoes or comfortable shoes?

Comfort, without any real hesitation. I walk a great deal, and badly designed shoes will ruin your day. Ideally you find something that manages both, but if I have to {compromise|murosa qilmoq}, it will not be on comfort.
How much money do you usually spend on shoes?

More than I used to, because I have {come round to|shu fikrga kelganman} the idea that cheap shoes are a false economy - they wear out in months. I would rather buy one decent pair a year than three cheap pairs, which works out {much the same|deyarli bir xil} in cost but is far better for your feet.
What is your favourite type of shoes?

Plain leather trainers, the kind that are casual enough for everyday but smart enough that you can wear them somewhere formal at a push. They are {versatile|koʻp maqsadli}, which for someone who owns three pairs of shoes in total is the main consideration.

p2.task: Describe a time you went to a noisy place.
bullets: and explain how you felt about the noise
p2.ans:
The noisiest place I have been to recently was a football match at the national stadium in Tashkent, which I went to with three friends about a year ago.

It was a World Cup qualifier, so the ground was completely full - around thirty-five thousand people - and the atmosphere was quite unlike anything I had experienced before. We were sitting fairly close to the section behind the goal where the organised supporters stand, which turned out to be a {mixed blessing|ham yaxshi, ham yomon}.

The noise was more or less constant for the whole ninety minutes. There was drumming, chanting and, whenever anything happened, a {roar|gulduros} that you felt physically rather than simply heard. At one point the home side scored, and the sound was genuinely {deafening|quloqni qomatga keltiradigan} - I remember it being difficult to think clearly for several seconds afterwards. We could not hear each other speak at all; the entire conversation between us for an hour and a half was conducted through {gestures|imo-ishoralar}.

What was interesting was how my reaction changed. For the first ten minutes I found it genuinely {overwhelming|bosim oʻtkazadigan} and slightly unpleasant, and I remember thinking I should have brought earplugs. But after a while I {got caught up in|berilib ketdim} it, and by the second half I was joining in with the chanting, which is not something I would ever have predicted about myself.

Afterwards my ears were {ringing|jiringlardi} for about an hour, and my voice had gone entirely, which I suppose was the price of admission. But I would go again without hesitation. I think it made me realise that noise is not a single thing - the same volume that is intolerable in a traffic jam becomes {exhilarating|ruhlantiruvchi} when it is shared and when everyone there has chosen to be part of it.

p3: Do you think people like noisy places?

Some do, in specific contexts. Noise that comes from a crowd - a stadium, a concert, a bazaar - creates a {sense of shared energy|umumiy ruh} that people actively seek out. What almost nobody enjoys is {involuntary|majburiy} noise, such as traffic or construction, where you have no connection to the source and no ability to leave.
Why do some people like to meet in places with loud music?

Partly because loud music {lowers inhibitions|tortinchoqlikni kamaytiradi} - conversation becomes less important, which suits people who find small talk difficult. It also creates a shared mood very quickly. And there is a practical element: in a loud venue you have to lean in to speak, which paradoxically makes interactions feel more {intimate|yaqin}.
What kinds of noises are there in our life?

I would divide them into three: natural sounds such as wind and rain, which most people find pleasant or neutral; mechanical noise - traffic, machinery, construction - which is the main source of complaint; and human noise, from conversation to music. The crucial difference is whether it is {predictable and controllable|oldindan bilinadigan va boshqariladigan}, because unpredictable noise is far more stressful.
Which area is exposed to more noise, the city or the countryside?

Cities, overwhelmingly, because of {traffic density|transport zichligi}, construction and the sheer concentration of people. Rural areas are not silent - agricultural machinery can be extremely loud - but the noise is intermittent and seasonal. The key difference is that city noise is {round the clock|kechayu kunduz}, which is why urban residents report far more sleep disturbance.
How would people usually respond to noises in your country?

There is a fairly high {tolerance|bardosh} for noise in general, particularly for celebrations - a wedding with loud music until midnight would rarely be complained about, because it is understood that everyone's turn comes. People are far less tolerant of construction noise, and complaints about it have become more common as building has {intensified|kuchaygan} in residential districts.
On what occasions do people need to be quiet?

In places of worship, at funerals, in libraries and examination halls, and in hospitals - situations where silence signals {respect or concentration|hurmat yoki diqqat}. There are also less formal expectations, such as on public transport late at night. In general, quiet is expected wherever noise would {intrude on|xalaqit bermoq} someone else's grief, rest or thought.

sessions.t2: A special day out that cost little money
p1: Do you live in a flat or a house?

I live in a flat, in a nine-storey building in a residential district of Tashkent. It is on the fourth floor, which I consider {the ideal compromise|eng maqbul yechim} - high enough to be quiet, low enough that the stairs are not a punishment when the lift breaks.
How long have you lived there?
Just over eight years. We moved there when I was fourteen, and although I complained about leaving my old neighbourhood at the time, I {grew to like|yoqtirib qoldim} it fairly quickly.
What do you like most about your flat?

How much light it gets. The main rooms face east, so mornings are extremely bright, which makes a small space feel far larger. I also appreciate that it is {well insulated|yaxshi isitilgan} - the winters here can be harsh and our heating bills are noticeably lower than my friends'.
Is there anything you don't like about your apartment?

The sound insulation is poor, so you hear the neighbours above rather more than you would like. And storage is {in short supply|yetishmaydi} - there is only one built-in cupboard for the whole flat, so we have had to be quite {inventive|ixtirochi} about where things go.
Which room do you like the most?

The living room, because it is where the family actually spends time together. It is the largest room and it also {doubles as|ikkinchi vazifasi} a guest room when relatives stay, which happens fairly often.
Would you like to move to another home in the future?

At some point, yes. I would like a place of my own once I am working, ideally with an extra room I could use as a study. I am {in no great rush|shoshilmayapman}, though - the flat is convenient and rents in Tashkent are high.
What kind of home would you like to live in?

Ideally a house with a small courtyard, in the traditional style, but somewhere close enough to the centre that I would not spend two hours a day commuting. That combination is {hard to come by|topish qiyin}, so I may have to {settle for|rozi boʻlmoq} a flat with a decent balcony.
Do you think it's better to live in a flat or a house?

It depends entirely on the stage of life. Flats are cheaper, more secure and much {less demanding|kamroq talab qiladi} in terms of maintenance, which suits young people and older people. A house makes far more sense for a family with children, because of the space and the outdoor area, but it comes with {considerable upkeep|katta parvarish}.

p2.task: Describe a special day out that cost you little money.
bullets: and explain why it was so special despite costing little
p2.ans:
The day I would like to describe was a walking trip through the old part of Tashkent that I did with two friends last spring, and which cost the three of us almost nothing.

The idea came about because we had been complaining that we never actually looked at our own city. One of my friends suggested that instead of going somewhere expensive, we should spend a Saturday walking from one end of the old town to the other with no fixed plan. We spent, between us, the price of three bus tickets and a large amount of bread and samsa from a bakery, so the entire day came to a {trivial amount|arzimas miqdor}.

We started at Chorsu bazaar early in the morning, when it is at its busiest and the traders are {calling out|chaqirib turishadi} over each other. From there we walked through the residential streets behind it, which almost no visitors see - narrow lanes with old wooden doors, where you can hear families through the walls. We ended up at a madrasa where a man showed us around for twenty minutes simply because we had asked a question, and later we sat on a wall eating lunch and watched a group of children playing football in an alley for the better part of an hour.

What made it special was precisely that nothing had been {organised or paid for|tashkil qilingan yoki toʻlangan}. There was no schedule, so the day could {unfold on its own|oʻz-oʻzidan kechdi}, and because we were not trying to get value out of an expensive ticket, we were not in a hurry. We talked for eight hours, which almost never happens otherwise.

It taught me something I keep {coming back to|qaytib kelaman}: the cost of a day and how memorable it is have almost no {correlation|bogʻliqlik}. Some of the most expensive days I have had have been forgettable, and that one, which cost nothing, I still describe to people two years later.

p3: What do people usually do in their leisure time?

It splits between {passive and active|passiv va faol} pursuits. The passive - watching, scrolling, listening - takes up the majority of most people's free hours, simply because it requires no planning. Active leisure covers sport, hobbies and socialising. Here, visiting relatives is a very significant category, far more so than in many countries.
How have advancements in technology affected people's leisure time?

It has made leisure {abundant and instant|behisob va bir zumda} - entertainment is permanently available, which was never true before. But it has also {blurred|xiralashtirgan} the line between leisure and work, since people check messages at all hours. And it has made leisure more solitary; activities that once required leaving the house and being with others can now be done alone on a screen.
Do you think people have more free time now than in the past?

Statistically, yes - working hours have fallen considerably over the last century and domestic appliances removed an enormous amount of housework. But people do not {feel|his qilish} they have more, because free time has become {fragmented|boʻlak-boʻlak} into small pieces between commitments. An hour broken into ten-minute gaps is far less useful than an uninterrupted hour.
Do older people also spend their leisure time actively?

Increasingly so. The stereotype of retirement as {sedentary|harakatsiz} is outdated - older people today are healthier and more likely to travel, exercise and study. Here in particular, older people are highly involved in community and family events, so their time is often {far from idle|umuman boʻsh emas}. What does change is intensity rather than activity.
What activities are popular among older people?

Walking, gardening and social gatherings, above all. Many take up hobbies they had no time for earlier - reading, crafts, occasionally learning a language. There is also a strong tradition here of older people spending time with grandchildren, which is both a {pleasure and a responsibility|zavq ham, mas'uliyat ham}.
Why do some people prefer spending their leisure time alone?

Because for many people, particularly those whose work involves constant interaction, solitude is genuinely {restorative|tiklovchi}. Being alone also removes the need to {accommodate|moslashish} anyone else's preferences, so you can do exactly what you want. And certain rewarding activities - reading, writing, making things - simply require uninterrupted concentration.
Do you think people will have more or less leisure time in the future?

My guess is more in theory and less in practice. Automation should reduce necessary working hours, and there is growing interest in shorter working weeks. But historically every {efficiency gain|samaradorlik oshishi} has been absorbed by rising expectations rather than converted into free time. Unless attitudes change, I suspect people will continue to feel {pressed for time|vaqt tanqisligida} regardless of the statistics.

sessions.t2: A journey that you did not enjoy
p1: What is your favourite colour?
Dark green, I would say. I find it {restful|tinchlantiruvchi} on the eye, and it works well in almost any setting without being {attention-seeking|e'tibor tortadigan} the way brighter colours are.
What do you like about your home?

Mainly the atmosphere rather than anything physical. It is {modestly furnished|oddiy jihozlangan}, but it is always full of people, and I think a home is defined by that far more than by how it looks.
What is your home like?

It is a single-storey house with four rooms arranged around a small courtyard, which is the traditional layout here. The courtyard has a grapevine over it, so in summer it stays {shaded|soyali} and is where we eat most meals.
What do you like most about your home?

The courtyard, without question. It effectively doubles the living space for half the year, and there is something very pleasant about eating outdoors without actually {leaving the house|uydan chiqmasdan}.
Is there anything you would like to change about your home?

The insulation, honestly. The house is old and the winters are {bitterly cold|qattiq sovuq} here, so heating it properly is expensive. I would also replace the windows, which are original and {let in a considerable draught|ancha shamol oʻtkazadi}.
Would you like to move to a different home in the future?

Not really, if I am honest. I would rather {renovate|ta'mirlash} this one than move, because it has been in the family for a long time and I am quite {attached to|bogʻlanib qolgan} it. If work took me elsewhere I would move, but it would not be by choice.

p2.task: Describe a journey that you did not enjoy.
bullets: and explain why you did not enjoy it
p2.ans:
The journey I want to describe was a trip from Bukhara to Tashkent about three years ago, which should have taken around six hours by road and which took just under twelve.

I was travelling for a university interview, so the timing genuinely mattered, and I had booked a seat on a minibus that was due to leave at six in the morning. It left at half past seven, because the driver was waiting for two more passengers, which was my first indication of how the day would go.

Things then {went from bad to worse|battar boʻldi}. About two hours out of the city the vehicle developed a fault with the cooling system, and we stopped at a roadside garage where the driver and a mechanic spent nearly three hours on it. There was nowhere to sit and it was well over forty degrees, so the twelve of us stood in whatever shade we could find. When we finally set off again, we hit a long {tailback|tirbandlik} caused by roadworks and lost another hour and a half.

I did not enjoy it for reasons that went beyond simple discomfort, although sitting in a hot minibus for twelve hours is unpleasant enough. The real problem was the {uncertainty|noaniqlik}: nobody could tell us how long the repair would take, so we could not decide whether to wait or find another vehicle. I also had no way of knowing whether I would arrive in time for the following morning, and that {gnawed at me|meni yeb qoʻydi} the entire day.

I arrived at around half past nine at night, exhausted and {utterly drained|butunlay holdan toygan}. In fairness, the interview went perfectly well the next day, so nothing was actually lost. But it taught me a lesson I have {taken to heart|jiddiy qabul qilganman} since: for anything that genuinely matters, travel the day before and pay for the reliable option.

p3: Why do people travel abroad or go on long-distance journeys?

For work, study, family and tourism, primarily. Long-distance travel for leisure is really about {novelty|yangilik} - seeing how differently other people live. There is also a substantial amount of travel driven by {necessity|zarurat} rather than choice: medical treatment, business, or visiting relatives who have emigrated.
Why do some people choose to work abroad?

Wages, most obviously - the same work can pay several times more elsewhere, which for many families is {transformative|hayotni oʻzgartiradigan}. Beyond money, people go for career opportunities that do not exist at home, better professional standards, and sometimes simply for the experience. For a significant number it is a {means to an end|maqsadga erishish vositasi}: they intend to earn, save and return.
What are the main reasons people travel to other countries?

Tourism and visiting family account for the majority. Business travel is significant, though it has fallen since remote meetings became normal. Education is another major reason, particularly among young people, and there is also growing {medical tourism|tibbiy turizm}, where people travel specifically for treatment that is cheaper or unavailable at home.
How often do people usually go on holiday?

It varies enormously by income. In wealthier countries, once or twice a year is typical. Here, a proper holiday away from home is less frequent - perhaps once a year or less - and a great deal of leisure time is spent visiting relatives instead, which serves a similar purpose at {a fraction of the cost|arzimagan xarajatda}.
Why do people need to go on holiday?

Because sustained work without a break {takes a measurable toll|sezilarli ta'sir qiladi} on health and performance. A holiday provides psychological distance, which is what actually allows recovery - simply not working while remaining at home rarely achieves it. Holidays also matter for relationships, since they provide uninterrupted time that ordinary weeks never do.
Do you think people travel more often nowadays than in the past?

Considerably more. Transport is faster and cheaper in real terms, visa rules have been {relaxed|yumshatilgan} in many regions, and booking takes minutes. Rising incomes in large developing countries have added enormous numbers of new travellers. The only real {check on|toʻsiq} this trend is environmental pressure, which has not yet affected behaviour much.
What are the benefits of travelling long distances?

The obvious one is exposure to different ways of doing things, which tends to make people less {dogmatic|qat'iy fikrli}. Long journeys also build practical independence - you learn to handle problems without a familiar support network. And there is value in the journey itself; long travel provides uninterrupted thinking time, which is increasingly {scarce|kam uchraydigan}.
What problems can people face when travelling abroad?

Language barriers and unfamiliar bureaucracy are the most common. Beyond that: health problems where you do not know the system, the risk of {being taken advantage of|aldanish} because you do not know local prices, and {culture shock|madaniy zarba}, which people underestimate. Practical difficulties such as lost documents or delayed transport are far more stressful abroad than at home.

sessions.t2: A special evening event you spent with friends
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I study journalism, which I chose partly because I like writing and partly because it is one of the few degrees where you are constantly {out of the classroom|sinfdan tashqarida}.
What do you like about your studies?

The practical assignments, mainly. We are expected to go out and actually interview people, which is {daunting at first|dastlab qoʻrqinchli} but has improved my confidence enormously. I also enjoy how {topical|dolzarb} it is - the material changes with the news.
Is there anything you dislike about your studies?

Some of the theory modules feel rather {dated|eskirgan}. We spend time on models of media that were developed before the internet, and the reality of how news actually {circulates|tarqaladi} now is quite different.
Do you enjoy listening to music?

Very much - it is more or less the {soundtrack to|ohangi} my day. I listen while commuting, studying and cooking, and I would find long periods of silence quite strange, which is probably a habit rather than a preference.
What kind of music do you usually listen to?

My taste is fairly {eclectic|rang-barang}. Mostly I listen to instrumental music when I am working, because lyrics are {distracting|chalgʻituvchi}, and more traditional Uzbek music at home. I also go through phases of listening to one artist {obsessively|qattiq berilib} for a month and then never again.
Do you ever listen to music with your friends?

Yes, usually in the car or when a few of us are cooking together. It becomes a sort of negotiation, since everyone wants to {take a turn|navbat olish}. I find it interesting how much you learn about people from what they play when they are given control.
Do you like buying shoes?

Not particularly. I see it as a {practical necessity|amaliy zarurat} rather than an enjoyable activity. Finding a pair that fits properly takes a long time, so once I do, I tend to buy the same thing repeatedly.
How often do you buy shoes?
Perhaps twice a year, and usually because something has {worn through|teshilib ketgan} rather than because I want a new pair. I would rather spend on one good pair than several cheap ones.
What kind of shoes do you usually wear?

Trainers, almost exclusively, because I walk a lot and comfort {trumps|ustun keladi} everything else for me. I do own one pair of formal shoes, which come out for weddings and interviews and spend the rest of the year in a box.
Do you prefer casual shoes or fashionable shoes?

Casual, without hesitation. I am not indifferent to how things look, but I would not tolerate {discomfort|noqulaylik} for the sake of appearance. The ideal is something plain enough to be {smart|chiroyli} and comfortable enough to walk in all day.

p2.task: Describe a special evening event which you spent with your friends.
bullets: where and when it took place
and explain why it was special to you
p2.ans:
The evening I want to describe was a farewell dinner we organised for one of our closest friends about eighteen months ago, the night before he left to study abroad.

There were seven of us, and we had known each other since school, so this was the first time any of the group had properly {left for good|butunlay ketmoq}. We booked a long table at a restaurant in the centre of Samarkand with a terrace, and we arrived at around seven expecting to stay for two or three hours. We were still there at one in the morning, by which point the staff were {stacking chairs around us|atrofimizda stullarni yigʻishardi} with impressive patience.

The evening itself was not elaborate. We ate, we told the same stories we have told a hundred times, and somebody had put together a collection of old photographs on a phone, which caused a great deal of laughter and a certain amount of {embarrassment|xijolat}. Towards the end of the night the tone shifted and people became unusually {candid|samimiy} - there were a few short speeches that nobody had planned, and one of them was genuinely moving.

What made it special was the awareness, which everybody had and nobody mentioned directly, that this particular group would probably never be {in one room again|bir xonada}. That gave the whole evening a quality it would not otherwise have had. Ordinary gatherings are pleasant and forgettable; this one was {charged|toʻyingan} with something else.

Looking back, I think it was the first time I really understood that friendships have {a shape|shakli bor} - that they belong to a period of life rather than continuing unchanged forever. We are all still in touch, but it is not the same, and I am glad we {marked the moment|lahzani nishonladik} properly rather than letting him leave with a message.

p3: Why do people need friends?

Because humans are fundamentally {social|ijtimoiy} creatures, and isolation has measurable effects on both mental and physical health. Friends provide emotional support, but also perspective - they will tell you things family often will not. And practically, friendships are how most people find work, information and opportunities, which is easy to overlook.
What makes someone a good friend?

Reliability first: doing what you said you would do. Beyond that, honesty, including when it is {unwelcome|yoqimsiz}, and discretion - keeping what is told to you. I would also say a good friend is genuinely pleased at your success rather than {quietly competitive|jimgina raqobatlashadigan}, which is much rarer than people assume.
Do you think it is easier to make friends when you are young?

Considerably easier. Children and students share {enforced proximity|majburiy yaqinlik} - the same classroom every day - and repeated contact is what friendships actually grow from. Adults have to create those conditions deliberately, and they have less time and more {caution|ehtiyotkorlik}. Friendships made young also benefit from being formed before people become guarded.
How have friendships changed because of technology?

Maintaining contact has become almost effortless, which means friendships now survive distance in a way they never used to. The {downside|salbiy tomoni} is that the ease of messaging can substitute for real contact, so people feel connected without actually spending time together. Technology has also {widened|kengaytirgan} friendship circles while arguably making each individual friendship shallower.
Is it better to have a few close friends or many friends?

A few close ones, in my view, though ideally you would have both. Close friendships are what actually provide support, and there is a natural {limit|chegara} to how many relationships anyone can genuinely maintain. A wide network has real practical value, but it should not be {confused with|chalkashtirmaslik kerak} friendship.
Why do some friendships last for many years while others end quickly?

The ones that last usually rest on shared values rather than shared circumstances. A friendship formed purely because you worked together tends to {dissolve|tarqab ketadi} when the circumstance does. Longevity also requires effort from both sides, and {tolerance|bagʻrikenglik} - people change, and a friendship survives only if both are willing to accommodate who the other has become.
Do you think people spend enough time with their friends nowadays?

Generally not. Work has expanded, commutes are longer and a great deal of leisure is spent on screens, so friendship tends to be the thing that {gets squeezed out|siqib chiqariladi} when time is short. The irony is that it is one of the strongest predictors of wellbeing, so it is precisely the wrong thing to {deprioritise|ikkinchi oʻringa qoʻymoq}.

sessions.t2: A tall building that you like or dislike
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student. I study architecture, which I am {two years into|ikki yildan beri oʻqiyman} and thoroughly enjoying, despite the workload.
What do you study?
Architecture - it combines design, structural engineering and history, so a typical week might include drawing, a physics-heavy lecture and an essay on twentieth-century urbanism.
What do you like most about your studies?

The studio culture. You work alongside your classmates for hours at a time, and you {learn as much from|shuncha oʻrganasiz} seeing how they solve a problem as from the tutors. I also like that the work is {tangible|koʻrinadigan} - at the end of a project there is something you can point at.
Is there anything you dislike about your studies?

The hours, mainly. Deadlines involve {all-night sessions|tunni bedor oʻtkazish} that I do not think are actually necessary - it is more a culture than a requirement. I also find the criticism sessions difficult, though I accept they are useful.
Do you live in a tall building?

Not particularly tall - I live on the third floor of a five-storey block. By the standards of most cities that is {nothing to speak of|arzimaydigan}, but in Termiz most housing is low-rise, so it is above average for here.
Do you like tall buildings?

I have {mixed feelings|ikki xil qarash}. As an architecture student I find them technically fascinating, and I think a well-designed tower can be genuinely beautiful. As a resident, I am less enthusiastic - they often create windy, {shaded|soyalangan} streets at ground level and can feel quite impersonal.

p2.task: Describe a tall building that you like or dislike.
bullets: and explain why you like or dislike it
p2.ans:
The building I would like to describe is the Tashkent Television Tower, which I like, and which I have visited twice.

It stands in the north of the capital and is around three hundred and seventy metres tall, which makes it easily the most visible structure in the city - you can see it from most districts. It was completed in the early 1980s, and it looks very much of its period: a slender concrete shaft rising out of three curved supporting legs, with an observation deck near the top that flares outwards and, higher still, a long {antenna mast|antenna ustuni}. The concrete is a pale grey and there is a decorative metal lattice around the base which, from a distance, gives it a slightly {ornamental|bezakli} quality that most towers of that era lack.

Functionally it is a broadcasting tower, so most of its height is purely technical. The part that the public uses is the observation deck and a rotating restaurant, which completes a full turn roughly every hour, so you see the entire city over a meal.

The reason I like it is partly personal and partly professional. Personally, it was the first tall building I ever went up, when I was about ten, and I remember being astonished that the city was so much larger than I had assumed. Professionally, I admire it because the engineering is genuinely impressive - it was built to {withstand|bardosh bermoq} a serious earthquake, which in this region is not a {theoretical concern|nazariy masala}, and the three-legged base is a direct response to that.

What I like most, though, is that it has become a {landmark|belgi, moʻljal} in the proper sense. People give directions by it and it appears in photographs of the city. A building that ordinary people use to {orient themselves|moʻljal olish} has earned its place, whatever anyone thinks of the style.

p3: Why do some people prefer living in tall buildings?

The views are the obvious attraction, along with better light and noticeably less street noise on the upper floors. Tall buildings also tend to be {centrally located|markazda joylashgan}, so residents are close to work and services. And modern towers often include facilities - parking, security, gyms - that are {impractical|amalga oshirib boʻlmaydigan} in low-rise housing.
What are the advantages of living in a high-rise building?

Beyond views and quiet, there is {security|xavfsizlik}, since access is controlled, and lower maintenance, because the building management handles the structure. From a city's perspective the benefit is {density|zichlik}: housing more people on less land reduces urban sprawl and makes public transport and services economically viable.
What are some disadvantages of living in tall buildings?

Dependence on lifts is the practical one - a breakdown is genuinely serious for anyone on the twentieth floor. There are also {evacuation|evakuatsiya} concerns in a fire or earthquake. Socially, high-rises can be {isolating|yolgʻizlantiradigan}: residents rarely know their neighbours, and there is no equivalent of the courtyard where people naturally meet. Families with small children also lose the convenience of a garden.
Why are more tall buildings being built in cities nowadays?

Principally because {land is scarce and expensive|yer tanqis va qimmat} in city centres, so building upwards is the only way to add housing without expanding outwards. Population growth and urbanisation drive the demand. There is also an element of {prestige|nufuz} - cities and developers use towers as symbols of modernity, which is not always a good reason.
Do you think cities should have more high-rise buildings or more low-rise buildings?

I would argue for a {mixture|aralash}, with density concentrated near transport hubs and lower-rise housing elsewhere. Cities that are entirely high-rise tend to feel inhuman at street level, whereas cities that refuse to build upwards {sprawl|yoyilib ketadi} outwards and become car-dependent. The middle option - medium-density blocks of five to eight storeys - is often the most liveable, and it is frequently overlooked.
What problems can tall buildings cause in crowded cities?

They {overshadow|soya tashlaydi} neighbouring streets and can create severe wind at ground level. They concentrate traffic at a single point, which local roads are often not designed for. And they put enormous pressure on {infrastructure|infratuzilma} - water, power, sewerage - which is rarely upgraded at the same rate. There is also the question of who they are built for, since towers frequently serve investors rather than residents.
Do you think tall buildings will become more common in the future?

Almost certainly, as urban populations continue to grow and land becomes more valuable. Construction technology has also advanced - {timber|yogʻoch} high-rises are now viable, which may reduce the environmental cost considerably. I would expect the emphasis to shift towards {mixed-use|aralash maqsadli} towers containing homes, offices and shops, since single-purpose buildings leave districts empty for half the day.

sessions.t2: A live sports event that you watched
p1: What clothes do you like to wear?

Fairly plain things - jeans, a shirt, a jumper in winter. I prefer {neutral colours|betaraf ranglar} and simple cuts, partly because they are easy to combine and partly because I have no real interest in following trends.
Do you prefer wearing comfortable clothes or fashionable clothes?

Comfort, though I do not think the two are {mutually exclusive|bir-birini istisno qiladigan}. I would simply rather not spend a whole day {conscious of|his qilib turish} what I am wearing. If something looks good and feels good, so much the better.
Which colour don't you like to wear?

Bright yellow or orange. They do not suit me at all and they {draw attention|e'tibor tortadi} in a way I find uncomfortable. I have nothing against them on other people - it is purely that they look wrong on me.
Do you know a lot of people in your hometown?

A fair number, yes. Bukhara is not a large city and my family has been there for generations, so you constantly {run into|duch kelasiz} people you know, or people who know your relatives, which is either pleasant or inconvenient depending on the day.
How well do you know the people who live around you?

Quite well. We live in a mahalla, where neighbours are involved in each other's lives to a degree that outsiders find {striking|hayratlanarli} - everyone contributes to weddings and funerals, so there is a real sense of {mutual obligation|oʻzaro majburiyat}.
Do you often talk to people in your neighbourhood?

Most days, though usually briefly - greetings, a short exchange about something practical. Longer conversations tend to happen at communal events. I would say we are on genuinely good terms without {living in each other's pockets|bir-birimizning hayotimizga aralashmasdan}.
What do you like most about your hometown?

The fact that so much of the old city has {survived intact|butunligicha saqlanib qolgan}. You can walk through streets that have barely changed in centuries, which is quite rare. I also like the pace - it is a city where nobody seems to be in a hurry.
Is there anything you would like to change about your hometown?

I would like to see more done for young people. There are very few career opportunities outside tourism, so a great many of my friends have {moved away|koʻchib ketgan}. It would also benefit from better public transport, since at the moment almost everything {depends on|bogʻliq} taxis.

p2.task: Describe a live sports event that you watched.
bullets: where and when you watched it
and explain what you enjoyed about it
p2.ans:
The event I would like to describe is a national league football match I watched in person at the stadium in Bukhara about two years ago, between our local side and a team from Tashkent.

I went with my brother and two of his friends on a Saturday afternoon in October. None of us were serious supporters - my brother is far more interested than I am - but the tickets cost very little and it seemed like a good way to spend an afternoon.

The stadium was perhaps two-thirds full, which was enough to create a real atmosphere without being uncomfortable. What struck me first was how different the game is in person. On television the camera {follows the ball|toʻpni kuzatadi}, so you only see a small part of what is happening; live, you can watch players moving into space long before the ball reaches them, and you realise how much of football is happening {away from the action|harakatdan uzoqda}.

The match itself was, by all accounts, not a particularly good one. It finished one-all, and the goals were both fairly {scrappy|tartibsiz}. But the crowd more than {made up for|oʻrnini qopladi} it - there was a constant running commentary from the men behind us, most of it critical and some of it genuinely funny, and when our side equalised in the last ten minutes the whole stand {erupted|portladi}.

What I enjoyed most was the {collective|jamoaviy} nature of it. Several thousand people, most of whom had nothing else in common, were all reacting to the same thing at the same moment. You cannot get that from a screen, however good the coverage is. I came away thinking that the sport is almost {beside the point|asosiy masala emas} - what people are really buying is a few hours of belonging to something.

p3: Do you think competition makes people more confident?

It can, but only under certain conditions. Competing and doing well clearly builds confidence, and even losing can, if it is {handled constructively|toʻgʻri qabul qilinsa}. But repeated failure in a highly competitive environment does the opposite - it teaches people to avoid the activity entirely. So the effect depends heavily on whether the competition is {well matched|teng kuchli} and how adults around the child react.
Why do some people enjoy competing with others?

Partly because competition provides {clear feedback|aniq natija} - you know exactly where you stand, which most of life does not offer. It also raises effort; people almost always perform better against someone than alone. And for some there is genuine pleasure in the {contest itself|kurashning oʻzi}, quite apart from winning.
Is rivalry stronger between neighbouring countries or between countries that are far apart?

Between neighbours, almost invariably. Proximity means shared history, disputed borders and constant comparison, and the similarities can matter more than the differences - people {measure themselves against|oʻzini solishtiradi} those most like them. Distant countries rarely generate the same feeling, because there is no {common ground|umumiy nuqta} to argue over.
What kinds of competitions do children usually take part in?

Sport is the most common, along with academic competitions - olympiads are taken very seriously here. Beyond that, music, art and debating contests, and increasingly things like robotics. Schools also run a great many informal competitions, which children take {every bit as seriously|xuddi shunday jiddiy} as the official ones.
Do you think competitions are beneficial for children?

On balance yes, provided they are not the only thing on offer. Competition teaches preparation, resilience and how to lose {gracefully|munosib tarzda}, which is a genuinely important skill. The danger is when winning becomes the sole measure of worth, at which point children start avoiding anything they might not be good at, which is exactly the opposite of what you want.
What can children learn from taking part in competitions?

That effort and results are connected, which is easier to see in a competition than in ordinary schoolwork. They also learn to {perform under pressure|bosim ostida ishlash}, to prepare systematically, and to deal with disappointment. Team competitions add cooperation, which is arguably more valuable than the competitive element itself.
Can competition sometimes have a negative effect on children?

Certainly. Excessive pressure can produce anxiety and, in extreme cases, {burnout|tamomila charchash} at an age when it should be unthinkable. It can also damage relationships between children and encourage {cutting corners|qoidani buzish} to win. And children who consistently lose may conclude that ability is fixed, which discourages them from trying anything difficult afterwards.

sessions.examiner: Older bald man with glasses (long name, unclear)
sessions.t2: A routine you think is a waste of time
p1: Do you live in a house or an apartment?
I live in an apartment, on the third floor of a five-storey block. It is not large, but the rooms are a decent size and it is {perfectly adequate|butunlay yetarli} for the three of us.
How long have you lived there?
About seven years now. We moved when my father changed jobs, and although I missed my old neighbourhood at first, I {grew to like|yoqtirib qoldim} this one fairly quickly.
What do you like most about the place where you live?

The location, above all. Everything I need is {within walking distance|piyoda yurish masofasida} - the market, the clinic, the bus stop - so I hardly ever need to drive anywhere, which in a city of this size is a genuine {luxury|hashamat}.
Are you good at remembering people's names?

Not especially, if I am honest. I remember faces extremely well and names very poorly, which is an {awkward combination|noqulay birikma} because you end up recognising someone without being able to greet them properly.
Is it difficult for you to remember new names?

It is, particularly when I meet several people at once. I think the problem is that I am usually {too preoccupied with|band boʻlib qolaman} making a good impression to actually listen when the name is said, so it never really {registers|yodda qolmaydi}.
How do you remember someone's name when you meet them for the first time?

I have started {repeating it back|takrorlab aytish} straight away - saying, nice to meet you, Aziz - which sounds obvious but works surprisingly well. If it is someone important I will also write it down afterwards, because writing something by hand {fixes it in my memory|xotiramga mustahkamlaydi} far better than typing.
Do you often feel stressed in your daily life?

Occasionally rather than constantly. There are certain periods - deadlines, exams - when the pressure {builds up|toʻplanib boradi}, but on an ordinary week I would say my life is fairly {manageable|boshqarsa boʻladigan}.
What usually makes you feel stressed?

Mostly having too many things due at the same time, and, more than that, {uncertainty|noaniqlik}. Waiting for a result or a decision I cannot influence is far more stressful for me than a large amount of work, because at least work {can be got through|bajarib boʻladi}.
What do you do when you feel stressed?

Physical activity helps more than anything - even a twenty-minute walk {takes the edge off|keskinlikni yumshatadi}. Beyond that, I find that writing down exactly what I have to do makes the problem look far smaller, because stress tends to {exaggerate|boʻrttirib koʻrsatadi} everything while it is still in your head.

p2.task: Describe a routine you do regularly but think is a waste of time.
bullets: and explain why you think it is a waste of time
p2.ans:
The routine I want to describe is the half hour or so I spend every morning scrolling through my phone before I get out of bed, which I have been doing for years and which I am fairly certain has never once {done me any good|menga foyda keltirgan}.

It happens every single day, usually between about seven and half past. The alarm goes off, I turn it off, and then instead of getting up I open one app, then another, and by the time I look at the clock, thirty or forty minutes have {evaporated|bugʻlanib ketgan}.

The reason I keep doing it is partly habit and partly a kind of excuse I tell myself - that I am easing into the day, or catching up on the news. In reality the news takes about four minutes and the remaining half hour is {aimless|maqsadsiz}. I think the honest explanation is that it requires no effort at all, and at seven in the morning that is genuinely appealing.

I consider it a waste of time for three reasons. First, I remember almost nothing of what I read, so nothing is actually {gained|qoʻlga kiritilgan}. Second, it makes the rest of the morning rushed, so I end up leaving the house without breakfast. And third - this is the one that bothers me most - it means the first thing I do every day is {react to|munosabat bildirish} other people's content rather than decide anything for myself.
