I have tried to break it several times, and the only thing that has ever worked is leaving the phone in another room overnight, which I always {abandon after a week|bir haftadan keyin tashlab yuboraman}. So I am aware of the problem and doing very little about it, which is probably the most honest part of this answer.

p3: Is it good for people to have a daily routine?

Broadly yes. A routine removes the need to make dozens of small decisions, which {frees up mental energy|aqliy kuchni tejaydi} for things that actually matter. It also makes difficult habits - exercise, study - far more likely to survive, because they stop depending on motivation. The risk is only when a routine becomes so rigid that it {stifles|boʻgʻadi} anything new.
Why do some people prefer to follow the same routine every day?

Mainly because predictability is {reassuring|tinchlantiruvchi}. Knowing what the day holds lowers anxiety, especially for people whose work is already unpredictable. There is also an efficiency argument: a well-established routine {runs on autopilot|oʻz-oʻzidan ishlaydi}, so you get more done with less effort. And some people simply dislike surprises.
Are there any routines that people should be forced to follow?

I would be cautious about the word forced, but there are certainly routines that should be {mandatory in specific contexts|ma'lum sharoitlarda majburiy} - safety checks for pilots or surgeons, for instance, where a checklist saves lives. In ordinary life, I think the state should encourage rather than compel; imposed routines tend to {breed resentment|norozilik keltirib chiqaradi} and rarely last.
What are the advantages of doing something regularly?

Consistency {compounds|jamlanib boradi} in a way that occasional effort does not - twenty minutes a day beats three hours once a month for almost any skill. Regularity also makes progress measurable, and it removes the daily negotiation about whether to do it, which is where most good intentions {fall apart|barbod boʻladi}.
Can having a strict routine have any disadvantages?

Certainly. An {inflexible|moslashuvchan boʻlmagan} routine makes people fragile - the moment something disrupts it, they cannot function. It can also lead to doing things out of habit long after they have stopped being useful, which is exactly what I described in my talk. And it can {crowd out|siqib chiqarish} spontaneity, which is where a lot of life's more interesting moments come from.
Do people's routines change as they get older?

Substantially, and usually in the direction of becoming more {settled|barqaror}. Young people's routines are {dictated by|belgilanadi} external things - school timetables, shift work - and tend to be chaotic. As people take on families their routines become tightly structured around others, and in retirement they often become gentler and more self-chosen. What is consistent is that routines tend to {harden|qotib qoladi} with age, which makes change harder.

sessions.t2: An ambition you have had for a long time
p1: Do you work or are you a student?

I am a student at the moment - I am in my third year, so studying {takes up|egallaydi} almost all of my week. I do a little tutoring at weekends, but that is very much {on the side|qoʻshimcha ravishda}.
What are you studying?

I am studying international relations, which covers politics, history, economics and a certain amount of law. It is quite a {broad|keng qamrovli} degree, which is exactly what appealed to me about it.
Why did you choose this subject?

Because I wanted to understand how decisions taken in one country {ripple out|tarqaladi} into others. I had also always been interested in languages and travel, and this was the one subject that seemed to {tie those threads together|bu qiziqishlarni birlashtirmoq}.
What do you enjoy most about your studies?

The seminars, without question. You are expected to {take a position|pozitsiya egallash} and defend it, and because the class comes from several different backgrounds, you very quickly discover how differently reasonable people can read the same event.
Do you enjoy singing?

I do, although I am under no illusions about my ability. I sing constantly when nobody is listening and it genuinely {lifts my mood|kayfiyatimni koʻtaradi}. In front of other people, however, I become extremely {self-conscious|uyatchan}.
When do you usually sing?

Almost always when my hands are busy with something else - cooking, washing up, walking home. It seems to happen {of its own accord|oʻz-oʻzidan} when my mind is only half engaged, which I suspect is true for most people.
Did you enjoy singing when you were a child?

Far more than I do now, because children have no {inhibitions|tortinchoqlik} about it whatsoever. We sang in class, at family gatherings, in the street. I think the self-consciousness {creeps in|sezdirmay keladi} somewhere around twelve, and most people never quite lose it.
Do you prefer singing alone or with other people?

Alone, for the reasons I mentioned - there is no audience to judge you. That said, singing in a group at a wedding or a celebration is a completely different experience, because nobody is really listening to any individual voice, so the {pressure disappears|bosim yoʻqoladi}.

p2.task: Describe an ambition you have had for a long time.
bullets: what you have done about it so far
and explain why this ambition is important to you
p2.ans:
The ambition I want to describe is my intention to study for a master's degree abroad, ideally in Europe, which is something I have been {working towards|intilib kelmoqdaman} for close to six years now.

I first had the idea when I was about sixteen. A former student from my school came back to give a talk about studying in Germany, and what struck me was not the prestige of it but the way he described being taught - that students were expected to {challenge|e'tiroz bildirish} the lecturer rather than transcribe what was said. That sounded like a completely different world from the one I was in, and the idea {lodged itself|oʻrnashib qoldi} and never left.

What I have actually done about it is less glamorous than the ambition itself. I chose my undergraduate degree specifically because it would qualify me for the programmes I want. I have spent three years working on my English, which is why I am sitting this exam. I have been {putting money aside|pul jamgʻarib kelyapman} from tutoring since my first year, and I have also started emailing academics whose work I have read, two of whom have actually replied, which was {genuinely encouraging|chinakamiga ruhlantiruvchi}.

The reason it matters so much to me is partly practical - the research facilities and the career opportunities are simply on another scale. But the deeper reason is that I want to test myself somewhere where nothing is familiar and nobody knows my family. I suspect that is where you {find out what you are actually capable of|aslida nimaga qodirligingizni bilib olasiz}.

I am realistic about the odds. Funding is the obstacle, not admission, and it may take another two or three years. But it is the one thing in my life I have never {wavered about|ikkilanmoq}.

p3: Do your friends have the same ambitions as you?

Some do, some very much do not. Two of my closest friends are working towards more or less the same thing, which is useful because we {keep each other accountable|bir-birimizni nazorat qilamiz}. Others are entirely focused on starting businesses here, which I respect just as much - it is a different route rather than a {lesser|pastroq} one.
Is it important for young people to have ambitions?

I think so, provided the ambition is their own. Having something to aim at gives structure to decisions that would otherwise be {arbitrary|tasodifiy} - what to study, where to live. The danger is ambition that has been {inherited from|meros qilib olingan} parents, because people can spend a decade pursuing something they never actually wanted.
What kinds of ambitions do young people in Uzbekistan usually have?

Studying or working abroad is an extremely common one, along with starting a business - entrepreneurship has become far more {aspirational|orzu qilinadigan} here in the last few years. IT is another major one, for obvious reasons. Underneath most of them is the same goal: {financial independence|moliyaviy mustaqillik} earlier than the previous generation managed it.
Do you think society values some ambitions more than others?

Undoubtedly. Ambitions that produce visible status - wealth, a prestigious profession, going abroad - are celebrated, while equally demanding ones are {overlooked|e'tibordan chetda qoladi}. Somebody who wants to be an outstanding teacher in a village school is pursuing something genuinely difficult, but it {carries little social weight|ijtimoiy ogʻirligi kam}, and I think that is a loss.
Are people without ambitions at a disadvantage?

Practically, often yes - ambition {opens doors|eshiklarni ochadi} because it makes people prepare and take risks. But I would distinguish between having no ambition and having no visible ambition. Plenty of people are quietly content, and contentment is not a {deficiency|kamchilik}. The people genuinely at a disadvantage are those who want something and have been persuaded they cannot have it.
Why are ambitious people important to society?

Because almost everything that changes for the better was {driven by|harakatga keltirilgan} somebody who was not satisfied with how things were. Ambitious people take the risks that create jobs and solve problems. The qualification I would add is that ambition needs to be {channelled|yoʻnaltirilgan} towards something useful - unchecked personal ambition can be extremely destructive.
Do you think it is possible to live a happy life without having any ambitions?

Absolutely, and I would go further - there is good evidence that constant striving makes people {less|kamroq} happy, not more. Ambition postpones satisfaction by definition, because there is always a next target. Someone who takes pleasure in ordinary things and has close relationships may well be happier than someone {chasing|quvib yuruvchi} a goal they will always move. Happiness and achievement are simply not the same currency.

sessions.t2: A person who likes growing plants
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I work - I finished my degree last year and I am now employed at a small trading company, where I mainly handle {customer accounts|mijozlar bilan ishlash} and documentation.
Do you plan to continue working here in the future?

For the next couple of years, yes. The company is small enough that I have real responsibility, which would not happen at my level in a large firm. Longer term I would like to move into management, so I am {keeping my options open|imkoniyatlarni ochiq qoldiryapman}.
What kind of websites do you often visit?

A fairly small number that I use repeatedly - news sites, a couple of professional resources for work, and video platforms in the evening. I also spend more time than I should on forums, where people discuss things {in depth|chuqur} rather than in short posts.
What kind of website do you own?

I do not own one, to be honest. I did build a very simple personal page a few years ago when I was learning some basic coding, but I never {maintained|yuritmadim} it and it has long since disappeared. It is something I would like to {come back to|qaytib kelmoq} eventually.
What kinds of websites are common in your country?

Messaging and social platforms dominate, Telegram above all - it is used here for news, shopping and business as much as for conversation. Beyond that, {classified advertising|e'lonlar} sites where people buy and sell, and government service portals, which have improved {beyond recognition|tanib boʻlmas darajada} in the last few years.
How often do you go shopping?

For food, two or three times a week, because I prefer buying fresh rather than doing one enormous weekly shop. For anything else, perhaps once a month, and usually only when something has genuinely {worn out|eskirgan}.
Do you prefer shopping online or going to shops?

Online for anything standardised, since the choice is {vastly wider|ancha keng} and you can compare reviews before committing. For food and clothes I still much prefer going in person - {sizing is unpredictable|oʻlchamlar noaniq} and I like to see produce before I buy it.

p2.task: Describe a person who likes growing plants at home or in a garden.
bullets: how much time they spend on it
and explain why you think they enjoy it
p2.ans:
The person I want to describe is my aunt, who lives on the edge of Termez and has turned what is really quite a small plot of land into something close to a {working garden|toʻliq bogʻ}.

She is in her late forties and she works as an accountant, so the gardening is entirely a hobby, which makes the scale of it more impressive rather than less.

What she grows is remarkably varied for the space. Along one wall there are tomatoes, peppers and herbs in summer; there is a grapevine trained over a wooden frame that provides shade for the whole courtyard; and she has two apricot trees and a pomegranate that she is inordinately proud of. Indoors she keeps perhaps twenty pots, mostly things that can {tolerate|chiday oladigan} being forgotten about for a week, which is a sensible choice given her working hours.

In terms of time, she is out there for an hour before work most mornings, watering and checking the leaves, and then a good part of Saturday. She is very {systematic|tizimli} about it - she keeps a notebook recording what was planted where and when, which is presumably the accountant in her. She also makes her own compost and is deeply {sceptical of|shubha bilan qaraydigan} anything chemical.

As for why she enjoys it, I think there are two things. The first is that her job is entirely {abstract|mavhum} - numbers on a screen - and gardening produces something you can hold. She has said as much herself. The second is that it is the one part of her life that {cannot be hurried|shoshirib boʻlmaydi}. A plant takes the time it takes regardless of deadlines, and I suspect that is genuinely restful for someone whose working year is built around them.

p3: Is it common for people to grow plants in your country?

Extremely common, for cultural and practical reasons alike. Almost any house with a courtyard will have grapevines or fruit trees, and people in flats keep pots on their balconies. Growing at least some of your own food is regarded as {perfectly ordinary|butunlay odatiy} here rather than as a hobby, and the climate is {favourable|qulay} for it.
Why do people grow plants in their homes?

Partly for appearance and air quality, but I think the psychological side matters more. Caring for something living is a well-known {stress reliever|stressni kamaytiruvchi}, and it gives a sense of progress that is rare in daily life. Indoor plants also make a space feel {lived in|yashaladigan} rather than merely furnished.
Why do people like growing vegetables and fruits?

The obvious answer is taste and cost - anything picked that morning is {incomparably better|taqqoslab boʻlmas darajada yaxshi} than something transported for a week. But there is also a strong element of control: you know exactly what has gone onto it. And for many people here it is simply {handed down|avloddan avlodga oʻtgan} - they grow what their parents grew.
Why do some people prefer to buy vegetables from shops?

Convenience, above all. Growing food requires land, time and a certain amount of knowledge, and city life supplies none of those. Shops also offer {year-round variety|yil davomida xilma-xillik} that no garden can match. And frankly, gardening involves a lot of failure at the start, which {puts people off|odamlarni bezdiradi} before they see any results.
Do you think growing plants will continue to be popular in the future?

In terms of ornamental and indoor plants, I expect interest to grow, especially as people become more aware of how much time they spend {cooped up indoors|uy ichida qamalib}. Food growing is more complicated: {plot sizes|yer maydonlari} are shrinking as flats replace houses, so the scale will fall even if the interest does not.
How can people grow plants in apartments?

More easily than most people assume. Balconies take containers perfectly well, and herbs, tomatoes and peppers all grow in pots. Indoors, a south-facing window is enough for a great deal, and {grow lights|oʻsish lampalari} have become cheap enough to make even dark flats workable. The main constraints are watering discipline and {drainage|suv oqizish}, both of which are easily solved.

sessions.t2: A time you helped someone solve a problem
p1: Can you describe the place where you live?

I live in a flat in the north of Tashkent - three rooms, a kitchen and a small balcony, on the fourth floor. The building is not new, but the rooms are {generously sized|keng} in a way modern flats rarely are.
What do you like about your flat?

The balcony, mostly. It looks out over a small park, and I have put a chair and some plants out there, so it has become the place where I {wind down|dam olaman} in the evening. I also appreciate how much light the flat gets.
What do you dislike about your flat?

The sound insulation is poor, so you hear the neighbours above rather more than you would like. Storage is also {in short supply|yetishmaydi} - there is one built-in cupboard for the whole flat, so it looks {cluttered|tartibsiz} however much I tidy.
Do you pick up rubbish if you see it on the ground?

Sometimes, though I will admit not always. If it is in a park or somewhere I am {personally attached to|shaxsan bogʻlangan}, I usually will. On a busy street I tend not to, which is a slightly uncomfortable thing to admit, because the {logic|mantiq} is exactly the same.
How do you feel when you see rubbish on the ground?

Genuinely irritated, particularly in an otherwise attractive place. It sends a signal that nobody cares, and that {tends to be self-reinforcing|oʻzini oʻzi kuchaytiradi} - one discarded bottle very quickly becomes twenty. Clean streets seem to {stay clean|toza qoladi} for exactly the same reason.
Do you think recycling is well-developed in your country?

Not yet, if I am honest. There are {isolated initiatives|alohida tashabbuslar} - separate bins in some districts, private collection for plastic and cardboard - but there is no nationwide system, so most waste still goes to landfill. It has improved noticeably in the last five years, though, so the direction is {encouraging|umidli}.

p2.task: Describe a time when you helped someone to solve a problem.
bullets: and explain how you felt about helping them
p2.ans:
The occasion I would like to describe is when I helped a colleague at work {untangle|hal qilmoq} a problem with a shipment that had gone badly wrong, about eight months ago.

She had joined the company only a few weeks earlier, and a consignment she was responsible for had been held at the border because one of the accompanying documents had been issued with the wrong company name on it. The supplier was {unresponsive|javob bermayotgan}, the client was calling twice a day, and she was, understandably, {out of her depth|imkoniyatidan tashqarida} - it was her first serious problem and nobody had shown her what to do.

What I did was fairly methodical rather than clever. I sat down with her and we went through the paperwork line by line until we could identify exactly which document was wrong and who had issued it. I then made two phone calls, one to a customs broker I had dealt with before, who explained that the document could be {reissued|qayta rasmiylashtirilishi} rather than corrected, which saved about a week. After that I let her make the remaining calls herself, and I simply sat with her while she did it, because the difficulty by then was confidence rather than knowledge.

The shipment cleared four days later, which was a far better outcome than anyone had expected.

How I felt about it was, oddly, more complicated than simple satisfaction. I was pleased, obviously. But what {stayed with me|esimda qoldi} was the realisation that the problem existed only because nobody had trained her. I had been in exactly the same position two years earlier and somebody had helped me then, so it felt less like doing a favour than like {passing something on|estafetani uzatish}. Since then I have made a point of sitting with new staff in their first month.

p3: What kind of jobs require helping others?

The obvious ones are healthcare, teaching and social work, where helping is the substance of the job. But I would argue almost every job involves it - customer service, law, even engineering, where you are solving somebody's problem. What distinguishes the caring professions is that the help is {emotional as well as practical|amaliy ham, hissiy ham}, which is why they are so draining.
What do you think the government should give to society, time or money?

It has to be both, but if I had to choose, I would say money is easier for a government to provide and time is what is actually {in short supply|tanqis}. Funding a hospital is straightforward; ensuring officials actually spend time listening to the people affected by a policy is much harder. So I would say money is the {necessary condition|zarur shart} and time is what makes it effective.
In what ways should the government give its time to society?

Through genuine {consultation|maslahatlashuv} rather than the ceremonial kind - meeting communities before decisions are taken rather than announcing them afterwards. Officials spending time in the schools and clinics they fund would also change how policy is written. And responding to complaints within a reasonable period is a form of giving time that people notice {immediately|darhol}.
Do you think a society can become too focused on individual success at the expense of community values?

I think it can, and there are societies where it has clearly happened. When success is measured purely individually, people begin to see shared institutions - public transport, state schools - as things for other people, and support for funding them {erodes|yemiriladi}. The result is a kind of {atomisation|parchalanish} where everyone is competing and nobody is responsible for anything collective. A degree of individual ambition is healthy; the question is whether anything is valued alongside it.
Do citizens need to do more to influence the decisions made by their government?

I think most citizens underestimate how much influence is available to them at the local level. National policy is difficult to affect, but decisions about a school, a road or a clinic are frequently {decided by whoever turns up|kim kelsa, oʻsha hal qiladi}. Beyond voting, that means attending meetings, signing petitions and making complaints formally rather than {grumbling privately|ichida norozi boʻlish}, which changes nothing.
How can people contribute more to their local community?

The mahalla system here already provides an obvious channel - people contribute to weddings, funerals and communal clean-ups {as a matter of course|oddiy hol sifatida}. Beyond that: volunteering with young people, helping elderly neighbours with things like paperwork or technology, and simply being willing to {take on|oʻz zimmasiga olmoq} the unglamorous organisational jobs that somebody has to do.
Why is it important for people to care about society as a whole?

Because almost everything that determines quality of life is {collective|jamoaviy} - clean air, safe streets, a functioning health system. None of it can be bought individually, however wealthy you are. There is also a practical argument: societies with high trust are measurably more prosperous, because cooperation is cheaper than {policing every transaction|har bir bitimni nazorat qilish}.
What can governments do to encourage people to become more involved in their communities?

Small structural things work better than campaigns. Funding community spaces, making volunteering count towards qualifications, and giving local bodies real {decision-making power|qaror qabul qilish vakolati} so that participation is not merely symbolic. The single most effective measure, though, is responsiveness: people get involved when they have seen that involvement actually {changes something|biror narsani oʻzgartiradi}.

sessions.t2: A speech or talk that was not interesting
p1: At what age did you first start using social media?

I was about thirteen, I think, when I made my first account, largely because everyone in my class had one and I did not want to {feel left out|chetda qolgandek his qilish}. Looking back, thirteen strikes me as {rather young|ancha yosh}, though it is younger still for children now.
Do you think you will continue using social media in the future?

Probably, though in a more limited way. I have already deleted two apps because I found they were {eating into|yeb qoʻyayotgan} my time without giving much back. I suspect I will keep the ones that are genuinely useful for staying in touch and {let the rest go|qolganlaridan voz kechish}.
Do you think recycling paper is important?

Yes, and for a very direct reason - paper comes from trees, and recycling it reduces both {deforestation|oʻrmonlarning kesilishi} and the energy needed to produce new paper. It is also one of the easiest materials to recycle, so there is very little {excuse|uzr} for not doing it.
Did you make anything out of paper when you were a child?

Constantly. We had art lessons where we made {cut-out|qirqib olingan} animals and greeting cards, and at home I went through a long phase of folding aeroplanes and trying to work out which design {stayed in the air|havoda ushlanib turadi} longest. It was cheap entertainment, which mattered.
What do young people usually talk about with their friends?

A great deal of it is about entertainment and technology - what to watch, which app to use, which course is worth taking. There is also plenty of {shop talk|kasbiy suhbat} about studies and jobs. What they rarely discuss openly is anything that makes them look {vulnerable|zaif}, at least outside a close circle.
Do young people enjoy talking to older people?

Many do, though I think it depends heavily on whether the older person treats it as a conversation or a {lecture|ma'ruza}. When an older person is genuinely curious about a young person's life, young people are usually delighted to talk. When the exchange is {one-directional|bir tomonlama}, they disengage very quickly.
What topics do you usually discuss with people your age?

Study and work plans, mostly - a lot of my friends are at the same stage of deciding what happens next. Beyond that, films, football and, increasingly, practical things like {renting|ijara} and money, which we never discussed at eighteen and now talk about constantly.
Do you think young people and older people have different ways of communicating?

Clearly, yes. Younger people communicate in short, frequent, informal bursts across several platforms, and they are comfortable with {silence in a conversation|suhbatdagi jimlik} being filled by a link or an image. Older people tend to prefer longer, less frequent exchanges and value a phone call where a young person would send a message. It is a difference of {medium and register|vosita va uslub} rather than of content.

p2.task: Describe a speech or talk that was not interesting for you.
bullets: what the speech or talk was about
where and when you heard it
and explain why you did not find it interesting
p2.ans:
The talk I want to describe was a compulsory careers presentation at my university, given by a visiting speaker from a recruitment agency, which lasted a little over ninety minutes and felt considerably longer.

It took place on a Friday afternoon in the main lecture hall, with perhaps two hundred of us in the room, which is already the {worst possible slot|eng yomon vaqt} for anything requiring concentration. Attendance was recorded, so nobody could leave.

The speaker was a man in his forties who clearly gave this same presentation regularly. The subject - how to find a job after graduating - could hardly have been more relevant to the audience, which is precisely what made the whole thing so {disappointing|umidsizlantiruvchi}. He read almost the entire session directly from slides that were {dense with text|matnga toʻla}, in a flat voice, without once looking up. There were no examples, no stories about actual candidates, and not a single question to the audience in ninety minutes.

Within about fifteen minutes the room had {switched off|diqqatini yoʻqotdi} almost completely. People were quietly scrolling, and by the end perhaps a third of the audience was still nominally paying attention.

What I found frustrating was not boredom exactly but the {waste|isrof} of it. He must have had hundreds of real examples - people who had been hired, people who had been rejected and why - and any one of them would have held the room. Instead we were given {generic advice|umumiy maslahat} that everyone present had already read online.

Honestly, the main thing I took away from it was a lesson about presenting rather than about careers: that expertise and the ability to communicate it are {entirely separate skills|butunlay ikki xil koʻnikma}, and that without the second, the first {falls on deaf ears|quloqqa kirmaydi}.

p3: Do you think talkative people are good at listening to others?

Not necessarily, and often the opposite. Some talkative people are simply {enthusiastic|ishtiyoqli} and listen perfectly well; others talk because they are uncomfortable with silence, and those people tend to be waiting for their turn rather than listening. The clearest sign is whether they ask questions that {build on|rivojlantiradi} what you actually said.
How can you tell whether someone is really listening to you?

Mainly by their response rather than their {body language|tana tili}, which is easy to fake. If somebody asks a follow-up question, or refers back to something you mentioned earlier in the conversation, they were genuinely listening. Anyone can nod and maintain eye contact while {miles away|xayoli boshqa joyda}.
What can people do to become better listeners?

The single most useful habit is {resisting the urge|istakni jilovlash} to prepare your reply while the other person is still speaking. Beyond that: asking a question before offering an opinion, tolerating a short silence rather than filling it, and - practically - removing the phone from the table, which does more for attention than any technique.
Why do some people find it difficult to listen to others?

Several reasons. Some are genuinely {preoccupied|band} with their own concerns and have no spare attention. Others have been conditioned by short-form content to expect constant novelty, so a long explanation feels intolerable. And for some it is {ego|manmanlik} - listening means accepting, at least temporarily, that the other person's view matters more than yours.
Is listening more important than speaking in a conversation?

I would say listening is the more {neglected|e'tiborsiz qolgan} of the two rather than the more important. A conversation where nobody speaks is not a conversation. But because people are trained to speak well and almost never trained to listen, listening is where most of the available improvement lies, and it is usually the reason conversations {break down|buziladi}.
Do people listen differently when they talk to friends and strangers?

Considerably. With strangers people listen more {attentively but more cautiously|diqqat bilan, ammo ehtiyotkorlik bilan} - they are gathering information and judging. With friends the listening is warmer but frequently lazier, because you assume you already know what they are going to say, and that assumption is where a lot of {misunderstandings|tushunmovchiliklar} between close people begin.
How can teachers encourage students to listen to each other?

Structurally, by designing activities where listening is {unavoidable|muqarrar} - group work where each student holds a different piece of information, or asking one student to summarise another's point before responding. Debate formats also work well. What does not work is simply telling a class to listen, because there is no {consequence|oqibat} attached to not doing it.
Has social media affected the way people listen and communicate with each other?

Substantially, and in two directions. It has made people far better at {communicating briefly|qisqa muloqot qilish} and at reaching others instantly. But it has also trained us to {broadcast rather than converse|suhbatlashish emas, e'lon qilish}, because posts are directed at nobody in particular and require no response. Comment sections in particular reward the loudest reaction rather than understanding, and I think that habit {carries over into|oʻtib ketadi} face-to-face conversation more than people realise.

sessions.t2: A childhood friend you remember well
p1: Can you describe your hometown?

I am from Bukhara, which is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia. The historic centre is almost entirely {intact|butunligicha saqlangan} - narrow streets, madrasas and covered bazaars - and around it there is a much more ordinary modern city where most people actually live.
Is your hometown a busy or quiet place?

It is somewhere {in between|oʻrtasida}. The tourist areas can be crowded in spring and autumn, but the residential districts are remarkably quiet, especially in the evening. Compared with Tashkent it feels {positively sleepy|juda osoyishta}.
Do you like your hometown?

Very much. What I appreciate most is that daily life happens on a human scale - you walk everywhere, you {run into|duch kelasiz} people you know, and nobody seems to be in a hurry. The one drawback is the narrow {range of|doirasi} career opportunities.
What websites do you use?

A fairly small number that I use repeatedly - news channels, a couple of academic databases for coursework, and video platforms. I also use an online dictionary constantly, which has probably done more for my English than anything else I {have at my disposal|ixtiyorimda bor}.
Do the websites you use help you a lot with your studies?

Enormously, yes. Lecture recordings and open-access journals give me material my own library simply does not hold. The {caveat|shart} is that you have to be disciplined about sources, because a great deal of what appears online is {unverified|tasdiqlanmagan} and would not survive a moment's scrutiny.

p2.task: Describe a childhood friend you remember well.
bullets: and explain why you remember this person so well
p2.ans:
The friend I would like to talk about is a boy named Sardor, who sat next to me in primary school for four years and who was, for most of my childhood, {inseparable from me|mendan ajralmas}.

We became friends in the most accidental way possible. On the first day of school we were seated alphabetically, and he happened to be next to me. That was the entire basis of it, which I think is true of most childhood friendships - they begin through {sheer proximity|shunchaki yaqinlik} rather than through anything you choose.

What we did together was fairly unremarkable and, at the time, completely absorbing. We walked to and from school every day, which was about twenty minutes each way and where most of our real conversations happened. We collected football stickers with an intensity that now seems {faintly absurd|birmuncha kulgili}, and we spent whole summers in the street outside his house playing until it got dark. He was also the person who taught me to ride a bicycle, largely by pushing me down a slope and {refusing to admit|tan olishdan bosh tortib} afterwards that he had let go.

I remember him so well for two reasons. The first is that he moved to Tashkent when we were fourteen, so the friendship ended {abruptly|toʻsatdan} rather than fading, and things that end suddenly tend to {stay sharp in the memory|xotirada yorqin qoladi}.

The second is that he was the first person outside my family who genuinely took my opinions seriously. At nine or ten that is a surprisingly powerful thing, and I suspect a certain amount of my confidence {can be traced back to|kelib chiqadi} those walks to school. We are still in occasional contact, though it is not the same, and I doubt it ever could be.

p3: Should people keep in touch with friends they made in childhood?

Where it is natural, yes - those friendships carry a shared history nobody else has, and old friends often see you more honestly because they knew you before you {constructed an image|imidj yaratish} of yourself. But I would not treat it as an obligation. People change, and forcing a friendship that has {run its course|oʻz vaqtini oʻtagan} serves nobody.
How important is childhood in our lives?

It is probably the single most formative period. Attitudes to risk, to learning and to other people are largely {laid down|shakllantiriladi} before adolescence, and they are extremely difficult to change afterwards. That said, I am wary of {determinism|oldindan belgilanganlik} - plenty of people have transformed a difficult start, so childhood shapes us without dictating the outcome.
Why are childhood friendships important?

Because they are where children first learn to negotiate, share and {resolve conflict|nizoni hal qilish} without an adult intervening. They also provide a sense of belonging outside the family, which is an important step towards independence. And practically, they are the first relationships a child chooses for themselves.
Do you think it is easier to make friends when you are a child or an adult?

Far easier as a child. Children have no {social baggage|ijtimoiy yuk} - no concern with status or background - and they see the same people every day, which is really what friendships grow from. Adults have to {engineer|sun'iy yaratish} those conditions deliberately, and they are more guarded because they have been disappointed before.
What can people learn from their childhood friends?

Very practical social lessons: how to apologise, how to lose, how to {stand up for yourself|oʻzingizni himoya qilish} without turning it into a fight. Children also pick up interests from each other - I would never have played football seriously if Sardor had not. And they learn, usually the hard way, that people can be {unpredictable|oldindan bilib boʻlmaydigan}.
Do friendships from childhood usually last for a long time?

Some do, but I think fewer than people assume. The ones that survive are usually those where the friendship was based on genuine {common ground|umumiy nuqta} rather than circumstance. Once people move away, marry or take different paths, a friendship that rested only on proximity tends to {quietly dissolve|jimgina tarqab ketadi}, and that is not really anyone's fault.
How has the way people make friends changed compared with the past?

The biggest change is that {geography matters far less|geografiya ahamiyatini yoʻqotdi}. A generation ago your friends were whoever lived near you; now people form close friendships through shared interests online and may not meet for years. That is a genuine gain for anyone with unusual interests. The loss is that friendships built entirely through screens rarely develop the {everyday intimacy|kundalik yaqinlik} that comes from simply being in the same place.

sessions.t2: A successful businessman you know
p1: What kind of place do you live in?

I live in a flat, in a four-storey block built in the eighties. It has three rooms and a small balcony, and although the building is not modern, the walls are thick and the rooms are {generously proportioned|keng} in a way newer flats rarely are.
Is the place where you live usually quiet or busy?

Mostly quiet. We are a few streets back from the main road, so the traffic noise is {muffled|boʻgʻiq}. It becomes busy twice a day around the school, and otherwise it is calm enough that you can hear birds, which in a city is not {something to take for granted|oddiy deb bilinadigan narsa}.
What do you like about the place where you live?

The neighbours, above all. Most of them have lived there for decades, so there is a genuine {sense of community|jamoaviylik hissi} - people look after each other's children and notice if something is wrong. I also like how convenient it is; everything I need is {within walking distance|piyoda yurish masofasida}.
What do you usually do at home?

Study, mostly, and cook, which I have come to enjoy more than I expected. In the evening I read or watch something with my family. I also spend a fair amount of time on the balcony, which has effectively become my {retreat|panohgoh}.
Do you prefer living in a quiet or busy place?

Quiet, without much hesitation. I like the idea of a busy area more than the reality of it - the constant noise is {mentally taxing|aqlan charchatadi} even when you stop noticing it. Ideally you live somewhere quiet that is only ten minutes from somewhere busy.
Do you think your home is a good place for relaxing?

On the whole yes, although it depends on the time of day. In the evening it is genuinely restful. During the day, when everyone is home and the television is on, it can be {surprisingly hard|kutilmaganda qiyin} to concentrate, so I often go out to a library if I need real quiet.

p2.task: Describe a successful businessman you know.
bullets: and explain why you consider them successful
p2.ans:
The person I want to describe is a man called Farrukh, who is the father of a close friend of mine and who owns a chain of furniture workshops and showrooms in Bukhara.

I have known him since I was about twelve, so I have watched the business grow from a single workshop with four employees into something that now employs, I believe, around seventy people and supplies hotels across the region.

The way he got there is less dramatic than people tend to expect. He trained as a carpenter, worked for somebody else for eight years, and started on his own with a loan from relatives and a rented shed. For the first three years, by his own account, he {barely broke even|zoʻrgʻa zararsiz ishladi} and worked seven days a week. The turning point came when a hotel was being built nearby and he {undercut|arzonroq taklif qildi} the imported alternative on price while delivering faster. That one contract led to others, and the business {snowballed|qor toʻpiday oʻsdi} from there.

What I find most interesting is how he runs it now. He still knows the name of every person who works for him, he pays wages on time even in bad months, which in this industry is not {a given|kafolatlangan narsa}, and he has trained a considerable number of young carpenters who have since gone on to open their own workshops - competitors, effectively, which he {seems entirely relaxed about|butunlay xotirjam qabul qiladi}.

I consider him successful not primarily because of the money, although he is comfortable. It is because he built something that survives without him being in the room, and because the people who work for him genuinely {speak well of|yaxshi gapiradi} him. That combination is rarer than commercial success on its own.

p3: What makes a businessman successful?

A combination of judgement and {persistence|qat'iyat}, since most businesses fail at least once before they work. Understanding customers rather than assuming you know what they want is critical, as is careful management of cash, which is what actually {sinks|choʻktiradi} most small firms. And timing and connections play a larger role than successful people usually {care to admit|tan olishni xohlaydi}.
What qualities does a successful businessman need?

{Resilience|bardoshlilik} first - the ability to keep going after a bad year. Then adaptability, because markets shift faster than plans do. Good judgement about people matters enormously, since most serious business problems come down to hiring or partnership. And honesty, which is not merely ethical: a reputation for {reliability|ishonchlilik} is the cheapest marketing available.
Why do some businesses become more successful than others?

Often because they solve a problem the competition has {overlooked|e'tibordan chetda qoldirgan}, or simply execute the same idea more consistently. Capital and timing matter too - two identical businesses launched two years apart can have completely different fates. And many are held back by the founder's unwillingness to {delegate|vakolat berish}, which puts a hard ceiling on growth.
How important is customer satisfaction for a business?

It is probably the single most important factor in the long term, because keeping an existing customer costs a fraction of what finding a new one does. Satisfied customers also {advertise on your behalf|nomingizdan reklama qiladi}, and word of mouth is far more credible than any campaign. In markets where products are nearly identical, service is often the only real {point of difference|farqlovchi jihat}.
What can businesses do to satisfy their customers?

Deliver what they promised, on time, and be honest when they cannot. Beyond that: train staff properly, make complaints easy to make rather than {burying|koʻmib tashlash} the contact details, and actually act on feedback instead of merely collecting it. {Anticipating|oldindan sezish} a need before the customer raises it is what separates good service from adequate service.
Why do some customers become loyal to a particular business?

Consistency, mainly - they know exactly what they will get. Trust is the other half: one occasion where a business acted {against its own short-term interest|oʻzining qisqa muddatli manfaatiga qarshi} to help a customer will buy years of loyalty. Habit and convenience also play a bigger part than most people would like to admit.
Should businesses focus more on making money or satisfying customers?

I would argue the choice is {a false one|soxta tanlov}. Profit is the result of satisfied customers, not an alternative to them. A firm that maximises short-term revenue at customers' expense {erodes|yemiradi} the thing that generates revenue in the first place. That said, a business that ignores its finances in the name of service will not survive either, so the honest answer is that both are constraints rather than goals.
How can businesses deal with unhappy customers?

Listen first and {resist the urge to defend|himoyalanish istagini jilovlash} immediately, because most complaints are about feeling ignored as much as about the fault itself. Then apologise plainly, fix it quickly, and where possible offer something beyond what was strictly owed. Handled well, a complaint frequently produces a more loyal customer than a {trouble-free|muammosiz} transaction would have.

sessions.examiner: Older man with a bald spot, name not remembered
sessions.t2: A place where you felt bored
p1: Where do you live?

I live in Tashkent, in a residential district in the north of the city. It is a fairly ordinary neighbourhood of apartment blocks and courtyards, about twenty minutes from the centre by metro, which makes it {extremely convenient|nihoyatda qulay}.
What do you like about the place where you live?

The courtyards, mainly. Each block has a shared yard with trees and benches, and in the evening it fills with children and older people, so there is a real {sense of life|hayot ruhi} to it. I also like that the metro is close enough to walk to.
Is there anything you would like to change about your neighbourhood?

Parking, above all - car ownership has grown far faster than the streets were designed for, and the yards are gradually being {taken over by|egallab olinmoqda} vehicles. I would also like more green space, since a lot of the original planting has been {built over|qurilib ketgan}.
Do you think you will continue living there in the future?

Possibly not. I am fond of it, but if my career takes me elsewhere I would move without much hesitation. I suspect I would {look back on it fondly|iliqlik bilan eslayman} rather than stay purely out of attachment.
Do you often use headphones?

Almost daily. They are {indispensable|ajralmas} on the metro, and I use them while studying because instrumental music helps me {tune out|e'tibor bermaslik} everything else. I do take them off near roads, though, after one close call a couple of years ago.
What do you usually use headphones for?

Music and podcasts, mostly, and listening practice for this exam, where you {pick up|ilgʻab olasiz} considerably more detail than through a speaker. I also use them for calls, simply because it leaves my hands free.
Do you prefer using headphones or listening to things without them?

Headphones, for anything I actually want to concentrate on - the sound is fuller and nothing competes with it. Without them, listening becomes a {background activity|fon mashgʻuloti}, which is fine for music while cooking but useless for anything demanding.
Do you have a favourite teacher?

Yes, my literature teacher in year nine. She was the first person who treated my opinion as though it {carried weight|ahamiyatga ega edi}, and she had a way of explaining a text that made it feel like something worth arguing about rather than memorising.
What makes someone a good teacher?

Patience, and a genuine interest in whether the class has understood rather than whether the material was covered. Good teachers also {pitch|moslashtirish} the same idea in several different ways until it lands, and - this is underrated - they are willing to admit when they do not know something.
Do you think teachers are important in your life?

Considerably. Two or three teachers have {shaped|shakllantirgan} what I chose to study and how I approach problems, which is a substantial influence for people I only saw a few hours a week. Information is available everywhere now, but motivation still {comes from people|odamlardan keladi}.

p2.task: Describe a place where you went and felt bored.
bullets: and explain why you felt bored
p2.ans:
The place I want to describe is a regional history museum in a small town a couple of hours outside Tashkent, which I visited on a school trip when I was about fifteen.

We went because it was the last week of the school year and the trip had evidently been arranged months earlier by somebody who had never actually been there. Around forty of us were {bussed in|avtobusda olib borildi} on a very hot morning and told we would be staying for three hours, which turned out to be roughly two hours and forty minutes longer than necessary.

What we did was walk slowly through four rooms and then sit in a corridor waiting for the bus. The exhibits themselves were not the problem - there were old agricultural tools, coins, and a reconstruction of a traditional room, all of which could have been genuinely interesting. The problem was entirely in the presentation. Everything sat behind {glass cases|shisha vitrinalar} with tiny typed labels giving a date and nothing else. There was nothing to touch, nothing to try, and no explanation anywhere of why any of it {mattered|ahamiyatli edi}. Our guide read from a prepared text in a completely {flat|jonsiz} voice and never once asked us a question.

Within twenty minutes the entire group had {switched off|diqqatini yoʻqotdi}. People were sitting on windowsills, and the teachers spent more energy keeping us quiet than the guide spent explaining anything.

Looking back, I felt bored not because the subject was dull but because the place had been arranged for the objects rather than for the visitors. Nobody had asked what a fifteen-year-old might want to know. It taught me that almost anything can be made {compelling|qiziqarli} with the right presentation - and, equally, that almost anything can be made {excruciating|azobli} without it.

p3: Why do some people get bored more easily than others?

Temperament accounts for a fair amount - some people have a high need for {novelty and stimulation|yangilik va qoʻzgʻatuvchi ta'sir} and become restless quickly. Habit matters too: anyone accustomed to fast-changing content finds slower activities harder to tolerate. And people with strong internal interests are rarely bored, because they can {entertain themselves|oʻzini band qila oladi}.
What do people usually do when they feel bored?

The default now is to {reach for a phone|telefonga qoʻl uzatmoq}, which provides instant distraction and very little satisfaction. Others eat, call someone, or start an unnecessary task simply to fill the time. Boredom is also a well-documented trigger for {impulsive behaviour|oʻylamasdan qilingan xatti-harakat}, from pointless shopping to snacking.
Do you think people nowadays get bored more easily than in the past?

They experience fewer {empty moments|boʻsh daqiqalar}, because any gap can now be filled. But I would argue their tolerance has dropped, so the same ten minutes of waiting feels far longer than it would have done twenty years ago. Boredom has essentially been {suppressed rather than resolved|hal qilinmay, bosilgan}.
Is it good for people to experience boredom sometimes?

Genuinely, yes. Boredom is uncomfortable, and that discomfort is what {prompts|turtki beradi} people to create, invent or simply think. Most good ideas arrive in unoccupied time rather than during concentrated work. Children who are never bored rarely develop the ability to {amuse themselves|oʻzini ovuntirish}, which is a real disadvantage later.
Why do children often get bored when they have nothing to do?

Partly because they have less experience of {self-direction|mustaqil tashabbus} - they are used to activities being organised for them. Toys that do everything also leave nothing for the child to contribute. And a good deal of what looks like boredom is really a request for {attention|e'tibor} rather than for entertainment.
How can people make their free time more interesting?

By choosing activities that require some {active participation|faol ishtirok} rather than consumption - making something, playing a sport, learning a skill. Planning helps too, because unplanned free time tends to {default to|oʻz-oʻzidan oʻtib ketadi} a screen. And variety matters: even an enjoyable activity becomes {stale|zerikarli} if it is the only one you ever do.

sessions.examiner: Elderly man with grey hair, nationality unclear
sessions.t2: A place where an event took place
p1: Describe your hometown.

I am from Samarkand, which is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. It is best known for Registan Square and the tiled monuments around it, but the greater part of it is an ordinary working city of around half a million people, with {wide streets|keng koʻchalar} and a great deal of greenery.
Is the place where you live noisy?

Not particularly. The tourist quarter can be lively, but our district is residential and the evenings are genuinely quiet. The main source of noise is construction, which has become {a permanent feature|doimiy holat} of almost every neighbourhood here.
How long have you been living there?
My whole life, so about twenty-three years. My family has been in the same district for three generations, which means I probably {take a great deal of it for granted|koʻp narsani oddiy deb bilaman}.
Do you know people in your neighbourhood well?

Yes, very well. We live in a mahalla, where neighbours are involved in each other's lives to a degree that visitors find {striking|hayratlanarli} - everyone contributes to weddings and funerals, so you inevitably know who everyone is.
Do you wear a watch?

I do, most days. It began as a practical habit, because I did not want to take my phone out during lectures, and now it feels {odd|gʻalati} without one. It has become part of how I dress as much as a way of telling the time.
How often do you wear a watch?

Essentially every day, apart from weekends at home when I am not going anywhere. I have worn the same one for about four years, and I have {grown attached to|koʻnikib qolganman} it in a way that is slightly disproportionate to what it cost.
What kind of watches do you like?

Simple, {understated|kamtarona} ones - a plain face, a leather strap, nothing that draws attention. I have never been interested in smartwatches, because I already have quite enough devices {competing for my attention|e'tiborim uchun kurashayotgan}.

p2.task: Describe a place you have been to where an event took place.
bullets: and explain how you felt about the place
p2.ans:
The place I would like to describe is Registan Square in Samarkand, and the event I want to talk about is a music festival that is held there every couple of years, which I attended two summers ago.

Registan is essentially a courtyard enclosed on three sides by enormous madrasas, all of them covered in blue and gold tilework, and it has been the ceremonial centre of the city for roughly six hundred years. For the festival, a stage is built at the open end and several thousand seats are laid out across the square, so the buildings themselves become the {backdrop|orqa fon}.

I went with my parents and my sister on the opening evening, which began at around eight, once the heat had {subsided|pasaygan}. The programme was a mixture of traditional Uzbek music and ensembles from other countries, and it ran for close to three hours. What made it extraordinary was the lighting: as the sky darkened, the facades were {lit from below|pastdan yoritilgan}, and the tiles, which look impressive enough in daylight, became genuinely spectacular.

How I felt about it is difficult to separate from the setting. I have walked through that square hundreds of times and I had, frankly, {stopped noticing it|e'tibor bermay qoʻygandim} - that is what happens with monuments in your own city. Seeing it used for something living rather than photographed by visitors {restored|tikladi} it for me.

There was also a thought I could not quite {shake off|yoʻqotib boʻlmadi}: that those madrasas were built as places of learning and debate, and that an evening of music in front of several thousand people was, in its way, closer to their original purpose than a quiet queue of tourists. That is probably why the place has stayed with me.

p3: Where do people from your country usually go for holidays?

A great many travel domestically - Samarkand, Bukhara and the mountains near Tashkent are the obvious destinations. Internationally, Turkey and the UAE are extremely popular because flights are affordable and visa requirements are {relaxed|yengil}. A substantial number of people, though, spend holidays visiting relatives, which serves much the same purpose {at a fraction of the cost|arzimagan xarajatda}.
How do people usually plan their holidays?

Increasingly online - people compare prices, read reviews and book directly, which was not the case even five years ago. Travel agencies still handle the more complicated trips and anything involving visas. And a great deal of planning is really {word of mouth|ogʻzaki tavsiya}: people go where friends and relatives have recommended.
Why do some people prefer travelling abroad for their holidays?

Partly {novelty|yangilik} - a different language and culture makes a week feel much longer than a familiar destination would. There is also the appeal of things not available at home, such as a coastline. And, honestly, a degree of {status|maqom} is attached to foreign travel, which people are not always willing to acknowledge.
Are there any places in your country that are popular with tourists?

Very much so. Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva form the standard route, and they are among the best-preserved historic cities anywhere on the old Silk Road. The Chimgan mountains attract visitors for hiking and skiing, and there is growing interest in the Aral Sea region, which is a rather {sobering|oʻylantiradigan} kind of tourism.
What type of accommodation do people in your country usually prefer?

Domestically, staying with relatives remains extremely common and is the default for most families. For paid accommodation, mid-range hotels are the norm, though guesthouses in restored traditional houses have become popular, particularly in Bukhara. Short-term rentals are growing quickly among younger travellers, mainly because they are {considerably cheaper|ancha arzon} and allow you to cook.

sessions.t2: A friend's house you liked but would not live in
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my third year of a degree in management, so studying {takes up|egallaydi} most of my week, although I do some part-time work at weekends.
What do you like most about your work or studies?

The case-study work. Rather than learning theory in the abstract, we {pull apart|tahlil qilmoq} what an actual company did and argue about whether it was the right decision. It is far more engaging than memorising models, and it {sticks|yodda qoladi} much better.
Do you like shopping?

In small doses. Buying something I have planned for is enjoyable, but {drifting around|aylanib yurish} shops with no purpose {wears me out|meni charchatadi} within half an hour. I am very much a targeted shopper.
How often do you go shopping?

For food, two or three times a week at the local market. For anything else, perhaps once a month, and usually only because something has {worn out|eskirgan} rather than because I particularly want something new.
What do you usually buy when you go shopping?

Mostly {everyday essentials|kundalik ehtiyoj mollari} - food and household items. Beyond that, books, and occasionally something for studying. I try to buy one decent item rather than several cheap ones, which {works out cheaper|arzonroqqa tushadi} over time.
Do you prefer shopping online or in stores?

Online for anything standardised, because the selection is {vastly wider|ancha keng} and you can compare reviews. For food and clothes I still prefer going in person - {sizing is unpredictable|oʻlchamlar noaniq} and I like to inspect fresh produce myself.
Would you like to have an expensive car in the future?

Not especially, if I am honest. I would want something {reliable|ishonchli} and economical rather than impressive. An expensive car seems to me a large amount of money spent on something that {loses value|qadrsizlanadi} the moment you drive it away.
Would you prefer to be a passenger or the driver when travelling by car?

A passenger, for longer journeys at least - you can read, sleep or simply look out of the window. Driving requires {sustained concentration|uzluksiz diqqat}, which after a few hours becomes genuinely tiring. For short trips I would rather drive, because you are {in control of|nazoratdasiz} the timing.
What kind of car would you like to have?

Something small and economical - a compact hatchback, ideally hybrid or electric if the charging infrastructure {catches up|yetib oladi}. My priorities would be fuel consumption, ease of parking and low running costs rather than {performance|quvvat}.

p2.task: Describe a friend's house that you liked but would not want to live in.
bullets: and explain why you would not want to live there
p2.ans:
The house I want to describe belongs to a friend of mine called Timur, whose family lives about forty kilometres outside Tashkent, at the foot of the hills.

It is a large traditional house built around a courtyard, which is where the family actually lives for most of the year. There is a grapevine trained over a wooden frame that covers almost the whole courtyard, so even in August it stays {pleasantly shaded|yoqimli soyada}. Inside, the rooms are enormous by city standards, with high ceilings and very little furniture, and the whole place has a kind of {unhurried|shoshmasdan} quality that is difficult to describe.

What I liked about it was partly the space and partly the silence. From the roof you can see the hills, and at night there is essentially no {light pollution|yorugʻlik ifloslanishi}, so you can see an astonishing number of stars. There is also a small orchard at the back, and the fact that you can walk out and pick an apricot off a tree in July struck me as a genuine {luxury|hashamat}.

The reason I would not want to live there is entirely practical. It is forty minutes' drive from anything - the nearest proper shop is fifteen minutes away, there is no public transport to speak of, and everything {hinges on|bogʻliq} owning a car. In winter the road becomes difficult, and the house is expensive and laborious to heat, because those high ceilings that look so impressive are {a nightmare|dahshat} in January.

So I enjoy visiting enormously, and I always come back slightly {envious|hasad qilgan}. But I think I would find the isolation frustrating within about a month, which is probably the honest test of whether you would actually live somewhere.

p3: What are the most important things to consider when choosing a house to live in?

Location comes first for most people - proximity to work, schools and transport determines how you spend your time far more than the house itself does. After that, cost relative to income, the condition of the building, and whether the space {suits the way you actually live|hayot tarzingizga mos keladi} rather than how you imagine you will live. Noise and neighbours are consistently {underestimated|kam baholanadi}.
What are the differences between choosing a house in the countryside and choosing one in the city?

In a city you are buying access - to work, services and people - and space is what you {sacrifice|qurbon qilasiz}. In the countryside space is cheap and access is the problem, so you are effectively buying a car and a commute alongside the house. Rural buyers also have to think about things a city dweller never does, such as water supply and {self-sufficiency|mustaqil ta'minot} in winter.
Why do some people prefer living in the countryside?

Space and quiet, primarily, and the cost - the same money buys several times more house. Many also want their children to grow up outdoors, and some are simply {worn down by|charchagan} the pace and noise of city life. There is also a certain {romantic idea|romantik tasavvur} of rural living which, I suspect, does not always survive the first winter.
Do you think people's housing preferences change as they get older?

Substantially. Young people prioritise being close to work and nightlife and will tolerate a small flat for it. Families want space and schools. Older people tend to {trade space back|joyni qaytarib almashtiradi} for convenience and accessibility - a single-storey home near a clinic becomes far more valuable than a large garden. So preferences tend to move outwards and then back in again.
What kinds of gifts are popular in your country?

For weddings and major celebrations, {household goods|uy-roʻzgʻor buyumlari} and textiles are traditional, and money in an envelope is extremely common and entirely acceptable. For smaller occasions, sweets, tea sets and flowers. Among younger people, practical gifts and gift cards have become more normal, which older relatives sometimes find {impersonal|shaxsiy emas}.
When do people usually give gifts?

Weddings above all, which here involve a great deal of {reciprocal giving|oʻzaro sovgʻa berish}. Beyond that, births, Navruz, the start of the school year and religious holidays. Visiting someone's home essentially always involves bringing something, usually sweets or fruit - arriving {empty-handed|quruq qoʻl bilan} would be considered impolite.

sessions.t2: A noisy place you have been to
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my second year at university, so studying is very much my {full-time occupation|asosiy mashgʻulot} at the moment.
What are you studying?
I am studying food technology, which combines chemistry, biology and a fair amount of engineering. It is far more {technical|texnik} than people assume when they hear the name.
Why did you choose this subject?

Partly because agriculture is such an important industry here and there is a real shortage of specialists. I was also drawn to it because it is {tangible|aniq, koʻrinadigan} - you can see the result of what you study on a shelf, which is more satisfying than something purely theoretical.
Do you like eating fruit?

Very much - I eat some almost every day. We are extremely fortunate here, because the fruit is genuinely {exceptional|ajoyib} in summer and costs very little. In winter the choice {narrows considerably|ancha torayadi}, which makes you appreciate the season more.
What is your favourite fruit?

Melon, without hesitation, particularly the varieties grown around Khorezm. They are {intensely sweet|juda shirin} and the season is short, which somehow makes them better. Apricots would be a close second.
Do you often eat vegetables?

Every day, more or less. Tomatoes and cucumbers appear in almost every meal here, and I cook with onions, carrots and peppers constantly because they {form the base of|asosini tashkil qiladi} most of what I make.
What vegetables do you usually eat?

In summer, tomatoes, cucumbers and peppers, all of which are {abundant and cheap|moʻl va arzon}. In winter the range shrinks and we {fall back on|qaytamiz} pumpkin, cabbage and carrots, which keep well. I have also started eating a lot more greens than I used to.

p2.task: Describe a noisy place you have been to.
bullets: and explain how you felt about being there
p2.ans:
The noisiest place I have been to recently is Chorsu bazaar in Tashkent on a Saturday morning, which I visited with my mother a few months ago to buy food for a family gathering.

We arrived at around eight, which is more or less the peak. Chorsu is an enormous covered market under a domed roof, with hundreds of traders inside and several times that number in the streets around it, and on a weekend it is {heaving|gavjum}.

The noise comes from every direction at once. Traders call out prices continuously, each one trying to be heard over the next, and because the dome is a hard enclosed surface, everything {echoes and amplifies|aks sado berib kuchayadi}. Add several thousand people talking, trolleys being dragged over concrete, and somebody's radio, and the result is a wall of sound you feel as much as hear. My mother and I had to {raise our voices|ovozimizni koʻtarish} to speak even standing side by side.

How I felt about it was genuinely mixed, and it changed as the morning went on. For the first twenty minutes I found it {overwhelming|bosim oʻtkazadigan} - I could not concentrate on what we were buying and I remember wanting to leave. But after a while something shifted and I stopped {resisting|qarshilik qilish} it. The noise stopped being an obstacle and became part of the experience, and by the time we left, two hours later, I had rather enjoyed myself.

What it made me realise is that noise is not a single thing. The same volume that is intolerable in a traffic jam becomes {invigorating|ruhlantiruvchi} in a market, because it is human and because you chose to be there. It is the noise you cannot escape that actually damages people.

p3: What places are usually noisy in your city?

Markets are the obvious ones, along with major road junctions and the areas around transport hubs. Construction sites have become a significant source in recent years, since building is happening almost everywhere. And {entertainment districts|koʻngilochar hududlar} in the evening, though that noise is at least {confined to|cheklangan} certain streets and hours.
Why are some places in cities noisier than others?

Mainly {traffic density|transport zichligi} and how the buildings are arranged - narrow streets with hard surfaces trap and reflect sound, whereas trees and open space absorb it. Land use matters too: districts that mix housing with commerce and industry are inevitably louder than purely residential ones, which is really a {planning decision|reja qarori} rather than an accident.
What problems can noise cause for people?

Sleep disturbance is the most immediate and the most serious, because almost every other health problem follows from poor sleep. There is solid evidence linking chronic noise exposure to raised blood pressure and stress hormones. It also {impairs|zaiflashtiradi} concentration and learning - studies of schools near airports show measurable effects on reading. And it affects quality of life in a way that is hard to quantify but that people {feel keenly|keskin his qiladi}.
What can be done to reduce noise in cities?

Several things work well. Traffic is the main source, so lowering speed limits, {resurfacing|qayta qoplash} roads with quieter asphalt and pedestrianising central streets all have measurable effects. Trees and green barriers absorb a surprising amount. Building regulations requiring proper {sound insulation|tovush izolyatsiyasi} in new housing help, and enforcing restrictions on construction hours costs almost nothing.

sessions.t2: Listening to something you were not interested in
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my final year, so a great deal of my time at the moment is {taken up by|band qilgan} my dissertation.
What do you study?

I study psychology, which is a much more {empirical|empirik} subject than most people expect. There is a great deal of statistics involved alongside the theory, and we spend a considerable amount of time on research design.
What is the most interesting part of your studies?

Cognitive psychology, without question - specifically how {unreliable|ishonchsiz} memory turns out to be. The idea that people confidently recall events that never happened is genuinely unsettling, and it has {changed how I listen to|qanday tinglashimni oʻzgartirdi} anyone describing something from the past, including myself.
Do you think you are a polite person?

I would like to think so, though it is an awkward thing to claim about yourself. I make an effort with greetings and with people in service jobs, who are {routinely overlooked|doimo e'tibordan chetda qoladi}. Whether I am always polite when I am tired is a different question.
Who taught you to be polite?

My parents, and particularly my grandmother, who was extremely {particular about|talabchan edi} how you addressed older people. Most of it was taught by example rather than instruction - children {absorb|oʻzlashtiradi} the way adults around them behave long before anyone explains the rules.
How do you usually show politeness to other people?

Small, consistent things: greeting people properly rather than {perfunctorily|shunchaki}, letting someone finish what they are saying, giving up a seat. I also try to thank people specifically rather than generally, because a vague thank you is {easy to see through|darrov sezilib qoladi}.
Are people in your country generally polite?

Broadly yes, particularly in terms of hospitality, which is taken extremely seriously here - a guest is treated with a formality that visitors often find remarkable. Politeness towards {strangers|notanish odamlar} in traffic or in a queue is perhaps less consistent, and the contrast between the two is quite noticeable.

p2.task: Describe a time when someone talked to you about something you were not interested in, but you kept listening.
bullets: and explain why you kept listening
p2.ans:
The occasion I want to describe is a long conversation with an elderly neighbour of ours, a man in his eighties, about the history and mechanics of beekeeping, which lasted the better part of two hours.

It happened last spring. I had gone round to help him move some furniture, and afterwards he offered tea, which here effectively means you are staying. He kept hives for around forty years before his eyesight {deteriorated|yomonlashdi}, and once the subject came up, he began at the beginning and worked steadily forward.

He explained how a colony is structured, how you tell when a hive is about to {swarm|koʻchish}, which flowering plants produce which kind of honey, and how the winters in the 1970s had affected his yields. He was extremely precise about all of it - dates, quantities, the prices he used to get.

I was not interested, in all honesty. I have no intention of keeping bees and I retained perhaps a tenth of what he told me. It was also, in places, {highly technical|juda texnik}, and he assumed a background knowledge I simply did not have.

I kept listening for three reasons. The first is straightforward: it would have been rude to cut him off, and in our culture you do not {curtail|qisqartirmoq} an older person mid-story. The second is that it gradually became obvious he did not have many people to talk to, and that the subject mattered to him far more than the information itself did.

The third reason is the one that surprised me. About an hour in, I stopped listening for content and started listening to how he talked about it, and the {sheer pleasure|chinakam zavq} he took in something so specific was genuinely moving. I left thinking that being interested in the person is a perfectly good substitute for being interested in the topic.

p3: What happens if you do not listen carefully when others are talking?

The immediate consequence is misunderstanding, which then takes far longer to {undo|tuzatish} than listening properly would have taken. Beyond the practical cost, people notice, and they feel {dismissed|e'tiborsiz qoldirilgan}. Repeated often enough, half-listening quietly damages a relationship, usually without either side being able to say exactly when it happened.
Why do some people talk about things that other people are not interested in?

Often they simply cannot tell - they are {absorbed in|berilib ketgan} the subject and miss the signals. Sometimes it is loneliness: the talking matters more than the topic. And occasionally it is a lack of {social awareness|ijtimoiy sezgirlik}, particularly with people who are used to being listened to and have never had to check.
Is it polite to stop someone when you are not interested in what they are saying?

It depends entirely on how it is done. {Cutting someone off|gapini boʻlish} abruptly is rude in almost any culture. But gently redirecting a conversation, or saying honestly that you need to leave, is perfectly acceptable and arguably kinder than {feigning|oʻzini koʻrsatish} interest for an hour. What matters is that the person does not feel their subject was worthless.
Why is it important to listen carefully when someone is talking to you?

Because most disagreements come from half-listening rather than from genuine difference. Careful listening also {defuses|yumshatadi} conflict remarkably quickly - people become far less defensive once they feel heard. And practically, it saves enormous amounts of time that would otherwise go into correcting avoidable mistakes.
How can people show that they are listening to someone?

{Body language|tana tili} helps - eye contact, an open posture, putting the phone away - but it is easy to fake. The genuine signals are in the response: asking a follow-up question, summarising what was said before disagreeing, or referring back to something mentioned earlier. Anyone can nod while {miles away|xayoli boshqa joyda}.

sessions.examiner: David (elderly British man, grey hair and glasses)
sessions.t2: A sports event you watched and enjoyed
p1: Is your hometown a busy or a quiet place?

Busy, without much doubt - Tashkent is the largest city in Central Asia and the traffic alone makes that obvious. That said, it is a city of {pockets|alohida hududlar}: the residential courtyards can be remarkably calm even a street away from something very loud.
What kind of facilities does your hometown offer?

Almost everything you would expect from a capital - a metro system, hospitals, universities, theatres, a great many parks. What has improved most noticeably in recent years is {public space|jamoat maydonlari}: pedestrian areas and renovated parks.
