What is still {lacking|yetishmayotgan} is parking and cycling infrastructure.
Do you know the people there well?

In my own mahalla, yes - neighbours are involved in each other's lives to a degree that visitors find {surprising|hayratlanarli}. Across the city as a whole, obviously not; Tashkent is far too large for that, and people tend to know their own district and very little beyond it.
How does it feel to be a teacher?

Rewarding and {draining in equal measure|bir xil darajada charchatadigan}. I teach English part-time at a centre, and the good moments - when something finally clicks for a student who has been struggling - are genuinely {exhilarating|ruhlantiruvchi}. The difficult part is that you are performing for four hours straight.
Is it easy to be a teacher?

Not at all, and I say that having assumed it would be. Explaining something clearly is a skill in itself, and managing a group of fifteen people with different levels and different motivations is {considerably harder|ancha qiyin} than the subject knowledge. Preparation also takes far longer than the lesson itself.
Do you like your teacher?

I do - my main lecturer this year is excellent. She is extremely {demanding|talabchan} but entirely fair, and she gives feedback that is specific rather than general, which is rarer than it should be. You always know exactly where you stand with her.
Which teacher do you like more, your secondary school teacher or your teacher at an educational centre?

They are difficult to compare, because the settings are so different. My school teachers had thirty students and a fixed syllabus, so there was very little room to {tailor|moslashtirmoq} anything. The centre teachers work with small groups by choice, so the teaching is far more {responsive|moslashuvchan}. On balance I learned more at the centre, but that is a matter of conditions rather than ability.
Do you like teaching?

Very much, more than I expected to. What I enjoy is that it forces you to understand something {thoroughly|puxta} - you cannot explain what you only half know. I also like the immediacy of it; you can see within seconds whether an explanation has worked.
What do you enjoy most about teaching?

The moment a student who has decided they are bad at something discovers they are not. Changing somebody's {self-assessment|oʻziga bergan bahosi} does far more for their progress than any amount of grammar, and it is the part of the job that {stays with you|esingizda qoladi} afterwards.

p2.task: Describe a sports event you watched and enjoyed.
bullets: where and when you watched it
and explain why you enjoyed it
p2.ans:
The event I would like to describe is a World Cup qualifying match that I watched at the national stadium in Tashkent about a year ago, with my brother and two of his friends.

It was an evening game in autumn, and the stadium was essentially full - somewhere around thirty-five thousand people. We had seats fairly close to the section where the organised supporters stand, which turned out to be both the best and the worst place to sit.

The match itself was, by any technical standard, not a good one. It finished one-all and both goals were rather {scrappy|tartibsiz}. What made the evening was everything around it. The noise was continuous for the full ninety minutes - drumming, chanting, and whenever anything happened, a {roar|gulduros} you felt physically rather than simply heard. When our side equalised in the last fifteen minutes, the sound was genuinely {deafening|quloqni qomatga keltiradigan}, and for a few seconds it was impossible to think clearly.

What I enjoyed most, though, was something I had not anticipated. Watching a match live is a completely different experience from watching it on television, because the camera {follows the ball|toʻpni kuzatadi} and you only see a fraction of what is happening. In the stadium you can watch players moving into space thirty seconds before the ball arrives, and you realise how much of football takes place {away from the action|harakatdan uzoqda}.

The other reason I enjoyed it is harder to define. Several thousand people, most of whom had nothing else in common, were all reacting to the same thing at the same instant. You cannot get that from a screen, however good the coverage is, and I came away thinking that what people actually buy a ticket for is a few hours of {belonging to something|biror narsaga mansublik}.

p3: Do competitions increase people's stress?

They certainly can, particularly when the {stakes|ulush, xavf} are high or when someone's identity depends on the result. A moderate amount of pressure actually improves performance - that is well established - but beyond a point it {tips over into|oʻtib ketadi} anxiety that damages it. The deciding factor is usually whether the person feels the competition is fair and whether failure is {recoverable|tuzatib boʻladigan}.
Why do many people think that competitions are unfair or unequal nowadays?

Because in many cases they genuinely are. Access to good coaching, equipment and training facilities depends heavily on money, so two competitors are rarely starting from the same position. In sport specifically there are also long-running concerns about {doping|dopingsi} and about the financial gap between wealthy clubs and everyone else, which makes the outcome feel {predetermined|oldindan belgilangan}.
What are the drawbacks of competing with others?

Constant comparison can {undermine|zaiflashtiradi} motivation, particularly for people who consistently lose - they conclude ability is fixed and stop trying. Competition can also damage relationships and encourage {cutting corners|qoidani buzish} to win. And it narrows the definition of success: things that cannot be measured against someone else tend to be treated as worthless.
Can competition have positive effects on people?

Definitely, when it is {well matched|teng kuchli}. Competition raises effort - almost everyone performs better against someone than alone - and it provides clear feedback, which most of life does not. It also teaches preparation, resilience and how to lose {gracefully|munosib tarzda}, which is a genuinely useful skill.
Does hosting an international sports event help improve relationships between countries?

It can, though I would be careful not to {overstate|boʻrttirib yubormoq} it. Hosting raises a country's profile, brings in visitors and creates informal contact between people who would otherwise never meet, and that does {soften|yumshatadi} mutual stereotypes. But sport can also intensify rivalry, and hosting is sometimes used quite deliberately to improve a government's image, which is a different thing from improving relations.
How can international sporting events bring people from different countries together?

Mainly by providing a shared framework where everyone {follows the same rules|bir xil qoidalarga amal qiladi} regardless of politics, which is rarer than it sounds. The informal side matters most - athletes living together, supporters travelling and discovering the hosts are ordinary people. Events that include cultural programmes alongside the sport tend to {leave a more lasting impression|uzoqroq taassurot qoldiradi} than the competition itself.

sessions.t2: A person who makes things by hand and with technology
p1: Where do you live?
I live in Namangan, in a residential district about fifteen minutes from the centre. It is a mixture of older houses with courtyards and newer apartment blocks, and my family is in one of the houses.
What do you like about the place where you live?

The courtyard, above all - it effectively doubles our living space for half the year. Beyond that, the neighbours, who have been there for decades, and the fact that the market is {a short walk away|bir necha qadam narida}, which matters more day to day than anything else.
Is there anything you would like to change about the place where you live?

The traffic on the main road, which has become considerably worse, and the lack of green space - a lot of the original planting has been {built over|qurilib ketgan}. I would also like better drainage, because heavy rain still {floods|suv bosadi} several streets every spring.
What is the most interesting thing about the place where you live?

Probably the flower growing. Namangan has a long tradition of it and there are growers on our street who have been cultivating the same varieties for generations. In spring the whole district {comes alive|jonlanadi} with it, and people travel from other regions to buy.
Do you think you are a polite person?

I would like to think so, though it is a difficult thing to claim about yourself. I make a conscious effort with greetings and with people working in service jobs, who are {routinely overlooked|doimo e'tibordan chetda qoladi}. Whether I manage it when I am tired is another matter.
Who taught you to be polite?

My parents, and especially my grandfather, who was extremely {strict about|qat'iy edi} how you addressed older people. Very little of it was taught explicitly - you {absorb|oʻzlashtirasiz} the way adults around you behave long before anyone explains the rules.
How do you usually show politeness to other people?

Through small consistent things: greeting people properly rather than {perfunctorily|shunchaki}, letting someone finish speaking, offering my seat. I also try to thank people for something specific rather than generally, because a vague thank you is {easy to see through|darrov sezilib qoladi}.
Why is it important to be polite?

Because it is the {lubricant|moylovchi vosita} of ordinary life - it costs nothing and prevents an enormous number of unnecessary conflicts. It also signals respect, which matters most precisely when you disagree with someone. Societies where basic courtesy {breaks down|buziladi} become exhausting to live in very quickly.
Are people in your country generally polite?

Broadly yes, particularly regarding hospitality, which is taken extremely seriously - a guest is treated with a formality visitors often find remarkable. Politeness towards {strangers|notanish odamlar} in traffic or in a queue is less consistent, and that contrast is quite noticeable.
Are children taught to be polite at school?

To some degree, yes - there is explicit teaching about respect for elders and teachers, and it is reinforced constantly. But I would say the {bulk of it|katta qismi} still comes from home. School can reinforce what a family has established; it struggles to create it {from nothing|yoʻqdan}.

p2.task: Describe a person you know who makes things, both by hand and using technology.
bullets: how they combine handwork and technology
and explain why you admire what they do
p2.ans:
The person I want to describe is a man called Bekzod, who is about thirty and who runs a small workshop in Namangan making furniture and decorative wooden panels.

I know him because he made a set of doors for my uncle's house, and I ended up spending an afternoon in his workshop while they were being fitted.

What makes him interesting is that he works in two completely different ways at once. He was trained traditionally - he spent years as an {apprentice|shogird} to an older carver and he still does the fine work entirely by hand, with chisels his teacher gave him. But he also bought a small computer-controlled cutting machine about four years ago, and he now designs everything digitally first.

The way he combines the two is genuinely clever. He draws the pattern on a computer, which lets him test proportions and {make adjustments|oʻzgartirish kiritish} in minutes rather than redrawing by hand. The machine then cuts the {repetitive|takrorlanuvchi} elements - the parts that are identical forty times over and that used to take days of dull work. Everything that requires judgement, though - the depth of a cut, the finishing, anything that will be looked at closely - he still does himself. He says the machine removes the drudgery and leaves the craft, which strikes me as {exactly the right way round|aynan toʻgʻri yondashuv}.

What I admire is that he refused to treat it as a choice. A lot of traditional craftsmen here regard machinery as {a betrayal|xiyonat}, and a lot of younger people who buy machines have no craft at all and produce things that are technically perfect and completely {lifeless|jonsiz}. He managed to take what each is good at, and as a result he produces more, charges less and has kept a skill alive that would otherwise be {dying out|yoʻqolib borayotgan}.

p3: What kinds of things do people like to make by hand?

Food is easily the most common, and here bread and preserves in particular. Beyond that, clothing and knitting, woodwork, and traditional crafts such as embroidery and ceramics, which remain genuinely alive in this country rather than being purely {decorative|bezak uchun}. People also increasingly make things for their homes, partly for cost and partly because the result is {unrepeatable|takrorlanmas}.
Why do some people prefer making things themselves rather than buying them?

The satisfaction of producing something is hard to match, and there is a {sense of ownership|egalik hissi} in an object you made that a purchase never provides. There are practical reasons too: better quality for the money, and exactly the size or colour you wanted. And for many people the process itself is {therapeutic|tinchlantiruvchi} - it is one of the few activities that fully occupies your attention.
What kinds of things do children like to make?

Younger children make things from paper, cardboard and modelling clay, largely because those materials {forgive mistakes|xatoga yoʻl qoʻyadi}. Older children move towards models, drawings and, increasingly, digital creations - videos, simple games, edited images. What is consistent is that they prefer making something they can {show to someone|kimgadir koʻrsatish} immediately.
Do children prefer making things by hand or using technology?

It varies with age and with what they have been exposed to. Younger children generally prefer physical materials, because the {feedback is immediate|natija darhol koʻrinadi} and they can touch the result. Older children often move to digital tools, partly because mistakes can be {undone|bekor qilish} and partly because the results look more professional. Ideally they should do both, since the skills are different.
Should schools teach art to children?

Absolutely, and not merely as a break from academic subjects. Art develops {fine motor skills|mayda motorika}, spatial reasoning and the tolerance for producing something imperfect and improving it. It also gives children who struggle academically a genuine chance to {excel|zoʻr boʻlish} at something, which changes how they see themselves across every subject.
How can schools help children develop their creativity?

By setting tasks with more than one correct answer, which most of the curriculum does not. Giving children {open-ended|cheklanmagan} materials and time without a specified outcome matters enormously. And, crucially, by not grading everything - creativity requires being willing to produce something bad, and that {disappears the moment|yoʻqoladi, agar} every attempt is assessed.

sessions.t2: Someone who wants to work in the medical field
p1: Do you work or are you a student?

I work - I finished my degree last year and I am now employed at a logistics company, although I still think of myself as a student in some respects, because I am {learning constantly|doimiy oʻrganmoqdaman}.
What do you do?

I am a junior coordinator, which mainly means tracking shipments, dealing with documentation and identifying where a delay has {crept in|paydo boʻlgan}. It is less glamorous than it sounds but it teaches you a great deal about how things actually work.
What do you like most about your work or studies?

Solving problems that have a visible result. When I find a route that saves two days on a delivery, that is a {tangible|aniq} improvement, and it is considerably more satisfying than work where you never see the outcome.
Is there anything you would like to change about your work or studies?

The amount of {repetitive|takrorlanuvchi} paperwork - a good deal of what I do could be automated and simply has not been yet. I would also like more structured training; most of what I know I learned by {trial and error|sinov va xato yoʻli bilan}, which is slow and occasionally expensive.
What kind of websites do you often visit?

News sites and a couple of industry resources for work, along with video platforms in the evening. I also use forums quite heavily, because people there discuss problems {in depth|chuqur} rather than in the short, shallow way social media encourages.
What do you usually use websites for?

Information first - news, reference material, anything work-related. After that, communication, and then entertainment. Increasingly I also use them for {routine transactions|kundalik amaliyotlar}: paying bills, booking tickets, dealing with official documents, all of which used to mean queuing.
What kind of websites are popular in your country?

Messaging and social platforms dominate, Telegram above all - it is used here for news, shopping and business as much as for conversation. Beyond that, {classified advertising|e'lonlar} sites and government service portals, which have improved {beyond recognition|tanib boʻlmas darajada} in recent years.
Do you prefer using websites on a computer or on your phone?

A computer for anything serious - a larger screen makes comparison and typing far easier, and I {take in|oʻzlashtiraman} written material better that way. The phone is for quick checks and messaging. I have noticed I read far more {superficially|yuzaki} on a phone, which is worth being aware of.

p2.task: Describe someone you know who wants to work in the medical field.
bullets: and explain whether you think they will succeed
p2.ans:
The person I want to describe is my cousin Kamila, who is in her fourth year at medical university in Tashkent and who intends to specialise in paediatrics.

She is two years older than me and we grew up spending most summers together, so I have watched this ambition develop {from the very beginning|boshidanoq}. Even as a child she was the one who {took charge|mas'uliyatni oʻz zimmasiga olardi} when someone fell over, and she was strangely unbothered by things the rest of us found alarming.

Her choice of specialisation was not accidental. Her younger brother was seriously ill for several months when she was around fourteen, and she spent a great deal of that period in hospital with him. What struck her, by her own account, was not the treatment but the difference the staff made - one doctor in particular took the time to explain everything to her parents in plain language, and she describes that as the moment she decided. So her motivation has always been quite {specific|aniq} rather than a vague desire to help people.

Medical training here is long and {notoriously demanding|juda mashaqqatli ekani ma'lum}. She works harder than anyone else I know, and she has already begun volunteering at a clinic in order to {gain practical exposure|amaliy tajriba orttirish} well before she is formally required to.

As for whether she will succeed, I am fairly confident she will, and not primarily because she is academically strong, although she is. It is her temperament: she stays calm, she listens properly, and she is very good at explaining complicated things simply - which in paediatrics matters as much as clinical knowledge, since you are effectively treating the parents as well as the child. If I have a concern, it is that she will {work herself into the ground|oʻzini charchatib qoʻyish}, because she finds it almost impossible to say no.

p3: Do you think biology is easier than other subjects?

It is easier to {get started in|kirishish} than physics or chemistry, because the early material is descriptive and requires less mathematics. But I would resist calling it easy - at a higher level it involves enormous amounts of detail and a great deal of statistics, and it is arguably harder precisely because living systems are so {variable|oʻzgaruvchan}. There are very few clean rules.
Why do some students find biology difficult?

Mainly the {sheer volume|hajmining koʻpligi} of terminology - there is a great deal to memorise before anything makes sense. It is also taught in many schools as a list of facts rather than as a set of connected mechanisms, so students never see why any of it {hangs together|bir-biriga bogʻlanadi}. And the amount of chemistry involved surprises people who chose it to avoid the hard sciences.
Should technology be used more in medicine?

Yes, though {selectively|tanlab}. Diagnostic tools using artificial intelligence already outperform humans in specific tasks such as reading scans, and remote consultation makes a genuine difference in regions where specialists are scarce. The caution I would add is that technology should {augment|toʻldirish} clinical judgement rather than replace it, and that patient data raises serious privacy questions that are not yet properly settled.
What are the advantages of using technology in medicine?

Earlier and more accurate diagnosis, above all, since machines do not {tire or lose concentration|charchamaydi va diqqatini yoʻqotmaydi}. Digital records prevent a great many avoidable errors, particularly with medication. Telemedicine removes distance as a barrier, which in a country with large rural areas is significant. And automating routine work {frees clinicians|shifokorlarni ozod qiladi} for the parts of the job only a person can do.
Should governments invest more money in medicine?

I think so, and the argument is economic rather than purely humanitarian - untreated illness costs far more in lost work and emergency care than prevention does. The important qualification is that investment must reach {primary care and rural provision|birlamchi va qishloq tibbiyoti}, not only flagship hospitals in the capital, which is a common failing.
What areas of medicine should governments invest in?

Primary care first, because most conditions are cheapest to treat early. Then training and retaining staff, since equipment is useless without people and {emigration|migratsiya} of qualified doctors is a real problem here. Beyond that, preventive public health - vaccination, screening, clean water - which produces {by far the best return|eng katta samara} per unit of money spent, and mental health provision, which is consistently underfunded.

sessions.t2: An interesting neighbour
p1: Do you like sports?

I do, though I am considerably more of a spectator than a participant. I follow football closely and I enjoy watching athletics, but my own involvement is fairly {modest|kamtarona} - mostly running and the occasional game with friends.
What sports do you enjoy watching?

Football above all, and I make a point of watching the national team. I also enjoy wrestling, which has a long tradition here, and I find athletics compelling during major championships, particularly the middle-distance events where the {tactics|taktika} are visible.
Do you often play sports?

Not as often as I should. I run two or three times a week, and I play football perhaps twice a month with friends. I would like to be more {consistent|izchil}, but it tends to be the first thing that {gets squeezed out|siqib chiqariladi} when I am busy.
What sports are popular in your country?

Football is by far the most popular to watch. In terms of participation and international success, wrestling, judo and boxing are our strongest, and they have a genuinely {deep-rooted|chuqur ildizli} tradition. Volleyball and tennis have also grown noticeably in recent years.
Do you prefer watching sports or playing them?

I enjoy both but for entirely different reasons. Playing is better for me - it is exercise and it {clears my head|boshimni tiniqlashtiradi}. Watching is more social, and there is a {shared drama|umumiy hayajon} to it that playing at my level certainly does not provide.
Do you like reading?

Very much, although I read less than I would like. I usually manage a chapter before bed, and I try to {alternate between|navbat bilan} fiction and non-fiction so that I do not get stuck in one register.
What kind of books do you enjoy reading?

Historical non-fiction mostly, and biographies, which I find far more {illuminating|yorituvchi} than general histories because you see events through someone actually living them. For fiction I prefer novels with a strong sense of place.
How often do you read?

Most evenings, for twenty or thirty minutes. It is not a great deal, but I have found that a small daily amount {adds up|jamlanadi} far more reliably than intending to read for three hours at the weekend and never doing it.
Did you read a lot when you were a child?

Far more than I do now. Reading was my main form of entertainment and I could {devour|yutib yubormoq} a book in a weekend. Now it {competes with|raqobatlashadi} a phone, which is not a fair contest, so although what I read is more demanding, the quantity has clearly fallen.
Do you prefer reading books or reading online?

Physical books for anything I want to think about, because I concentrate better and I remember where things were on the page. Online is better for articles and for anything I need to search. I have also noticed I read far more {superficially|yuzaki} on a screen, which is a real drawback.

p2.task: Describe an interesting neighbour you know.
bullets: how long they have been your neighbour
and explain how you get on with them
p2.ans:
The neighbour I want to describe is a man called Rustam, who lives directly opposite us and who has been there for as long as I can remember - certainly more than twenty years.

He is in his sixties now and retired, but he spent his working life as a railway engineer, which is where most of what makes him interesting {originates|kelib chiqadi}. He worked on the lines across the whole country, and he can tell you, in genuinely extraordinary detail, why a particular route takes the path it does, what the ground conditions were, and which bridge nearly {came to grief|halokatga uchrashiga sal qoldi} in the 1980s.

What makes him interesting, though, is not only the knowledge. It is that he has turned retirement into something quite unusual. About eight years ago he started building working models of the stations he had worked on, in considerable detail, in what used to be a storeroom in his house. There are now something like fifteen of them, complete with working lights. Children from the street are allowed in to look on condition they {touch nothing|hech narsaga tegmaslik}, a rule enforced with the seriousness of a museum.

He is also the unofficial {fixer|hal qiluvchi} of our street. If anything electrical stops working, people ask him before they call anyone, and he almost always knows why.

I get on with him extremely well, although I would describe the relationship as friendly rather than close. We talk for ten minutes in the street perhaps twice a week, and he has helped my family out several times without ever {making anything of it|buni pesh qilmasdan}. What I value most is that he treats young people as equals, which is not universal in his generation, and consequently everyone on the street {thinks highly of|yuqori baholaydi} him.

p3: Do you know your neighbours well?

Yes, unusually well by international standards. We live in a mahalla, where neighbours are involved in each other's lives {as a matter of course|oddiy hol sifatida} - everyone contributes to weddings and funerals, and people notice if something is wrong. It is closer than many people elsewhere would find comfortable, but it does mean nobody is really {left to cope alone|yolgʻiz qoldirilgan}.
What kind of people make good neighbours?

People who are {considerate without being intrusive|xalaqit bermay, e'tiborli} - who keep the noise down, look after shared space, and are willing to help without needing to be asked twice. Reliability matters: someone who will take a delivery or keep an eye on your house. And crucially, someone who can {let small things go|kichik narsalarni kechirish} rather than escalating them.
Is it important to have a good relationship with your neighbours?

Very, for practical and psychological reasons alike. Practically, neighbours are the people who can help {at short notice|qisqa muddatda} when nobody else can reach you. Psychologically, knowing the people around you produces a measurable sense of security. And a bad relationship with someone you cannot avoid seeing daily is {corrosive|ruhni yemiradi} in a way people underestimate.
What problems can people have with their neighbours?

Noise is the most common by a wide margin, followed by disputes over {shared space|umumiy joy} - parking, boundaries, rubbish. Pets and building work also generate a great deal of friction. What turns a minor issue into a lasting conflict is almost always how it was first raised: people who complain formally before speaking directly tend to {entrench|qat'iylashtirish} the problem.
Why do some people not know their neighbours?

Mobility, mainly - where people move every year or two, there is little reason to invest in the relationship. Working hours mean many people are simply never home at the same time. Apartment design contributes as well: buildings with no shared space give people nowhere to {cross paths|duch kelish}. And in large cities there is a certain {reserve|tortinchoqlik} about approaching strangers.
Has the relationship between neighbours changed compared with the past?

In cities, clearly - it has become more {distant and transactional|uzoq va rasmiy}. People once relied on neighbours for tools, childcare and information, and now they can buy or search for all three. Here the mahalla system has {slowed that decline|bu jarayonni sekinlashtirgan} considerably, but even so, younger families in new apartment blocks know their neighbours far less well than my parents' generation did.
What can people do to build better relationships with their neighbours?

Start small and start early - introducing yourself when you move in makes everything afterwards easier. Beyond that, {shared activity|umumiy faoliyat} works better than anything: a communal clean-up, a street celebration, anything that gives people a reason to stand in the same place. And being the first to offer help rather than to ask for it tends to {set the tone|ohangni belgilaydi}.

sessions.t2: A tall building you like or dislike
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my second year of a four-year degree, so studying is very much my {principal occupation|asosiy mashgʻulot} at the moment.
What are you studying?
I am studying civil engineering, which is a mixture of mathematics, materials science and design. There is far more {fieldwork|dala ishi} involved than people expect, which is the part I enjoy most.
Why did you choose this subject?

Because it produces something permanent. A building or a bridge you design may still be standing in eighty years, which is quite a {sobering thought|jiddiy oʻylantiradigan fikr}. I was also good at mathematics and wanted to apply it to something {concrete|aniq} rather than abstract.
Do you have a favourite teacher?

Yes, one of my lecturers in structural analysis. He is extremely {demanding|talabchan} but completely fair, and he has a habit of setting a problem that looks impossible and then showing you that it {breaks down into|boʻlinadi} three simple steps. Nobody teaches confidence better than that.
What makes a good teacher?

Patience, and genuine interest in whether the class has understood rather than whether the syllabus was covered. Good teachers can {explain the same idea|bir gʻoyani tushuntirish} in several different ways, and they are honest when they do not know something, which paradoxically makes students trust them more.
Do you think teachers are important?

Enormously. A good teacher can {shape a child's entire attitude to|bolaning butun munosabatini shakllantirmoq} a subject, and a poor one can put them off it permanently. Information is freely available now, but motivation and judgement still {come from people|odamlardan keladi}.
Have you ever had a teacher who influenced you?

Yes, my mathematics teacher in year ten. Until then I had assumed I was simply not a mathematical person, and she {took that assumption apart|bu fikrni yoʻqqa chiqardi} very patiently over about a year. I would not be studying engineering without her, which is a considerable thing to owe someone.
What do you usually buy when you go shopping?

Mostly {everyday essentials|kundalik ehtiyoj mollari} - food and household items. Beyond that, books and occasionally equipment for my course. I try to buy one good item rather than several cheap ones, which {works out cheaper|arzonroqqa tushadi} over time.
Do you prefer shopping online or in stores?

Online for anything standardised, because the selection is {far wider|ancha keng} and you can compare reviews. For clothes and food I much prefer going in person, since {sizing is unpredictable|oʻlchamlar noaniq} and I like to see what I am buying.
Do you often go shopping with other people?

Not usually - I am more efficient alone and I can be in and out in ten minutes. With friends it becomes a {social occasion|ijtimoiy tadbir}, which is enjoyable but takes three times as long. The exception is clothes, where I genuinely want a {second opinion|boshqa birovning fikri}.

p2.task: Describe a tall building you like or dislike.
bullets: and explain why you like or dislike it
p2.ans:
The building I would like to describe is the Tashkent Television Tower, which I like, and which I have been up twice.

It stands in the north of the capital and is around three hundred and seventy metres tall, which makes it comfortably the most visible structure in the city - you can see it from most districts. It was completed in the early 1980s and it looks entirely of its period: a slender concrete shaft rising out of three curved supporting legs, with an observation deck near the top that {flares outwards|kengayib chiqadi}, and above that a long antenna mast. The concrete is a pale grey, and there is a decorative metal lattice around the base which, from a distance, gives it a slightly {ornamental|bezakli} quality that most towers of that era entirely lack.

Functionally it is a broadcasting tower, so the great majority of its height is purely technical. The part the public uses is the observation deck and a rotating restaurant that completes a full turn roughly every hour, so you see the whole city {over the course of|davomida} a meal.

The reason I like it is partly personal and partly professional. Personally, it was the first tall building I ever went up, when I was about ten, and I remember being astonished that the city {extended so far|shunchalik uzoqqa choʻzilgan} beyond what I knew of it. Professionally, as an engineering student, I find the design genuinely impressive - it was built to {withstand|bardosh bermoq} a serious earthquake, which in this region is not a theoretical concern, and the three-legged base is a direct response to that.

What I like most, though, is that it has become a {landmark|moʻljal} in the proper sense. People give directions by it. A building that ordinary people use to {orient themselves|moʻljal olish} has earned its place, whatever anyone thinks of the style.

p3: Why do people like tall buildings?

The views are the obvious attraction, along with the sense of {scale|ulkanlik} - standing at the top of something very tall is genuinely impressive. Tall buildings also function as symbols of a city's ambition, which is why they appear on postcards. And architecturally, a well-designed tower can be beautiful in a way low buildings rarely {command attention|e'tiborni tortadi}.
What are the advantages of living in a tall building?

Better light and noticeably less street noise on the upper floors, along with views. Tall buildings tend to be {centrally located|markazda joylashgan}, so residents are close to work and services. Security is usually better because access is controlled, and modern towers often include facilities - parking, gyms - that are {impractical|amalga oshirib boʻlmaydigan} in low-rise housing.
What are the disadvantages of tall buildings?

Dependence on lifts is the practical one - a breakdown is genuinely serious for anyone on the twentieth floor - and {evacuation|evakuatsiya} in a fire or earthquake is a real concern. Socially they can be {isolating|yolgʻizlantiradigan}, since residents rarely meet. They also {overshadow|soya tashlaydi} neighbouring streets and create wind at ground level, which affects people who do not even live there.
How can tall buildings be decorated to make them more attractive?

Careful treatment of the facade matters most - varied materials, {setbacks|pogʻonali chekinish} and detail that rewards a close look, rather than an unbroken wall of glass. Lighting at night can transform a plain tower. Green walls and planted terraces both soften the appearance and help the environment. And the ground floor is critical: a tower with active, welcoming space at street level feels {entirely different|butunlay boshqacha} from one with a blank wall.
Should governments control the design of tall buildings?

To a degree, yes. Tall buildings affect everyone who lives near them - light, wind, traffic and skyline - so they are not purely a private matter. Regulation should focus on {impact|ta'sir} rather than taste: overshadowing, safety, infrastructure capacity and how the building meets the street. Controlling aesthetics directly is riskier, because official taste tends to produce {bland|bir xil} results.
Do you think there will be more tall buildings in the future?

Almost certainly, as urban populations grow and land becomes more expensive - building upwards is the only way to add housing without {sprawling outwards|yoyilib ketish}. Construction technology is also advancing; {timber|yogʻoch} high-rises are now viable and considerably greener. I would expect a shift towards {mixed-use|aralash maqsadli} towers, since single-purpose buildings leave districts deserted for half the day.
What makes a building attractive or unattractive?

Proportion above all - buildings that are badly proportioned look wrong even to people who cannot say why. Materials that {age well|yaxshi eskiradi} matter enormously; concrete that stains badly ruins an otherwise good design within a decade. And the relationship with its surroundings: a building that ignores its neighbours entirely tends to feel {arrogant|manman}, however impressive it is on its own.

sessions.t2: A friend from your childhood
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I work - I finished my studies two years ago and I have been employed since then, so my student days are {behind me|ortda qoldi}, though I do take short courses from time to time.
What work do you do?

I work in accounting for a medium-sized construction firm. Most of my time goes on {payroll|ish haqi} and reporting, and towards the end of each quarter it becomes considerably busier than the rest of the year.
Why did you choose that job?

Partly for {stability|barqarorlik} - accountants are needed in every industry, so the skill travels. But I also genuinely like the work: there is a correct answer, the figures either {reconcile|toʻgʻri keladi} or they do not, and I find that clarity satisfying in a way that more open-ended work is not.
Would you like to be a teacher?

Possibly, later on. I have thought about teaching accounting at a college once I have enough {practical experience|amaliy tajriba} to be worth listening to. I would not want to teach straight from theory, because students {see through that|buni darrov sezishadi} immediately.
Do you think you could be a teacher?

I think I could, with training. I am patient and I am reasonably good at explaining things, which colleagues tell me. What I would find hardest is managing a large group - holding the attention of thirty people is a completely {separate skill|alohida koʻnikma} from knowing the subject.
Did you have a favourite teacher?

Yes, my mathematics teacher in secondary school. He had a way of making a difficult problem look {approachable|yechsa boʻladigan} by breaking it into steps, and he never made anyone feel foolish for asking. A great deal of my confidence with numbers {traces back to|kelib chiqadi} his classes.

p2.task: Describe a friend from your childhood.
bullets: what you used to do together
and explain what this friendship meant to you
p2.ans:
The friend I want to describe is a boy called Javlon, who lived on the same street as us and who was my closest friend from roughly the age of six until we were fifteen.

We met in the most ordinary way - our mothers knew each other, and I was essentially {presented with|tanishtirildim} him as a playmate before either of us had any say in it. That is how most childhood friendships begin, I think. What was less ordinary is that it actually worked; we got on immediately and {stuck together|birga yurdik} for nine years.

What we did together was almost entirely outdoors. We played football in the street until it was too dark to see the ball, cycled to the canal in summer, and spent an entire autumn building what we insisted on calling a den out of scrap wood behind his house, which {collapsed twice|ikki marta qulab tushdi} before we gave up. In the winters we sat indoors and played chess, badly, for hours.

What the friendship meant to me is easier to see now than it was at the time. He was a far more {outgoing|kirishimli} person than I am naturally, and being around him pushed me into things I would otherwise have avoided - joining teams, speaking up, talking to people I did not know. I think a noticeable part of my personality was {shaped by|shakllantirilgan} nine years of trying to keep up with him.

It also taught me how to disagree with someone without losing them. We argued constantly, sometimes seriously, and it never once {occurred to either of us|ikkalamizning ham xayolimizga kelmadi} that the friendship might end over it. That turns out to be a genuinely useful thing to have learned early, and I am not sure I would have learned it anywhere else.

p3: What do you think of making friends online?

I think it is entirely legitimate, and the scepticism about it is largely {generational|avlodlar orasidagi farq}. Online friendships form around shared interests rather than geography, which for anyone with unusual interests is a genuine advantage. The limitation is that they rarely develop the {everyday intimacy|kundalik yaqinlik} that comes from simply being in the same place, and it is harder to judge someone you have never met.
Do we benefit from having friends with different personalities?

Enormously. Friends who think differently {challenge|shubha ostiga oladi} assumptions you would otherwise never examine, and they notice things you miss. A circle of people who all agree with you is comfortable and intellectually {stagnant|turgʻun}. The practical benefit is also real - different personalities are useful in different situations.
Would you only make friends with people who are similar to you?

No, and I think that would be a mistake, although it is the natural tendency - people gravitate towards those who {resemble them|oʻziga oʻxshaydi}. Some common ground is necessary, obviously, or there is nothing to build on. But the friendships that have taught me most have been with people whose background and opinions were quite {unlike|farqli} mine.
How and where do people in your country make friends these days?

School and university remain the main sources, simply because of repeated daily contact. After that, the workplace, and here the mahalla, where neighbours become friends {almost by default|deyarli oʻz-oʻzidan}. Among younger people, online communities and shared-interest groups have grown considerably, and sports clubs and language centres are also {fertile ground|qulay muhit}.
In what situations would people be willing to get to know new people?

Where there is a {shared purpose|umumiy maqsad} and a reason to speak - a course, a team, a work project, a long journey. People are far more open when the conversation has a natural excuse. They are much less willing in purely social settings with no structure, which is exactly why networking events feel so {forced|sun'iy} to most people.

sessions.t2: An enjoyable evening with friends
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my third year at university, so studying accounts for most of my week, although I tutor a couple of evenings to {cover my own expenses|xarajatlarimni qoplash}.
What do you like about your studies?

The practical assignments. Rather than learning theory in the abstract, we are given a real problem and expected to {work it through|hal qilib chiqish} ourselves, which is far more engaging and considerably more memorable than a lecture.
What do you dislike about your studies?

The amount of {rote learning|yodlash} in some modules - there are courses where success depends entirely on memorising definitions, and I have never found that a good test of anything. Some of the material also feels rather {dated|eskirgan} compared with what people actually do in the field.
Do you like listening to music?

Very much - it is more or less the {soundtrack to|ohangi} my day. I listen while commuting, studying and cooking, and long periods of silence feel slightly strange to me, which is probably a habit rather than a genuine preference.
Where do you usually listen to music?

On the bus and in my room, mostly, through headphones. I also listen while cooking, which is when I play it out loud. I rarely listen in company, because everyone {has their own taste|oʻz didi bor} and it becomes a negotiation.
Does music change the way you feel?

Considerably, and quite reliably. Something with a strong rhythm will {lift my mood|kayfiyatimni koʻtaradi} within a couple of minutes, and slower instrumental music genuinely helps me concentrate. I have learned to be careful with sad music, because it {amplifies|kuchaytiradi} whatever I already feel rather than balancing it.
Do you ever listen to songs that you dislike?

Occasionally, and usually not by choice - in a taxi, at a wedding, in a shop. Sometimes something I initially disliked {grows on me|asta-sekin yoqib qoladi} after enough exposure, which makes me suspect that a fair amount of taste is simply {familiarity|tanishlik}.

p2.task: Describe an enjoyable evening you have spent with your friends.
bullets: when and where it took place
and explain why the evening was so enjoyable
p2.ans:
The evening I want to describe was a dinner we organised at the end of the summer, about a month ago, at the home of one of my friends whose parents were away.

There were six of us, all people I have known since school, which is the important detail: since we left, everyone has {gone their separate ways|har biri oʻz yoʻlidan ketdi} - two are studying in Tashkent, one has started working, and getting all six of us in the same place now requires weeks of planning.

We had agreed that everyone would bring or cook one thing, which was, in retrospect, an {ambitious|jasoratli} arrangement given that at least half of us cannot cook. The result was a table with three salads, no main course to speak of and an enormous quantity of bread, which became the joke of the evening. We ended up ordering food at about ten o'clock.

What we actually did was talk, for close to seven hours. We arrived at seven and the last person left after two in the morning. Somebody found old photographs on a phone, which produced a great deal of laughter and a certain amount of {embarrassment|xijolat}, and at some point the conversation turned serious and we talked about what everyone genuinely wanted from the next few years - the kind of conversation that only happens {well past midnight|yarim tundan keyin}.

The reason it was so enjoyable was not the food, obviously. It was that there was nowhere else any of us had to be. Our meetings now are usually two hours squeezed between other commitments, and you spend most of that {catching up on facts|yangiliklarni aytib berish}. Seven unhurried hours is a completely different thing - it is long enough for the conversation to {go somewhere|biror joyga yetib borish}, and that is what I had been missing without quite realising it.

p3: Should governments spend money on large programmes that bring people together?

I think there is a reasonable case for it, provided the spending is {proportionate|mutanosib}. Festivals, public spaces and community sports facilities produce benefits that are real but difficult to measure - lower isolation, higher trust, better mental health. The objection is that such money could go to health or education instead, and the honest answer is that {social cohesion|ijtimoiy jipslik} is cheap to maintain and extremely expensive to repair once it has broken down.
What do friends usually do when they are together?

It depends on age, but in most cases the activity is really a {pretext|bahona} for the conversation. Younger people eat out, play sport or watch something; older people tend to meet at home. What is consistent is that the best time with friends tends to be {unstructured|rejasiz} - the activity finishes and the talking carries on.
Why do people enjoy spending time with their friends?

Because friends are people you have chosen, so there is less {obligation|majburiyat} and more genuine common ground than with family or colleagues. They also provide a kind of understanding that comes from being at the same stage of life. And practically, being with people you are comfortable with is one of the most reliable ways of {improving your mood|kayfiyatni koʻtarish} that exists.
Is it easier for people to make friends when they take part in group activities?

Considerably, yes. A shared activity provides a {natural excuse|tabiiy bahona} to speak and something to talk about, which removes the awkwardness that makes purely social settings so difficult. Repetition matters too - a weekly class produces friendships far more reliably than a single event, because familiarity {accumulates|jamlanadi} without anyone having to force it.
Do you think people spend enough time with their friends nowadays?

Generally not. Work has expanded, commutes are longer and a great deal of leisure time goes to screens, so friendship tends to be the thing that {gets squeezed out|siqib chiqariladi} when the week is full. The irony is that close friendship is one of the strongest predictors of wellbeing, which makes it precisely the wrong thing to {deprioritise|ikkinchi oʻringa qoʻymoq}.

sessions.t2: A building you like to visit
p1: What do you like about your flat?

The light, above all - the main rooms face south, so it is {bright|yorugʻ} from the morning onwards, and that makes a small space feel considerably larger. I also like the balcony, which has become where I {wind down|dam olaman} in the evening.
Is there anything you would like to change about your flat?

The kitchen, which is {cramped|tor} and poorly designed, so two people cooking {get in each other's way|bir-biriga xalaqit beradi}. I would knock down one wall and open it up, because the kitchen is where my family actually spends time.
Do you live in a flat or a house?
A flat, on the fifth floor of a nine-storey block. It has three rooms and a balcony, and although it is not large, it is {perfectly adequate|butunlay yetarli} for the four of us.
What is your favourite room in your flat?

The living room, because it is where everybody {converges|yigʻiladi} in the evening. It is the largest room and it also {doubles as|ikkinchi vazifasi} a guest room when relatives stay, which happens fairly often.
Generally, what is more popular in your country, living in a flat or a house?

It divides quite sharply by location. In cities, flats are the norm, mainly because of cost and availability. Outside cities, houses with courtyards remain {overwhelmingly|mutlaqo} the preference, partly for space and partly because the courtyard is central to how families here actually live.
What are the advantages of living in a house?

Space, obviously, and the outdoor area, which for families with children is a genuine {asset|boylik}. You also have far more control - you can extend or alter it without anyone's permission, and you are not affected by neighbours above and below. Many people here also grow food, which a flat {rules out|imkonsiz qiladi}.
Would you prefer to live in a flat or a house in the future?

A house, ideally, if I can find one close enough to a city not to spend two hours a day commuting. That combination is {hard to come by|topish qiyin}, so realistically I may {settle for|rozi boʻlmoq} a flat with a decent balcony for quite a while.
When you were a child, who taught you to be polite?

My parents, and particularly my grandmother, who was extremely {particular about|talabchan edi} greetings and how you spoke to older people. Very little of it was explicit - children {absorb|oʻzlashtiradi} the way adults behave long before anyone sets out the rules.
Do you think children should be taught to be polite at school?

Yes, though school should {reinforce|mustahkamlash} rather than replace what happens at home. What school can do uniquely is teach politeness among equals - taking turns, disagreeing without insulting - because that only arises {within a group|guruh ichida}. Expecting teachers to instil manners from nothing is an unrealistic burden.
Are people in your country generally polite?

Broadly yes, particularly regarding hospitality, which is taken extremely seriously - a guest is treated with a formality that visitors often find remarkable. Politeness towards {strangers|notanish odamlar} in traffic or in a queue is less consistent, and the contrast between the two is quite {striking|sezilarli}.

p2.task: Describe a building that you like to visit.
bullets: what and where the building is
and explain why you like visiting it
p2.ans:
The building I want to describe is the Alisher Navoi National Library in Tashkent, which I try to visit whenever I am in the capital.

It is a large building near the centre, and architecturally it is quite {imposing|salobatli} without being beautiful in any obvious way - a lot of stone and glass, with a very wide entrance staircase. The interior, though, is exceptional: high ceilings, enormous reading rooms with rows of wooden desks, and a quality of {stillness|sukunat} that you very rarely encounter in a city.

I go perhaps five or six times a year, which is as often as I am in Tashkent. I usually spend the whole day there. I work on whatever I have brought with me, and I always spend an hour or two in the collections, mostly looking at material on regional history that is simply {unavailable|topilmaydi} anywhere near where I live. The catalogue is now digital, which has made finding things dramatically easier than it was even five years ago.

The reason I like visiting is partly practical and partly something harder to name. Practically, I get more done in four hours there than in an entire day at home, because the environment makes it embarrassing to open your phone and because nobody can reach you.

The other reason is the atmosphere. There is something genuinely affecting about a room containing two hundred people, all working silently on entirely unrelated things. It produces a sense of being part of something {larger|kattaroq} without any obligation to interact, which is a combination almost nowhere else offers.

I also like that it is a public building, free to enter, and that the people using it {range from|dan tortib} schoolchildren to retired academics. That feels increasingly rare and worth {valuing|qadrlash}.

p3: Do you think it is important to preserve historic buildings?

Yes, strongly. They are the most {tangible|koʻrinadigan} connection a society has to its own past - a photograph tells you what something looked like, but standing in a building tells you how people lived. There is also a practical argument: historic districts support tourism and, once a building is {demolished|buzib tashlangan}, the loss is absolute.
Why is it important to preserve them?

For identity, above all - places without visible history tend to feel {interchangeable|bir-biridan farqsiz}. They are also an educational resource that cannot be reproduced, and, less romantically, they are economically valuable, since heritage tourism depends entirely on them. There is also an environmental argument now: restoring a building is usually far {greener|ekologik toza} than demolishing it and building anew.
How do people decide which buildings should be preserved?

Usually through a combination of {architectural merit|me'moriy qiymat}, historical significance and rarity - a plain building may be preserved because it is the last of its kind. Public attachment carries real weight as well, and sometimes overrides expert opinion. The difficulty is that the criteria involve judgement, so decisions are frequently {contested|bahsli}, particularly where the land is valuable.
Who should be responsible for preserving historic buildings?

It has to be shared. The state should set the legal framework and fund what cannot pay for itself, since preservation is a {public good|jamoat manfaati}. Owners have a duty of maintenance, but they need support, because the cost of proper restoration is often {prohibitive|koʻtarib boʻlmas} for an individual. And local communities should have a real voice, since they are the ones who live with the result.
What is the difference between living in an old building and living in a modern building?

Old buildings tend to have better proportions, thicker walls and more character, but they are expensive to heat and maintain and rarely {accommodate|moslashadi} modern requirements without serious work. Modern buildings are efficient, well insulated and practical, and are often {architecturally forgettable|me'moriy jihatdan esda qolmaydigan}. In short, you are trading comfort against character.
Do people prefer living in old buildings or modern buildings?

Most people, given a free choice, prefer modern - the practical advantages are considerable and the running costs are lower. A {minority|ozchilik} strongly prefer older buildings and will accept the inconvenience for the character. Interestingly, in many cities the old buildings are the more expensive, which suggests that once {scarcity|kamyoblik} enters the picture, preference and price diverge.
What can people learn from historic buildings?

A great deal about how people lived - room sizes, heating, what was considered private. They also show what a society valued, since resources went to what mattered most. And technically, older buildings often demonstrate {passive|passiv} solutions to heat and ventilation that modern construction solved with machinery, which is now being {rediscovered|qayta kashf etilmoqda} for environmental reasons.
Do you think more historic buildings will disappear in the future?

Some will, inevitably - pressure on urban land is only increasing and maintenance is expensive. But I am cautiously optimistic, because public awareness has grown considerably and legal protection is stronger than it was a generation ago. The buildings most {at risk|xavf ostida} are the ordinary ones - modest houses and industrial buildings that nobody classifies as important until they have already gone.

sessions.t2: A shop or store that you often visit
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my second year of a degree in information systems, so studying is very much my {full-time occupation|asosiy mashgʻulot} at the moment.
Which subject are you interested in?
Within my course, databases and data analysis interest me most. Outside it, I read a fair amount of history, which has {no bearing on|aloqasi yoʻq} my degree but which I find genuinely absorbing.
Is this subject difficult to study?

Parts of it are. The programming itself becomes straightforward with practice, but the theoretical side - how data is structured and {optimised|optimallashtirilgan} - is considerably harder, and it demands a kind of precision that takes a long time to develop.
Why did you choose this subject?

Partly for {pragmatic|amaliy} reasons, since the job market is strong and the skills are portable. But I also like problems that have a definite answer - your code either works or it does not, and I find that {immediate feedback|bevosita natija} far more satisfying than subjects where everything is a matter of interpretation.
What do you like most about this subject?

The moment something that has been failing for hours suddenly runs correctly. It sounds trivial, but that {sense of breakthrough|yorilish hissi} is genuinely addictive and it makes the preceding frustration feel {worthwhile|arzigulik}.

p2.task: Describe a shop or store that you often visit.
bullets: and explain why you like going to this shop
p2.ans:
The shop I want to describe is a small second-hand bookshop about ten minutes' walk from my university, which I have been visiting for roughly three years.

It is on a side street off one of the main roads, occupying what was clearly once a flat, and you would {walk straight past it|e'tibor bermay oʻtib ketasiz} if you did not know it was there. There is no sign beyond a small painted board, and the window display has, as far as I can tell, not changed since I first went in.

It sells second-hand books almost exclusively, in Uzbek, Russian and English, and the stock is {wildly unpredictable|juda notekis}. There are rows of ordinary paperbacks and then, without any apparent logic, a shelf of technical manuals from the 1970s. Nothing is organised in any system I have ever managed to identify, which is either the charm of it or the problem with it depending on your mood.

I go perhaps twice a month, usually with no particular intention of buying anything. I spend twenty minutes or half an hour working through a few shelves, and I leave with something about half the time.

The reason I like it comes down to two things. The first is the {element of chance|tasodif omili}. Online, you find exactly what you searched for, which is efficient and slightly {joyless|zavqsiz}. In that shop you find things you did not know existed, and three or four books that genuinely changed what I am interested in were {pure accidents|sof tasodif}.

The second is the owner, an older man who never {pesters you|bezovta qilmaydi} but who, if you ask about one book, will produce two more you should read instead. He is almost always right, and that kind of knowledge is not something any algorithm has {replicated|takrorlagan} yet.

p3: What is the difference between shopping in the past and shopping nowadays?

The scale of {choice|tanlov} is the biggest difference - people once bought from whatever was locally available and now have access to almost anything. Shopping has also become faster and more {impersonal|shaxssiz}: the relationship with a particular trader who knew your family has largely disappeared. And it has shifted from a planned weekly event to something continuous, which you can do at two in the morning from your bed.
What is the difference between young people and older people when they go shopping?

Younger people are far more comfortable buying {sight unseen|koʻrmasdan} online, and they rely heavily on reviews and comparison. Older people generally prefer to inspect what they are buying and value a knowledgeable assistant, and many treat shopping as a {social outing|ijtimoiy chiqish} rather than a transaction. Older shoppers also tend to be more brand-loyal, whereas younger ones {chase the best price|eng yaxshi narxni quvadi}.
Do you think it is better to go shopping alone or with friends?

It depends entirely on the purpose. Alone is far more efficient - you know what you want and you are not {waiting around|kutib turish} for anyone. With friends it becomes an enjoyable way to spend an afternoon, and a {second opinion|boshqa birovning fikri} is genuinely useful for clothes. The risk is that company encourages spending you had not planned.
Why do some people enjoy shopping with other people?

Because for them the shopping is really the {pretext|bahona} and the company is the point - it provides several hours of unhurried conversation with something to do. There is also practical value in advice, and a certain amount of {reassurance|dalda}: spending money is easier when somebody else has agreed it is a good idea.
Do you think people shop more than they did in the past?

Considerably more, yes. Goods are cheaper relative to income, credit is easily available and buying now takes seconds rather than a trip across town. {Fast fashion|tez moda} in particular has changed how often people replace things. There is a growing {counter-movement|qarshi harakat} towards buying less and better, but it is still very much a minority.
How has online shopping changed the way people shop?

It has removed the constraints of distance and opening hours entirely, which is a genuine advantage for anyone outside a major city. It has also made comparison automatic, which has {driven prices down|narxlarni tushirgan}. The costs are real, though: local shops have struggled, returns generate an enormous amount of waste, and the {convenience|qulaylik} makes impulsive buying considerably easier than it used to be.

sessions.t2: A time you changed your opinion
p1: Do you use headphones?

Every day, more or less. They have become {an essential part of|ajralmas qismi} my routine - on the metro, while studying, during calls - and I would feel oddly {exposed|himoyasiz} without them on a long journey.
What do you usually use headphones for?

Music and podcasts mainly, but also to {block out|toʻsib qoʻymoq} background noise when I am revising. I use them for listening practice too, where you {pick up|ilgʻab olasiz} far more detail than through a speaker.
When did you first start using headphones?

Around eleven, when my parents bought me a very cheap pair for a school trip. They were {nothing to speak of|arzimas} and broke within a couple of months, but I remember being genuinely excited about them at the time.
Do you prefer headphones or earphones?

Over-ear headphones for anything at home - the sound is fuller and they are comfortable for hours. Earphones for travelling, purely because they {fit in a pocket|choʻntakka sigʻadi}. The compromise is that earphones {run out of battery|batareyasi tugaydi} at the least convenient moments.
Do you like singing songs?

I do, though I am under no illusions about my ability. I sing constantly when nobody can hear me, and it genuinely {lifts my mood|kayfiyatimni koʻtaradi}. In front of other people I become extremely {self-conscious|uyatchan}.
Do you often sing?

Most days in some form, even if it is only {humming along to|ohangini xirgoyi qilish} something. Properly singing, with any intention of sounding good, is much rarer - perhaps at family gatherings a few times a year.
Where do you usually sing?

In the shower, in the kitchen, and walking home when the street is empty. Essentially anywhere I am alone and my hands are busy, which suggests it happens {of its own accord|oʻz-oʻzidan} rather than as a decision.
Do you think singing can make people feel happier?

I think it genuinely can, and there is reasonable evidence behind it - singing affects breathing and releases the same chemicals as exercise. Group singing in particular produces a strong sense of {connection|bogʻliqlik}, which is presumably why almost every culture has developed it {independently|mustaqil ravishda}.

p2.task: Describe a time when you changed your opinion about something.
bullets: how long it took you to change
and explain how you feel about it now
p2.ans:
The opinion I want to talk about is my view of public transport, which I held firmly for years and which turned out to be almost entirely {unexamined|oʻylab koʻrilmagan}.

Until I was about nineteen, I regarded the metro and buses as something you used because you could not afford anything better. Owning a car was the obvious goal, and I assumed that anyone who continued taking the bus after they could drive was simply {making do|chidab yashayapti}. I would not have defended this seriously if challenged - it was less an argument than an assumption I had absorbed from the people around me.

What changed it was a combination of two things. The first was practical: I started a part-time job in the centre and, after a few months of being driven, I worked out that the metro was consistently faster at peak times and cost a {fraction|arzimagan qismi} of what fuel and parking did. The second was a module in my course on urban planning, where we looked at data comparing cities. Seeing how much of a city's land goes to roads and parking, and what that {does to|qanday ta'sir qiladi} the places people actually live, was genuinely difficult to argue with.

It took perhaps six months in total, and it was {gradual rather than sudden|toʻsatdan emas, asta-sekin}. I remember arguing the old position for a while after I had privately stopped believing it, which I think is quite common.

How I feel about it now is mostly interest in the process rather than satisfaction at the conclusion. What struck me afterwards was that I had held a confident view for years without ever having been given a reason for it. Since then I have tried to be more honest about which of my opinions I actually have evidence for, and it is a {smaller number|kamroq raqam} than I would like.

p3: Why do people sometimes change their opinions?

Usually because of new evidence or direct experience, which is considerably more persuasive than argument. Changing circumstances matter too - people's views on tax or childcare shift when their own situation does. And sometimes it is simply {maturity|yetuklik}: opinions formed at seventeen rarely survive close inspection at thirty.
What kinds of things can influence people's opinions?

Personal experience first, then the people around them, since we {take our cues from|ibrat olamiz} those we trust. Media framing is powerful, particularly on subjects where people have no direct experience. Education matters, and so does {repetition|takrorlash} - an idea encountered often enough starts to feel true regardless of the evidence.
Do young people change their opinions more easily than older people?

Generally yes, and for good reasons: they have invested less in their positions and are still {actively forming|shakllantirmoqda} them. Older people have more experience to weigh new claims against, which is valuable, but they also risk {dismissing|rad etish} anything that conflicts with a long-held view. Openness is a habit rather than a function of age, though.
Is it important to listen to opinions that are different from our own?

Essential, and for self-interested reasons rather than merely polite ones. You cannot know whether your own position is sound unless you have {heard the strongest version|eng kuchli koʻrinishini eshitish} of the opposite case. Environments where everyone agrees produce confident, brittle thinking, and people in them are consistently surprised by the world.
Can people's opinions be influenced by their friends?

Very considerably, and usually without anyone noticing. Views tend to converge within a group, partly through persuasion and partly because disagreeing is {socially costly|ijtimoiy jihatdan qimmat}. That influence is strongest in adolescence but does not disappear - adults simply choose friends who already agree with them, which produces the same result by a different route.
How does social media affect people's opinions?

It has two effects that pull against each other. It exposes people to far more views than any previous generation encountered, which should broaden them. But the algorithms {reward engagement|faollikni ragʻbatlantiradi} rather than accuracy, so the most extreme version of any argument travels furthest, and people are gradually shown more of whatever they already responded to. The result is that many users feel better informed while actually seeing a {narrower|torroq} picture.

sessions.t2: An occasion when you woke up early
p1: Do you usually wake up early?
I do, and by choice rather than obligation these days. I am usually up by six, and the first hour, before anyone messages me, is easily my most {productive|samarali} part of the day.
What do you usually do when you wake up early?

I make tea, and then I do whatever requires the most concentration - reading or writing - because my mind is {sharpest|eng tiniq} then. I deliberately avoid my phone for the first half hour, which makes a noticeable difference to how the rest of the day goes.
Is it easy for you to wake up early?

It is now, though it took a couple of months to establish. The thing that actually made it work was going to bed earlier rather than {forcing myself up|oʻzimni majburan turgʻizish} on insufficient sleep, which I tried first and which failed completely.
What do you like about waking up early?

The quiet, above all - nothing is expected of you yet, so the time is genuinely your own. I also like arriving at the day {ahead of it|undan oldinda} rather than chasing it, because a rushed start seems to set the tone for everything that follows.
Where do you live?

I live in Bukhara, in a house with a courtyard in a district about fifteen minutes from the historic centre. My family has been in the same house for three generations, so I have very {deep roots|chuqur ildizlar} there.
Is it noisy where you live?

Not particularly. We are away from the main road, so traffic noise is {muffled|boʻgʻiq}, and the evenings are genuinely quiet. The main disturbance is construction, which has become {a permanent feature|doimiy holat} of almost every neighbourhood in recent years.
How long have you lived there?

My whole life - around twenty-two years. I have travelled and spent time in Tashkent, but I have never lived anywhere else, which probably means I {take a good deal of it for granted|koʻp narsani oddiy deb bilaman}.
What do you like about the place where you live?

The courtyard, which effectively doubles our living space for half the year, and the neighbours, who have been there for decades. There is a genuine {sense of community|jamoaviylik hissi} - everyone contributes to weddings and funerals, so nobody is really {left to manage alone|yolgʻiz qoldirilgan}.

p2.task: Describe an occasion when you woke up early.
bullets: and explain how you felt about it
p2.ans:
The occasion I want to describe is a morning last summer when I got up at half past three to climb a hill outside Bukhara and watch the sunrise, with two friends.

The reason for the absurd hour was straightforward arithmetic. The sun rises here at around five in July, the drive takes forty minutes, and the walk up takes about an hour, so working backwards we arrived at half past three, which sounded far more reasonable the night before than it did at the time.

I had slept perhaps four hours and I remember the first twenty minutes as genuinely {unpleasant|yoqimsiz} - it was cold, none of us spoke, and I was privately certain the whole thing was a mistake. We drove out in the dark, parked at the bottom, and walked up with torches, which was slower than expected because the path is {uneven|notekis} and none of us had thought to check it in daylight.

We reached the top at about twenty to five, with fifteen minutes {to spare|zaxira}. What happened over the next half hour is difficult to describe without sounding sentimental. The sky changed colour very gradually, then very quickly, and the whole plain below us {came into view|koʻrinishga keldi} in stages. It was completely silent apart from the wind, and none of us said anything for several minutes, which for the three of us is genuinely unusual.

How I felt afterwards was a strange mixture of exhaustion and {elation|zavq}. I was useless for the rest of the day and fell asleep at eight in the evening. But it is one of very few mornings from that entire year that I remember in any detail, and that has stayed with me: the things worth remembering almost always seem to require some amount of {discomfort|noqulaylik} first.

p3: Why do some people prefer waking up early?

Partly {chronotype|biologik soat} - some people genuinely are more alert in the morning, and that is largely biological rather than a matter of discipline. Beyond that, early hours are uninterrupted, so people who need concentration find them valuable. And many simply prefer starting the day {ahead of schedule|jadvaldan oldinda} rather than in a rush.
What are the benefits of waking up early?

Uninterrupted time before demands begin, which is where a great deal of serious work gets done. Early risers also tend to have more {regular|muntazam} sleep patterns, since going to bed early follows naturally. There is a psychological benefit too: {a calm start|xotirjam boshlanish} noticeably affects how the rest of the day feels.
Do people nowadays wake up earlier or later than in the past?

Later, on the whole, and they sleep less. Artificial light {decoupled|ajratib yubordi} human routines from daylight, and screens have pushed bedtimes later still. Agricultural work once forced early rising on most of the population; office work and flexible hours have removed that {compulsion|majburiyat} for many people.
Why do some people find it difficult to wake up early?

Most often because they are simply not sleeping enough - the problem is at the other end of the night. {Biological variation|biologik farq} is real as well; genuine evening types find early mornings physically difficult rather than merely unwelcome. And inconsistent schedules make it far harder, because the body never {settles into|koʻnikadi} a rhythm.
Should children be encouraged to wake up early?

Younger children, yes, since regular routines help them enormously. For {adolescents|oʻsmirlar} I would be more careful: there is strong evidence that their body clocks genuinely shift later during puberty, and several school systems have {pushed start times back|dars vaqtini kechiktirgan} for that reason, with measurable improvements. So the principle should be adequate sleep rather than early waking as such.
Do you think people's sleeping habits will change in the future?

I suspect they will become more {flexible rather than earlier|erta emas, moslashuvchan}. Remote and shift work already allow people to arrange sleep around their own rhythms, and awareness of how much sleep affects health has grown considerably. Against that, screens and round-the-clock entertainment {pull in the opposite direction|teskari tomonga tortadi}, so I would expect the gap between the well-informed and everyone else to widen.

sessions.t2: A successful sportsperson
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my third year of a degree in management, so studying {accounts for|egallaydi} most of my week, although I do a little part-time work at weekends.
Why did you choose to study this subject?

Mainly because it is {broadly applicable|keng qoʻllanadigan} - almost every organisation needs people who can plan and coordinate, so it does not {tie you to|bogʻlab qoʻymaydi} one industry. I was also drawn to the fact that a great deal of it is about people rather than purely about numbers.
What do you dislike about this subject?
