A certain amount of {repetition|takrorlanish} between modules - the same frameworks come up in three different courses. Some of the theory also feels rather {removed from practice|amaliyotdan uzoq}, and when I did a placement I noticed that nobody in the company used any of it by name.
Do you prefer comfortable shoes or good-looking shoes?

Comfort, almost without exception. I walk a great deal and badly designed shoes will {ruin your day|kuningizni buzadi}. Ideally you find a pair that manages both, but if I have to {compromise|murosa qilmoq}, it will never be on comfort.
Do you often buy expensive shoes?

Not often, but I have {come round to|shu fikrga kelganman} the idea that cheap shoes are a false economy - they wear out within months and you replace them three times. One reasonably good pair a year {works out much the same|deyarli bir xil chiqadi} in cost and is far better for your feet.
Do you ever get tired?

Of course, though usually it is {mental rather than physical|jismoniy emas, aqliy} fatigue. A day of lectures leaves me far more drained than a day of walking, which I find slightly {counter-intuitive|kutilganidan boshqacha}.
When would you feel tired?

Mid-afternoon is my {low point|eng past nuqta}, roughly between three and five, and again late at night if I have been reading for several hours. I only notice the second one when I realise I have read the same paragraph twice.
Do you think school is tiring?

Genuinely, yes, and I think adults {underestimate|kam baholaydi} it. Sitting still and concentrating for six hours is demanding, and the schedule is rarely designed around when young people can actually {take things in|oʻzlashtirish}. The homework on top of it is what makes it exhausting.
What things make you feel tired?

Long hours in front of a screen, mostly. Oddly, doing nothing is more {draining|kuch oladigan} than being busy, because boredom {saps your energy|energiyangizni soʻrib oladi}. Crowded, noisy places also leave me exhausted even if I have barely moved.

p2.task: Describe a successful sportsperson who did a good job during an important event in their life.
bullets: and explain why you admire what they did
p2.ans:
The person I would like to describe is Bakhodir Jalolov, the Uzbek heavyweight boxer, and the event I want to talk about is his Olympic final.

He is a boxer in the super-heavyweight division, which is the category with the most prestige in amateur boxing, and he had already been world champion before the Games. He is an unusually {tall|baland boʻyli} fighter for the division, which is exactly what makes his style so distinctive - he fights at a distance rather than {trading punches|zarbalar almashish} in close, which requires enormous discipline.

What happened at the final is that he did precisely what he had said he would do. There was a great deal of pressure at home, because no Uzbek had ever won gold in that division, and the expectation {weighed on|bosim oʻtkazdi} the whole team. He went into the ring and fought a completely {composed|bosiq} contest - no wild exchanges, no attempt to finish it early, just a patient, controlled performance over three rounds. He won on points and became Olympic champion.

What I admire is not really the victory itself, since plenty of athletes win. It is the {temperament|xarakter} behind it. The obvious thing to do in a final, with a whole country watching, is to try to produce something spectacular, and that is usually how people lose. He {stuck to|sodiq qoldi} a plan that was unglamorous and effective, which takes more confidence than taking a risk does.

The other reason I admire him is what came afterwards. He has been extremely {vocal about|ochiq gapirgan} the need for proper facilities for young boxers in the regions, and he has put his own money into it. An athlete who uses their position to {open doors for|yoʻl ochib bermoq} the people coming after them is doing something considerably harder than winning a medal.

p3: What qualities should a person have to be successful?

{Persistence|qat'iyat} above all, because almost everything worth achieving involves a long period where nothing visible happens. Beyond that, the ability to {take criticism|tanqidni qabul qilish} without being discouraged by it, and a realistic view of your own weaknesses. Talent matters, but it is {wildly overrated|haddan tashqari ulugʻlanadi} compared with consistency.
Why is determination important for success?

Because progress is almost never {linear|chiziqli} - there is a plateau in the middle of learning anything where effort produces no visible result, and that is where most people stop. Determination is essentially the willingness to keep working through that stage. It also matters because setbacks are {inevitable|muqarrar}, and what separates people is how quickly they resume.
What are the benefits of engaging in different sports for children?

Physically, different sports develop different abilities - swimming builds endurance, gymnastics builds coordination and balance - so variety produces a far more {rounded|har tomonlama} athlete. It also reduces overuse injuries, which are a genuine problem in early specialisation. Socially, team sports and individual sports teach quite different lessons, and children benefit from {both|ikkalasidan ham}.
Can everyone be successful in sports?

Not at the highest level, no - elite sport depends heavily on physical characteristics that cannot be trained, and that is simply {a fact|haqiqat}. But if success means improving, staying healthy and enjoying it, then almost anyone can succeed. The problem is that sport is often presented purely as competition, which {discourages|ruhdan tushiradi} the majority who will never win anything.
What kinds of sports are popular among children in your country?

Football by a wide margin, for boys especially, because it requires almost no equipment. Wrestling and judo have a {deep-rooted|chuqur ildizli} tradition here and are heavily supported. Among girls, gymnastics, volleyball and increasingly tennis. Swimming is growing but remains limited by the number of pools, which is really a question of {infrastructure|infratuzilma}.
Why is gymnastics popular among girls?

Partly visibility - it is one of the sports where women receive genuine attention and have well-known role models, which matters enormously for participation. It also starts very young, when flexibility is natural, and it requires relatively little space. I would add that it is culturally regarded as {appropriate|munosib} for girls in a way some other sports unfortunately still are not.
What is the relationship between sports and success?

Sport teaches the mechanics of success in an unusually {visible|koʻrinarli} way - the connection between preparation and result is immediate and undeniable, which is rarely true in school or work. It also teaches how to lose, which is arguably the more useful lesson. The transfer is not automatic, though; it depends on how the sport is {coached|murabbiylik qilinadi}.
Do successful sportspeople influence children?

Considerably, and more than most adults realise. Children {model themselves on|oʻrnak qilib oladi} people they admire, and an athlete's habits and attitudes are copied along with their technique. That cuts both ways, which is why behaviour off the field matters - an athlete who behaves badly is {teaching that too|buni ham oʻrgatadi}, whether they intend to or not.
Is success in sports more dependent on talent or hard work?

At the very top, you need both - the gap between the best and the merely very good is usually {genetic|irsiy}. But below that level, hard work is far more decisive than people assume, and a great many naturally gifted athletes are {overtaken|ortda qoldiriladi} by less talented ones who trained properly. Talent determines the ceiling; work determines whether you ever reach it.
Should children be encouraged to participate in different sports?

Definitely, and for both physical and psychological reasons. Early specialisation increases injury risk and {burnout|charchash}, and children who try several sports are more likely to find one they genuinely enjoy and stay with. It also delays the moment at which a child decides they are {no good at sport|sportga layoqatsiz}, which is a conclusion a lot of people reach far too early.

sessions.t2: A problem you had with technology
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my second year of a degree in information systems, so studying is very much my {principal occupation|asosiy mashgʻulot} at the moment.
What do you like about your studies?

The problem-solving. You are given something that does not work and you have to {trace the fault|xatoni topish} yourself, which is far more engaging than being told the answer. There is also an unusually clear measure of progress - your code either runs or it does not.
Why did you choose to study this subject?

Partly for {pragmatic|amaliy} reasons, since the job market is strong and the skills are portable internationally. But I also like that it {rewards curiosity|qiziquvchanlikni ragʻbatlantiradi} - almost everything I know beyond the syllabus I learned because something broke and I wanted to understand why.
Do you often use headphones?

Almost daily. They are {indispensable|ajralmas} on the metro, and I use them while working because instrumental music helps me {shut out|toʻsib qoʻymoq} everything else. I take them off near roads, though, after a close call a couple of years ago.
When do you usually use them?

Commuting and studying, mainly, and for calls because it leaves my hands free. I also use them for listening practice, where you {pick up|ilgʻab olasiz} considerably more detail than through a speaker.
What kind of headphones do you use?

Over-ear ones at home, because the sound is fuller and they stay comfortable for hours. I keep a cheap wired pair in my bag as a backup, since wireless ones {invariably|doimo} run out of battery at the worst possible moment.
Do you think headphones are useful?

Very, though the benefit is as much about {privacy|shaxsiy makon} as about sound. They let you create a small private space in a crowded place, which in a city is genuinely valuable. The drawback is that they also make it very easy to {disengage from|aloqani uzish} the people around you.

p2.task: Describe a problem you had with a piece of technology.
bullets: and explain how you felt about the whole experience
p2.ans:
The problem I want to describe happened with my laptop about eighteen months ago, roughly two weeks before a major coursework deadline, which is of course exactly when these things happen.

The machine had been slowing down for a while and I had been {putting off|kechiktirib yurgandim} doing anything about it. Then one evening it simply would not start - it reached the manufacturer's logo and restarted, over and over, in a loop. I had about three weeks of work on it, and although I knew perfectly well that I should have been backing up, I had not done so for over a month. That is the detail that made it a genuine crisis rather than an inconvenience.

What I did, after an hour of {increasingly desperate|tobora umidsiz} restarting, was stop and approach it methodically. I searched the exact error on my phone, which told me it was almost certainly a failing storage drive rather than anything catastrophic. I then borrowed an external enclosure from a friend, took the drive out, connected it to his computer, and managed to {recover|tiklash} about ninety-five per cent of my files over the following two days. The drive itself was {beyond saving|tuzatib boʻlmas edi}, so I bought a replacement and reinstalled everything from scratch.

How I felt went through three distinct stages. The first was {sheer panic|toza vahima}, which lasted about an hour and was completely unproductive. The second was a kind of grim focus once I had a plan. The third, once it was over, was mostly {embarrassment|xijolat}, because the entire situation had been avoidable.

What I took from it is genuinely useful: I now have automatic backups running to two places, and I have never once thought about it since. The lesson was not really about technology at all - it was that the cost of {taking precautions|ehtiyot chorasini koʻrish} is always trivial compared with the cost of not having taken them.

p3: How has technology changed people's daily lives?

It has {compressed|qisqartirgan} time and distance more than anything else. Tasks that once required a day - paying a bill, sending a document, finding information - now take seconds. It has also changed where work happens, since a great many jobs are no longer {tied to|bogʻliq} a place. The less visible change is that it has made everybody permanently reachable, which is a mixed blessing.
What are the main advantages of using technology in everyday life?

Convenience and access, principally. Banking, healthcare appointments and official documents can be handled without queuing, which saves an enormous amount of collective time. It has also {democratised|hamma uchun ochiq qilgan} information - a student anywhere can watch lectures from leading universities. And for people with disabilities, assistive technology has been genuinely {transformative|hayotni oʻzgartiruvchi}.
Are there any disadvantages to relying on technology?

Several. The obvious one is {fragility|zaiflik} - when a system fails, people often have no manual alternative, as my own experience showed. There is also skill loss: fewer people can navigate without a phone or do arithmetic in their head. And there are real concerns about {privacy|maxfiylik} and about how much of daily life now depends on a handful of companies.
Do you think people use technology too much nowadays?

Many do, though I would distinguish between use and {dependence|qaramlik}. Using a device for six hours of productive work is not the problem; the problem is the hours that pass without any decision having been made to spend them. The platforms are {deliberately designed|ataylab ishlab chiqilgan} to be difficult to put down, so I think it is unfair to frame it purely as a failure of willpower.
How has technology changed the way students learn?

It has made material {universally available|hamma uchun ochiq} and allowed people to learn at their own pace, which is a genuine revolution for anyone outside a major city. Collaboration is far easier too. The downside is that access is not understanding, and the constant availability of answers {discourages|qaytaradi} the struggle that actually produces learning.
What are the benefits of using technology in education?

It allows teaching to be {differentiated|tabaqalashtirilgan} - software can adapt to a student's level in a way one teacher with thirty pupils cannot. Simulations make abstract ideas visible, particularly in science. It also removes geographic barriers entirely, which matters a great deal in a country with large rural regions, and it {frees teachers|oʻqituvchilarni ozod qiladi} from marking routine work so they can spend time on the parts that need a person.

sessions.examiner: Younger woman with glasses, Indian appearance
sessions.t2: A person whose interview you saw
p1: Do you live in a house or a flat?

I live in a house with a courtyard, which is the traditional arrangement here. It is not large, but the courtyard effectively {doubles the living space|yashash joyini ikki barobar oshiradi} for half the year, and that is where the family actually spends its time.
What do you like about your home?

The courtyard, above all - there is a grapevine over it, so even in August it stays {pleasantly shaded|yoqimli soyada} and we eat most of our summer meals out there. I also like that the house is old enough to have real character, which newer buildings tend to {lack|yetishmaydi}.
Would you like to move to a different type of home in the future?

Possibly, though not by choice. If work took me to Tashkent I would have to live in a flat, and I would {miss the outdoor space|ochiq joyni sogʻinardim} enormously. Given a free choice I would stay in a house, ideally closer to a city centre.
How long have you lived there?
My whole life - about twenty years. My family has been in the same house for three generations, which means I probably {take a great deal of it for granted|koʻp narsani oddiy deb bilaman}.
Do you like wearing shoes?

In the sense that I have no choice, yes. What I actually like is taking them off - we remove shoes indoors here, and after a long day that is one of the {small pleasures|kichik zavqlar} of coming home.
What kind of shoes do you usually wear?

Plain trainers, almost exclusively, because I walk a lot and comfort {trumps|ustun keladi} everything else for me. I own one pair of formal shoes which {come out|chiqariladi} for weddings and interviews and spend the rest of the year in a box.
Do you prefer comfortable shoes or fashionable shoes?

Comfortable, without hesitation. I am not indifferent to how things look, but I would never {tolerate|chidamoq} discomfort for the sake of appearance. The ideal is something plain enough to be smart and comfortable enough to walk in all day.
How often do you buy new shoes?

Perhaps twice a year, and almost always because something has {worn through|teshilib ketgan} rather than because I want a new pair. When I find a pair that fits properly I tend to {stick with|sodiq qolmoq} that model for years.
Have you ever bought a pair of shoes that you didn't like?

Yes, once online, which was a mistake I have not repeated. They looked quite different in person and the fit was {marginally wrong|ozgina notoʻgʻri} in a way that only became obvious after an hour of walking. Returning them was {more trouble than it was worth|arzimasdi}, so they sat in a cupboard for a year.

p2.task: Describe a person whose interview you saw.
bullets: and explain why the interview was interesting to you
p2.ans:
The interview I want to describe was with a well-known Uzbek film director, which I came across on YouTube roughly a year ago and which ran for close to an hour.

I found it {by chance|tasodifan} late one evening while scrolling, and I genuinely only intended to watch the first few minutes. I ended up watching the whole thing without {so much as glancing at|hatto bir qarab ham qoʻymay} my phone.

What made it unusual is that it was not the standard {promotional exercise|reklama tadbiri} where a public figure talks about their latest project. The interviewer spent most of the hour asking about failure, which is a subject famous people are rarely willing to {open up about|ochilib gapirmoq}. He talked about two films that had {flopped badly|katta muvaffaqiyatsizlikka uchradi}, about the years when he could not raise funding, and about seriously considering leaving the industry altogether. What struck me was how {candid|samimiy} he was - there was none of the polished, rehearsed quality you normally get.

There was one moment in particular that has {stayed with me|esimda qolgan}. He said that talent is enormously overrated and that what actually separates people is the willingness to keep working when nobody is watching and nobody is paying. He put it very bluntly, and coming from someone who had clearly {paid his dues|qiyinchiliklarni boshidan kechirgan}, it did not sound like an empty motivational slogan.

The reason it was interesting to me is that it changed how I think about accomplished people. I had tended to see them as somehow {a different breed|boshqa toifadagi odamlar}, and that interview made it obvious that they mostly just {persevere|sabr bilan davom etadi} for longer than everyone else. I found that far more encouraging than any success story, because persistence is something you can actually choose.

p3: Why do people like watching interviews?

Because they offer something a written profile cannot: {unfiltered|filtrlanmagan} personality. You judge someone by how they react in real time rather than by how they are described. There is also curiosity about the gap between a public image and the person behind it, and practically, interviews are easy to {consume|iste'mol qilish} while doing something else.
What makes an interview interesting to watch?

Preparation, mostly - an interviewer who has genuinely researched the subject asks questions that cannot be answered with a rehearsed line. Willingness to {follow up|izchil davom ettirish} rather than move to the next item on a list matters enormously. And the subject has to be prepared to be honest; a guest who is {entirely guarded|butunlay ehtiyotkor} makes even a good interviewer look weak.
What skills does a person need to be a good interviewer?

Listening above all - the best interviewers abandon their prepared question when something more interesting appears. They need the confidence to {sit through a silence|jimlikka chidash}, because people fill silences with the things they did not intend to say. And they need to be able to press someone without becoming {hostile|dushmanona}, which is a surprisingly fine line.
Do you think interviews are important when choosing someone for a job?

They are useful but {overrated|ortiqcha baholangan} as a predictor. The research is fairly clear that unstructured interviews are poor at forecasting performance, because they mainly measure confidence and similarity to the interviewer. {Structured|tuzilgan} interviews with the same questions for everyone, combined with a practical task, work far better. So the interview should be one element rather than the decision.
What questions are usually asked in a job interview?

The standard ones about background and why you want the role, which everybody prepares for and which reveal very little. More useful are {behavioural|xatti-harakatga oid} questions - describe a time when something went wrong and what you did - because they require a real example. Many employers also ask about weaknesses, which almost always produces a {rehearsed|yodlab olingan} answer.
What makes a person successful in a job interview?

Preparation that is specific to that organisation rather than generic. Concrete examples instead of claims - saying you are organised means nothing, describing a project you ran means something. And {composure|xotirjamlik}: the ability to take a moment before answering rather than filling the silence. Asking good questions at the end also leaves a {disproportionately strong|haddan tashqari kuchli} impression.
Do you think job interviews will be different in the future?

I expect so. Remote interviews are already standard and are unlikely to {revert|qaytmaydi}, and automated screening is spreading, which raises genuine questions about fairness and {bias|xolislik yoʻqligi} in the algorithms. I would also expect more practical assessment - work samples and trial tasks - because employers increasingly recognise that an hour of conversation tells them {remarkably little|juda kam narsa}.

sessions.t2: A time you helped someone solve a problem
p1: Do you often feel tired?

Not constantly, but there are certainly periods - around deadlines - when it {accumulates|toʻplanib boradi}. On an ordinary week I would say my energy is fairly {steady|barqaror}, provided I sleep properly, which is the variable that matters most.
What do you usually do when you feel tired?

I try not to {reach for|qoʻl uzatmoq} coffee straight away, because it only postpones the problem. A short walk outside or twenty minutes of something completely unrelated is usually enough to {recharge my batteries|kuchimni tiklash}. If it is genuine exhaustion, I sleep.
What makes you feel tired?

Long stretches in front of a screen, above all. Oddly, doing nothing is more {draining|kuch oladigan} than being busy, because boredom {saps your energy|energiyangizni soʻrib oladi}. Crowded, noisy environments also leave me exhausted even when I have barely moved.
Do you think people feel more tired nowadays?

I think they report feeling more tired, and there are plausible reasons. People sleep less than previous generations, screens {interfere with|xalaqit beradi} sleep quality, and work follows them home so there is no clear end to the day. Physical labour has declined, but {mental fatigue|aqliy charchoq} has clearly replaced it.
Do you use social media?
Yes, though less than I did. I have deliberately {pared it back|kamaytirganman} to two platforms, because I found the rest were taking time without giving much in return.
Which social media platform do you use most?

Telegram, by a wide margin - here it functions as far more than social media. It is where news, study groups, shopping and most organised communication happen, so it is {woven into|chirmashib ketgan} daily life in a way that would surprise people from other countries.
How often do you use social media?

Several times a day, but in short bursts rather than long sessions. My screen time report says about an hour and a quarter, most of it in pieces of two or three minutes, which is the part I find {faintly alarming|biroz tashvishli}.
What do you usually do on social media?

Mostly messaging and keeping up with study and news channels. I post very rarely - perhaps a few times a year - because I have never been comfortable {broadcasting|e'lon qilish} my life. So I am very much a reader rather than a contributor.
Do you think you spend too much time on social media?

Probably, yes, though the number is less concerning than the pattern. It is not an hour I chose to spend; it is an hour that {disappeared in fragments|boʻlak-boʻlak yoʻqoldi} while I was waiting for things. I have started leaving my phone in another room when I study, which has made a measurable difference.

p2.task: Describe a time when you helped someone solve a problem.
bullets: and explain how you felt afterwards
p2.ans:
The occasion I want to describe is when I helped a classmate prepare for a resit examination that she was, by her own account, certain she was going to fail.

This was last year. She had failed a statistics module by a small margin and had one attempt left, with about five weeks to prepare. The real problem was not the mathematics, which she was perfectly capable of. It was that she had convinced herself she was {incapable of|qodir emas} the subject, and consequently she had been avoiding it entirely - she had not opened the material since the first failure.

What I did was mostly structural rather than academic. We sat down and worked out exactly which topics had appeared in the failed paper, which {narrowed|toraytirdi} an enormous syllabus to about six areas. Then we agreed a fixed schedule - two hours on four evenings a week, in a library, together, which mattered because studying alone was precisely where she {came unstuck|qiynalib qolardi}. I did very little actual teaching; most of the time she explained a method back to me, and the gaps became obvious as she went.

The thing that made the real difference was none of that, though. About a fortnight in she solved a problem she had failed three times before, and I watched her {attitude shift|munosabati oʻzgarishi} in the space of an afternoon. After that she barely needed me.

She passed comfortably.

How I felt afterwards was mostly {relief|yengillik}, and then something more interesting. I had assumed the obstacle was knowledge and it was almost entirely confidence. That has {stayed with me|esimda qolgan} since, and it has changed how I respond when somebody says they are bad at something - the statement is usually a {symptom|alomat} rather than a fact.

p3: Why do people help each other?

A mixture of motives. Genuine {empathy|hamdardlik} accounts for a great deal - most people find it uncomfortable to watch someone struggle. There is also {reciprocity|oʻzaro yordam}: helping builds relationships you may need later. And in societies like ours there is a strong cultural expectation, particularly towards neighbours and relatives.
What kind of problems do people usually need help with?

Practical ones, mainly - moving, repairs, official paperwork, which here can be genuinely {impenetrable|tushunib boʻlmas}. Technology is an increasingly common one, especially across generations. People are far more {reluctant to|istamaydi} ask for help with money or emotional difficulties, which is unfortunate, because those are where help matters most.
Do you think people are more willing to help friends than strangers?

Generally yes, and that is natural - there is an existing obligation and you will see the consequences. Helping a stranger involves {uncertainty|noaniqlik}: you do not know whether the person is genuine or how much will be asked. That said, people often help strangers {more generously|saxiyroq} in an emergency, precisely because there is no ongoing relationship to manage.
Why is it important to help people in your community?

Because a community where people help each other is measurably more {resilient|bardoshli} - problems get solved before they become crises. It also builds the trust that makes everything else cheaper and easier, from leaving a key with a neighbour to organising anything collectively. And practically, you are likely to need it yourself at some point.
Should children be taught to help other people?

Yes, though through {doing rather than telling|aytish emas, qilish orqali}. Organised volunteering, helping younger pupils, community projects - these teach far more than a lesson about kindness. It also {broadens their world|dunyoqarashini kengaytiradi}, because most children only ever encounter people much like themselves.
Do you think people nowadays help each other as much as they did in the past?

Differently rather than less. Face-to-face help between neighbours has probably declined in cities, where {anonymity|anonimlik} and busyness reduce the sense of obligation. But people now help strangers at a scale that was previously impossible - crowdfunding for someone's operation on the other side of the country is a genuinely new form of generosity. So the impulse has been {redirected|yoʻnaltirilgan} rather than lost.
What can governments do to encourage people to help others?

Practical measures work better than campaigns: funding community organisations, making volunteering count towards qualifications, and giving tax relief for donations. Protecting people who help from {liability|javobgarlik} also matters - many hesitate in emergencies for fear of the consequences. And simply making it {easy|oson} to volunteer, with proper matching and training, removes the main barrier, which is not unwillingness but not knowing where to start.

sessions.examiner: Older Russian woman with blonde hair
sessions.t2: An article about a health problem
p1: Where do you live?

I live in Tashkent, in a residential district in the north of the city - a fairly ordinary neighbourhood of apartment blocks arranged around shared courtyards, about twenty minutes from the centre by metro.
What do you like about the place where you live?

The courtyards, mainly. Each block has a yard with trees and benches, and in the evening it fills with children and older people, so there is a real {sense of life|hayot ruhi} to it. The metro being close enough to walk to is the other advantage.
How long have you lived there?
About nine years. We moved when I was starting secondary school, and although I complained about leaving my old area at the time, I {grew attached to|koʻnikib qolganman} this one fairly quickly.
Is there anything you would like to change about your neighbourhood?

Parking, above all - car ownership has grown far faster than the streets were built for, and the courtyards are gradually being {taken over by|egallab olinmoqda} vehicles. I would also like more green space, since a lot of the original planting has been {built over|qurilib ketgan}.
Do you think you are good at doing things?

At some things, certainly - I am reasonably {methodical|tizimli}, which helps with anything that has to be done carefully rather than quickly. I am considerably worse at anything requiring manual skill, as my family will {readily confirm|bajonidil tasdiqlaydi}.
How did you feel after doing it well?

There is a particular {satisfaction|qoniqish} in finishing something properly that is quite different from being praised for it. It is quieter, and it lasts longer. Praise from other people fades within an hour; knowing you did it well {stays with you|esingizda qoladi}.
Do you often say thank you to people?

Constantly, almost to the point of being {reflexive|avtomatik}. It costs nothing and it changes the tone of an interaction immediately, particularly with people in service jobs, who are {routinely overlooked|doimo e'tibordan chetda qoladi}.
When do you usually say thank you?

In all the ordinary situations - shops, taxis, when somebody holds a door. But I try to be more {specific|aniq} when it actually matters: thanking someone for a particular thing they did rather than offering a general thank you, which is easy to {see through|sezib qolish}.
Do you think people say thank you enough nowadays?

In person, broadly yes - the habit is still strong here. Where it has {fallen away|susaygan} is online and in written communication, where people make requests and simply disappear once they have what they needed. I also think gratitude towards institutions and public workers is {thinner|kamroq} than it used to be.

p2.task: Describe an interesting article you read recently which is related to a health problem.
bullets: and explain why you found it interesting
p2.ans:
The article I want to describe was about sleep deprivation, which I read about three months ago on a science news site that a friend had sent me.

It was not a short piece - it ran to perhaps three thousand words - and it summarised about a decade of research on what happens when people consistently sleep less than seven hours. I had clicked on it expecting the usual {recycled advice|qayta-qayta takrorlanadigan maslahat} about avoiding screens before bed, and it was considerably more substantial than that.

What I learned from it genuinely surprised me. The first point was that the effects {accumulate|jamlanadi}: losing an hour a night for a fortnight produces roughly the same impairment as not sleeping for a whole night, and crucially, people in that state consistently rate their own performance as normal. In other words, you cannot {judge|baholay olmaysiz} your own impairment. The second point was about the range of systems involved - the article described effects on memory consolidation, on the immune response, and on appetite regulation, which is apparently why poor sleep is so strongly {linked to|bogʻliq} weight gain. The third was that catching up at weekends recovers far less than most people assume.

The reason I found it interesting is that sleep is treated almost everywhere as the thing you {sacrifice|qurbon qilasiz} first when you are busy, and students in particular wear it as a kind of badge. The article made the case that this is not a neutral trade - that you are not buying extra hours but {borrowing against|hisobidan olmoq} the quality of all the others.

It changed my behaviour, which very few articles do. I now treat a fixed bedtime as {non-negotiable|muhokama qilinmaydigan} during exam periods, and my concentration is noticeably better for it.

p3: What can people do to stay healthy?

The fundamentals are unglamorous and well established: sleep properly, move daily, eat mostly unprocessed food, and avoid smoking. Beyond that, {routine check-ups|muntazam tekshiruv}, because most serious conditions are far cheaper and easier to treat when caught early. And managing stress, which {underlies|asosida yotadi} a surprising proportion of physical complaints.
What are the most common health problems in your country?

Cardiovascular conditions are the leading cause of death here, as in most countries, followed by diabetes, which has risen noticeably with changes in diet. Respiratory problems are significant in cities because of {air quality|havo sifati}. And I would add that mental health is almost certainly {under-reported|kam qayd etilgan} rather than uncommon, because there is still some stigma attached to seeking help.
How would you describe the general level of health among people in Uzbekistan?

It has improved considerably - life expectancy has risen and infant mortality has fallen sharply over the last twenty years. The traditional diet is reasonably good, with a great deal of fresh produce. The {concerning trends|tashvishli tendensiyalar} are rising rates of obesity and diabetes, particularly in cities, as diets become more processed and people become more {sedentary|harakatsiz}.
Why do some people have unhealthy lifestyles?

Cost and time are the honest answers. Unprocessed food takes longer to prepare and in many places costs more, and exercise requires time that people working long hours do not have. Habit matters enormously - patterns established in childhood are {remarkably persistent|juda barqaror}. And the consequences are distant while the pleasure is immediate, which is a trade humans handle {notoriously badly|juda yomon}.
What effect does advertising have on people's choice of unhealthy food?

A substantial one, particularly on children, who cannot reliably distinguish entertainment from {persuasion|ishontirish}. Advertising works less by changing what people think than by keeping products {top of mind|esda turgan} and normalising frequent consumption. There is also the sheer volume of it: unhealthy products are advertised far more heavily than fresh food, which has {no marketing budget|reklama byudjeti yoʻq} behind it.
Do you think advertisements for harmful foods should be controlled?

I do, particularly where children are the audience. Several countries have {restricted|cheklagan} advertising of high-sugar products during children's programming and the evidence suggests it reduces consumption without harming legitimate business. For adults I would favour {transparency|shaffoflik} - clear labelling - over outright bans, since adults are entitled to make informed choices.
What can governments do to encourage people to live healthier lives?

The measures that work are mostly structural rather than educational. Making the healthy option the {easy|oson} one - safe cycling routes, affordable fresh food, parks within walking distance - changes behaviour far more than information campaigns do. Taxes on sugary drinks have produced measurable results in several countries. And investing in {preventive|profilaktik} care rather than only treatment gives by far the best return per unit of money spent.

sessions.examiner: British woman, short blonde hair and glasses
sessions.t2: A time you worked with others on a project
p1: Do you enjoy shopping?

In small doses. Buying something I have planned for is enjoyable, but {wandering around|aylanib yurish} shops with no particular purpose {wears me out|meni charchatadi} within half an hour. I am very much a targeted shopper.
How often do you go shopping?
For food, two or three times a week at the local market, because I prefer buying fresh. For anything else, perhaps once a month, and usually only because something has {worn out|eskirgan}.
What do you usually buy when you go shopping?

Mostly {everyday essentials|kundalik ehtiyoj mollari} - food and household items. Beyond that, books, and occasionally something for my studies. I try to buy one decent item rather than several cheap ones, which {works out cheaper|arzonroqqa tushadi} over time.
Do you prefer shopping alone or with other people?

Alone, for efficiency - I know what I want and I can be out in ten minutes. With friends it becomes a {social occasion|ijtimoiy tadbir}, which is enjoyable but takes three times as long. The exception is clothes, where a {second opinion|boshqa birovning fikri} is genuinely useful.
Do you like singing?

I do, though I am under no illusions about my ability. I sing constantly when nobody can hear me, and it genuinely {lifts my mood|kayfiyatimni koʻtaradi}. In front of other people, however, I become extremely {self-conscious|uyatchan}.
How often do you sing?

Most days in some form, even if it is only {humming along to|ohangini xirgoyi qilish} something. Properly singing, with any intention of sounding good, happens perhaps a few times a year at family gatherings.
Did you enjoy singing when you were a child?

Far more than I do now, because children have no {inhibitions|tortinchoqlik} about it at all. We sang in class and at celebrations without a second thought. The self-consciousness {creeps in|sezdirmay keladi} somewhere around twelve, and most people never quite lose it.
Do you prefer singing alone or with other people?

Alone, because there is nobody to judge you. Singing in a group at a wedding is a completely different matter, though - nobody is listening to any individual voice, so the {pressure disappears|bosim yoʻqoladi} entirely and it becomes genuinely enjoyable.

p2.task: Describe a time when you worked with other people on a project.
bullets: and explain how the experience went
p2.ans:
The project I want to describe was a market research assignment in my second year, which four of us worked on over about six weeks.

The task was to survey small retailers in Urgench about how they were handling online payment, and then produce a report with recommendations. The four of us had been {assigned|biriktirilgan} rather than choosing each other, which turned out to matter.

My role, slightly by accident, became coordinator. In the first week it became obvious that everybody was waiting for someone else to begin, so I wrote out the stages, put dates against them and allocated the interviews. Beyond that I handled the data analysis, because I was the only one comfortable with spreadsheets, and I wrote the final section.

How it went was genuinely mixed, and I think that is more instructive than if it had gone smoothly. Two of the group were excellent - one of them conducted interviews far better than I could have. The fourth person contributed almost nothing until the final week, which produced a certain amount of {resentment|norozilik} and some difficult conversations. We eventually agreed that he would take on the presentation, which he did well, and in hindsight the problem was partly ours: nobody had asked at the start what each person was actually good at, so he had been {landed with|boʻyniga ilingan} a task that did not suit him.

We got a strong mark, and the recommendations were {well received|yaxshi qabul qilindi} by one of the shop owners, who actually implemented one of them.

What I took from it is that the technical work was never the hard part. Coordinating four people's time and {managing the awkward conversation|noqulay suhbatni boshqarish} early rather than late is what determines whether a group project works, and nobody had ever taught us how to do that.

p3: What are the advantages of working with other people?

You get a wider range of skills and perspectives, so problems are approached from several angles rather than one. Work can be {divided|taqsimlanadi} so more is achieved in the same time. And there is accountability: people are considerably less likely to let a task slip when others are {depending on|bogʻliq} them. Discussion also tends to expose weak ideas early.
Do you think children should be taught how to work with others?

Definitely, and explicitly rather than by simply being put in groups and left to it. Cooperation is a skill with identifiable components - listening, dividing work fairly, {handling disagreement|kelishmovchilikni hal qilish} - and these can be taught. It is also one of the things employers consistently say graduates {lack|yetishmaydi}, which suggests schools are not doing it well.
How can schools teach children to work as a team?

By designing tasks that genuinely cannot be completed alone, where each student holds a different piece of information, so cooperation is {unavoidable|muqarrar} rather than optional. Assigning and rotating roles helps, as does assessing the process and not only the final product. And teaching children how to give feedback to a peer without {causing offence|xafa qilmasdan}, which is rarely taught at all.
What can governments do to encourage people to work together?

Fund the places where cooperation happens - community centres, sports clubs, shared workspaces - because people cooperate when they are in the same room. Supporting cooperatives and community organisations through tax treatment helps. And {involving people|odamlarni jalb qilish} genuinely in local decisions, because nothing builds cooperation faster than a shared project whose outcome actually matters.
How important is it for different countries to work together?

Essential, because the serious problems {transcend borders|chegaralardan oshib ketadi} - climate, pandemics, trade, water. Here specifically, water management in Central Asia cannot be solved by any one state acting alone; the Aral Sea is the clearest possible demonstration of what happens when countries {pursue|intiladi} their interests separately.
Why is cooperation between countries important?

Practically, because shared problems need shared solutions and because trade makes everyone better off. But I would add a less obvious reason: regular cooperation {builds familiarity|tanishlikni hosil qiladi}, and countries that work together routinely are far less likely to let a dispute {escalate|keskinlashmoq}. The habit of cooperating is itself a form of security.

sessions.t2: An interesting video you watched
p1: Do you like singing?

I enjoy it, though I would not claim any talent. I sing more or less constantly when I am alone, and it reliably {lifts my mood|kayfiyatimni koʻtaradi}. With an audience I become very {self-conscious|uyatchan}, which is a shame.
How often do you sing?
Every day in some form - usually {humming along to|ohangini xirgoyi qilish} whatever is playing while I cook or walk. Deliberate singing, where I am actually trying, is much rarer.
Did you enjoy singing when you were a child?

Enormously, and without any self-consciousness whatsoever. We sang at school and at family gatherings and nobody {gave it a second thought|ikkinchi marta oʻylab ham koʻrmasdi}. That changes around adolescence, and in my case it never really changed back.
Do you prefer singing alone or with other people?

Alone when I am just enjoying it. In a group, though - at a wedding, for instance - it is a different experience entirely, because no individual voice is {picked out|ajralib turadi} and the self-consciousness disappears. Group singing is probably the more enjoyable of the two.
Where is your hometown?
My hometown is Namangan, in the Fergana Valley in the east of the country. It is one of the largest cities in Uzbekistan, although it still {retains|saqlab qolgan} a fairly traditional character.
What do you like most about your hometown?

The {sense of community|jamoaviylik hissi}. Neighbours genuinely know one another, which is something you lose in bigger cities. I also like how green it is - the valley is extremely fertile, and the city is known above all for flower growing.
Has your hometown changed much in recent years?

Considerably. There has been a great deal of new construction, several roads have been widened, and the centre has been {redeveloped|qayta qurilgan}. Some of it is a clear improvement; some older buildings have been lost in the process, which I think is a genuine {shame|achinarli}.
Would you like to continue living in your hometown in the future?

Possibly later in life. At the moment I want to be somewhere with more career opportunities, which realistically means Tashkent or abroad. But I can easily imagine {settling down|joylashib qolmoq} there eventually, because it would be a far better place to raise a family.

p2.task: Describe an interesting video you watched recently.
bullets: and explain why you found it interesting
p2.ans:
The video I want to describe is a documentary about how the shipping container changed world trade, which I came across on YouTube a few months ago and which ran for about forty minutes.

I found it {by accident|tasodifan} - it appeared in my recommendations late one evening and I clicked on it more or less {out of idleness|zerikkanimdan}, fully expecting to watch two minutes of it.

The film explained that before the 1950s, loading a ship was done by hand, sack by sack and crate by crate, and that a vessel could spend a week in port. An American businessman had the apparently obvious idea of putting goods into standard steel boxes that could go straight from a lorry onto a ship without being {unpacked|ochilmagan}. The documentary then traced everything that followed: the cost of shipping {collapsed|keskin tushdi} by something like ninety per cent, which suddenly made it economically sensible to manufacture goods on the other side of the world. Entire industries relocated. Port cities that could not handle containers {went into decline|tanazzulga yuz tutdi}, and new ones grew where there had been nothing.

What made it interesting was the realisation that something so {mundane|oddiy} - a metal box with standard dimensions - reshaped the global economy more profoundly than most inventions we actually celebrate. The film made the point that we tend to credit dramatic technologies and {overlook|e'tiborsiz qoldiramiz} unglamorous ones that turn out to matter far more.

It also changed what I notice. Since watching it I find myself thinking about the {supply chain|ta'minot zanjiri} behind ordinary objects, which had genuinely never occurred to me before. Any video that leaves you noticing something you previously ignored has, I think, {earned its time|vaqtini oqlagan}.

p3: What kinds of videos are popular in your country?

Short entertainment clips dominate, along with music videos and comedy. There is also substantial interest in {educational content|ta'limiy kontent} - language learning and exam preparation in particular, which here is an enormous category. Cooking and travel videos do well, and so do vlogs, which appeal because viewers feel they {know|tanish} the person.
Why do people enjoy watching videos online?

Convenience above all - content is available instantly, on any subject, at any length. Video is also {undemanding|talab qilmaydigan} compared with reading, so you can absorb it while doing something else. And the recommendation algorithms are extremely effective at {serving up|taklif qilish} material that matches your interests, which makes stopping genuinely difficult.
What types of videos are popular among young people?

Short-form clips are dominant, along with gaming content, music and anything humorous. Tutorials of every kind do very well, because young people {default to|avtomatik murojaat qiladi} video rather than text when they want to learn something practical. And there is a strong appetite for commentary and reaction content, which is essentially a {social|ijtimoiy} experience rather than an informational one.
Do people prefer watching short videos or longer videos?

Short, by an enormous margin, measured by volume. But I think that reflects how people {stumble into|duch keladi} content rather than what they value. Long documentaries and podcasts have also grown substantially, which suggests there is real appetite for depth when people choose {deliberately|ataylab} rather than scroll.
How have videos changed the way people learn?

They have made demonstration {universally available|hamma uchun ochiq}, which is transformative for anything you learn by watching - a repair, a technique, an experiment. Learners can also {pause and repeat|toʻxtatib, qayta koʻrish} at their own pace. The limitation is that watching is passive, and watching someone do something competently creates a {false sense|soxta tuygʻu} of being able to do it yourself.
Do you think people spend too much time watching videos nowadays?

Many do, yes. The platforms are deliberately engineered to {maximise watch time|koʻrish vaqtini koʻpaytirish} with autoplay and endless feeds, so it requires conscious effort to stop. My concern is less the total hours than the {displacement|siqib chiqarish} - the time comes out of sleep, exercise and face-to-face contact rather than out of nothing.
What kind of videos do you think will be popular in the future?

I would expect more {interactive and personalised|interaktiv va shaxsiylashtirilgan} content, with AI generating or adapting material for individual viewers. Immersive formats will probably grow as the hardware improves. But I suspect the underlying appeal will not change - people have always wanted stories told well, and video is simply the current {vehicle|vosita} for that.

sessions.examiner: Very polite woman who smiled constantly
sessions.t2: A long-term ambition you have had
p1: What is your hometown like?

I am from Samarkand, which is one of the oldest cities in the world. The historic centre is extraordinary - Registan, Shah-i-Zinda - but most of the city is an ordinary working place of about half a million people, with {wide streets|keng koʻchalar} and a great deal of greenery.
Do you like your hometown?

Very much. What I appreciate most is the balance it {strikes|topgan}: it is large enough to have a university and proper facilities, but small enough that getting around is never {exhausting|charchatadigan}. Living somewhere with visible history is also quite a privilege.
Are you a student or do you work?
I work - I finished my studies last year and I am now employed at a travel company, mostly handling bookings and {itineraries|sayohat rejalari} for groups coming to the region.
Why did you choose that job?

Partly because it {draws on|foydalanadi} what I studied, and partly because I wanted work that involved people from different countries. Growing up in Samarkand, you watch visitors arrive and realise how little most of them know about the place, and I liked the idea of {bridging that gap|bu farqni bartaraf etish}.
Do you like your job?

On the whole, yes. It is {seasonal|mavsumiy}, so the spring and autumn months are extremely intense and the winter is quiet, which takes some getting used to. What I enjoy most is that no two groups are the same, so it never becomes {routine|bir xil}.
Do you enjoy shopping?

Reasonably, though I would not call it a hobby. I enjoy markets far more than shopping centres, because there is some {interaction|muloqot} involved and you can often negotiate. Malls I find rather impersonal.
How often do you go shopping?

For food, two or three times a week. For anything else, perhaps once a month, and even then it is usually because something needs {replacing|almashtirish} rather than because I particularly want something new.
Do you prefer shopping online or going to traditional shops?

Traditional shops for food and clothing, because I want to see what I am buying and the quality {varies enormously|juda farq qiladi}. Online for electronics and books, where the item is identical wherever you buy it and the selection is far wider.
Do you compare prices when you go shopping?

Almost always for anything that is not urgent. I will check two or three sellers or {browse online|internetda koʻrib chiqmoq} first, because the difference can be considerable. For small everyday items I do not bother, since the time is worth more than the saving.
Why do you compare prices?

Mostly because the {spread|farq} between sellers here is far wider than people assume - I have seen the same item at twice the price two streets apart. It is also a habit from a period when money was tighter, and habits of that kind tend to {stick|saqlanib qoladi} even once the circumstances change.

p2.task: Describe a long-term ambition that you have had.
bullets: what you have done to achieve it
and explain why it matters to you
p2.ans:
The ambition I want to describe is my intention to open a small tour company of my own, specialising in the parts of this region that visitors never see.

I first had the idea when I was about eighteen, before I had any real idea what it would involve. I had been taken by an uncle to a village roughly two hours from Samarkand where a family still makes paper by hand using a technique that had essentially {died out|yoʻqolib ketgan} and was revived about thirty years ago. There were no visitors there at all, and I remember thinking that this was far more interesting than the fifth monument of the day, and that somebody ought to be {bringing people here|bu yerga odamlarni olib kelish}.

That was seven years ago, and most of what I have done since has been {deliberately aimed at|ataylab yoʻnaltirilgan} it. I studied tourism rather than something more conventional, which my parents were not entirely happy about. I took the job I have now specifically because it would teach me the operational side - how bookings, permits and logistics actually work, which is the part that {sinks|choʻktiradi} most small operators. I have also spent three years quietly building relationships with craftsmen and families in villages across the region, and I have been {putting money aside|pul jamgʻarib kelyapman} since my first salary.

Why it matters to me comes down to two things. The first is straightforwardly that I would rather build something of my own than {spend thirty years|oʻttiz yil sarflash} executing someone else's plan.

The second is less commercial. The crafts in those villages are {disappearing|yoʻqolib bormoqda} because they cannot pay, and the only realistic way to keep them alive is to make them economically viable. If I can do that for even three or four families, I would consider it {worth the effort|mehnatga arzigulik}, whatever the business is worth.

p3: Why do people have ambitions?

Partly because ambition gives structure to decisions that would otherwise be {arbitrary|tasodifiy} - what to study, where to live, what to refuse. It also provides a sense of direction and progress, which people need. And some of it is social: ambition is {rewarded and expected|ragʻbatlantiriladi va kutiladi}, particularly of young people, so there is a degree of pressure involved.
What kinds of ambitions do young people usually have?

Studying or working abroad is extremely common here, along with starting a business - entrepreneurship has become far more {aspirational|orzu qilinadigan} in the last few years. Technology careers are another. Underneath most of them is the same thing: {financial independence|moliyaviy mustaqillik} earlier than the previous generation managed it.
Do you think ambitions change as people get older?

Substantially, and usually in a predictable direction. Young people's ambitions tend to be about {achievement and status|yutuq va maqom}; later they shift towards security, family and doing work that feels worthwhile. Many people also {narrow|toraytiradi} their ambitions, which is sometimes realism and sometimes regret, and it is not always easy to tell which.
Is it important to have a long-term ambition?

It helps enormously, because it makes short-term decisions easier - you have a criterion for saying no. But I would not treat it as essential. Plenty of people find their direction by {following opportunities|imkoniyatlar ortidan borish} rather than planning, and an ambition held too rigidly can stop you noticing a better path. The risk of having none is {drifting|oqim boʻylab suzish}.
What can people do to achieve their ambitions?

Break it into stages with dates, because an ambition without intermediate steps stays a wish. Acquire the specific skills rather than the general ones. Talk to people who have already done it, which {saves years|yillarni tejaydi} of avoidable mistakes. And accept that it will take considerably longer than you expect - almost everyone {underestimates|kam baholaydi} the timescale by a factor of two.
Why do some people give up on their ambitions?

Most often because progress is {non-linear|notekis} - there is a long middle stage where effort produces nothing visible, and that is where people conclude it is not working. Financial pressure forces many to abandon plans for perfectly rational reasons. And some discover the ambition was never really theirs, which is arguably not giving up at all but {correcting|toʻgʻrilash} a mistake.

sessions.t2: Something you saved money to buy
p1: Are you a student or do you work?
I am a student - I am in my second year at university, so studying is very much my {full-time occupation|asosiy mashgʻulot}, although I tutor a couple of evenings a week.
What do you enjoy most about your subject?

The practical sessions. Reading about a process is one thing, but {carrying it out yourself|oʻzing bajarish} makes it real, and you remember it far longer. There is also a genuine satisfaction when something you have set up actually works.
Is there anything you dislike about your subject?

The volume of memorisation in certain modules - there are courses where success depends almost entirely on learning definitions, which I have never thought a good test of anything. Some of the material also feels {dated|eskirgan} compared with current practice.
Did you make things with paper when you were a child?

Constantly. We had art lessons where we made {cut-out|qirqib olingan} figures and cards, and at home I went through a long phase of folding aeroplanes and testing which design {stayed in the air|havoda ushlanib turadi} longest. It was cheap entertainment, which mattered.
What kind of things did you make with paper?

Aeroplanes and boats mostly, and later rather more ambitious things - I remember building a model of our house out of card that {collapsed|qulab tushdi} almost immediately. At school we made decorations for Navruz, which was the one lesson everybody actually {looked forward to|intiqlik bilan kutardi}.
Do people in your country recycle paper?

To some extent, and it is improving. There are collection points in larger cities and some schools run paper drives, but there is no comprehensive national system yet, so a great deal still goes to landfill. Older people are often better at it than younger ones, mainly out of a habit of {not wasting anything|hech narsani isrof qilmaslik}.

p2.task: Describe something you saved money to buy.
bullets: how long you saved for it
and explain how you felt when you finally bought it
p2.ans:
The thing I saved for was a laptop, about three years ago, when I was starting university and my old one had reached the point where it {took ten minutes to start up|ishga tushishiga oʻn daqiqa ketardi}.

The model I wanted cost roughly four months of what I was earning at the time, and I was determined to buy it without asking my parents - partly out of {pride|gʻurur} and partly because they were already paying my tuition.

It took five months in the end. I was teaching two evenings a week and on Saturdays, and I decided to {set aside|ajratib qoʻymoq} everything from the Saturday shifts and live on the rest. To make that work I had to be reasonably {disciplined|intizomli}: I stopped eating out, which turned out to be where most of my money had been {quietly disappearing|bilinmay ketardi}, and I started taking the bus rather than a taxi. For the first month I wrote down every expense, which was genuinely {eye-opening|koʻzni ochadigan} - I had no idea how much small purchases were adding up to.

There were two points where I nearly {gave in|taslim boʻldim}. Once there was a sale and I came very close to buying a cheaper model, and once my phone broke and I had to {dip into|olib ishlatmoq} the savings, which set me back about three weeks.

When I finally bought it, the feeling was not quite what I had expected. There was satisfaction, certainly, but it had far more to do with the saving than with the laptop. I had proved to myself that I could {see something through|boshlagan ishni oxiriga yetkazish} over months rather than days, and honestly that turned out to be worth more than the machine. I have been considerably more careful with money ever since, and I now save {automatically|avtomatik} rather than having to decide each month.

p3: Why do people save money?

For security first - an {emergency fund|favqulodda jamgʻarma} is what stops an unexpected problem becoming a crisis. Beyond that, for specific goals: housing, education, weddings, which here can be extremely expensive. And some people save simply because the habit gives them a sense of {control|nazorat} over their circumstances, which is a psychological benefit rather than a financial one.
Is it easy for young people to save money?

Not particularly. Incomes are lowest at the start of a career while costs - rent, equipment, travel - are proportionally high. There is also considerable social pressure to spend, and credit and instalment plans make {deferring|kechiktirish} payment extremely easy. What young people do have is time, and even small amounts saved early {compound|jamlanadi} remarkably.
What do people usually save money for?

Housing and education are the two largest categories almost everywhere, and here weddings should be added, since they involve substantial cost. Beyond those, cars, travel and increasingly technology. A smaller number save without a specific target, purely as a {safety net|xavfsizlik yostigʻi}, and I would argue that is the most sensible form of saving.
Should parents teach their children how to save money?

Absolutely, and earlier than most do. Children handle money for the rest of their lives, yet financial habits are usually left {entirely to chance|butunlay tasodifga}. Practical teaching works best - giving a child a small regular amount and letting them make mistakes with it teaches more than any lecture, because the consequences are {real but harmless|haqiqiy, ammo zararsiz}.
Do you think people save more money now than they did in the past?

Less, I suspect, at least in proportion to income. Credit is far more available, goods are cheaper and more tempting, and buying something now {takes seconds|bir necha soniya oladi} rather than requiring a trip and a decision. Previous generations also had fewer options and a stronger cultural expectation of {thrift|tejamkorlik}. Against that, saving is easier to automate now, which helps those who do it.

sessions.t2: A person who likes growing plants
p1: Where is your hometown?

My hometown is Bukhara, in the south-west of the country. It is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia, and the historic centre is almost entirely {intact|butunligicha saqlangan} - narrow streets, madrasas and covered bazaars.
What do you like about your hometown?

The scale of it, mostly. Everything happens at a pace you can {keep up with|ergasha olasiz}, you walk everywhere, and you constantly run into people you know. The history is remarkable, but honestly it is the ordinary daily life I would miss.
Would you like to live there in the future?

Possibly, though not immediately. The {range of|doirasi} career opportunities is narrow, so for the next few years I expect to be in Tashkent. I can very easily imagine returning once I have established myself, because it would be a far better place to raise a family.
Who was your favourite teacher at school?

My literature teacher in year nine. She was the first person who treated my opinion as though it {carried weight|ahamiyatga ega edi}, and she had a way of making a text feel like something worth arguing about rather than something to memorise.
What did you like about this teacher?

She never {spoon-fed us|tayyor javob bermoq} answers. She would ask a question and then wait, sometimes uncomfortably long, until somebody {took the plunge|jur'at qilib gapirdi}. That patience taught us to think for ourselves, which is a rare thing for a teacher to prioritise over covering the syllabus.
Do you still remember your teachers from school?

Most of them, which surprises me slightly. I remember how they made me feel about a subject far more clearly than anything they actually taught, which I think {says something|biror narsani anglatadi} about what teaching really consists of.
What kind of clothes do you usually wear?

Fairly plain things - jeans, a shirt, a jumper in winter. I prefer {neutral colours|betaraf ranglar} and simple cuts, partly because they combine easily and partly because I have no real interest in following trends.
Do you prefer comfortable or fashionable clothes?

Comfort, though I do not think the two are {mutually exclusive|bir-birini istisno qiladigan}. I would simply rather not spend a day {conscious of|his qilib turish} what I am wearing. If something looks good and feels good, so much the better.
Do you spend a lot of money on clothes?

Not a great deal. I buy a few items a year and I would rather spend more on something that will last several seasons than replace cheap things constantly - which {works out cheaper|arzonroqqa tushadi} anyway, quite apart from the waste involved.

p2.task: Describe a person who likes growing plants at home or in a garden.
bullets: how they look after their plants
and explain why you think they enjoy it
p2.ans:
The person I want to describe is my grandmother, who has spent most of her life gardening and who is, without exaggeration, the most {devoted|sadoqatli} plant grower I know.

She lives in a house on the edge of Bukhara with a courtyard that she has turned into something close to a {miniature nursery|kichkina koʻchatxona}. She grows an enormous variety for the space: grapes trained over a wooden frame, apricot and pomegranate trees, tomatoes and herbs in summer, and along the whole length of one wall, roses, which are what she is genuinely known for. Neighbours come to ask her advice, which she gives {at considerable length|ancha batafsil}.

The care she puts in is remarkable. She is out there at six in the morning before it gets hot, watering, {pruning|butamoq} and checking the leaves for disease. She makes her own compost from kitchen waste and is deeply {sceptical of|shubha bilan qaraydigan} chemical fertilisers, insisting that if you {look after the soil|tuproqni parvarish qilsang}, the plants take care of themselves. She also keeps the entire plan in her head - what was planted where and when - without ever writing anything down.

As for why she enjoys it, I think there are several reasons. It gives her a clear routine and a reason to be outside, which matters a great deal now that she is retired. There is also the obvious {satisfaction of seeing results|natijani koʻrish qoniqishi}: you plant something, you wait, and eventually it produces, which is a kind of progress that very little else in life offers so visibly.

But more than anything, I think it is her way of {passing something on|biror narsani meros qilib qoldirish}. Half of what grows in that courtyard came from cuttings her own mother gave her. For her the garden is really a {living record|tirik yilnoma} of her family, and that is not something you can buy.

p3: Why do some people like growing plants?

Partly for the results - fresh produce or flowers you could not buy in that condition. But the psychological side matters more: gardening is a well-documented {stress reliever|stressni kamaytiruvchi}, it gets people outdoors, and it teaches patience, because nothing about it can be {rushed|shoshirilgan}. For many it is also inherited, something they grew up watching.
What are the benefits of growing plants at home?

Practically, cheaper and fresher food, and better air quality indoors. Psychologically, caring for something living has a measurable effect on mood, and it provides a sense of progress that is rare in daily life. It also {reconnects people|qayta bogʻlaydi} with where food actually comes from, which city children in particular rarely see.
Do people in your country often grow plants in their gardens?

Extremely often - it is close to universal where people have land. Almost any house with a courtyard has grapevines or fruit trees, and growing at least some of your own food is regarded as {perfectly ordinary|butunlay odatiy} rather than as a hobby. The climate is {favourable|qulay}, which helps enormously.
Is it better to grow plants in a garden or at home?

They serve different purposes. A garden allows real food production and larger plants, which a flat {rules out|imkonsiz qiladi}. Indoor growing is more limited but far more {accessible|qulay} - anyone with a windowsill can do it, and it works year-round regardless of weather. For most people in cities, indoor and balcony growing is the only realistic option.
Do you think children should learn how to grow plants?

Yes, and I would say it is one of the more {underrated|kam baholangan} things a school can teach. It demonstrates biology in a way no textbook manages, it teaches patience and responsibility, and it gives children a direct sense of where food comes from. There is also good evidence that children who grow vegetables are far more willing to {eat them|ularni yeyish}.
Why are some people not interested in gardening?

Time and space, principally - it is difficult to care about plants you have nowhere to put. Gardening also involves a lot of early failure, which {puts people off|odamlarni bezdiradi} before they see any result. And it is slow, which in a culture that increasingly expects immediate outcomes makes it feel {unrewarding|samarasiz} to some.
How can cities encourage people to grow more plants?

Allotments and community gardens on unused land are the most effective measure, and they cost very little. Requiring {planted terraces|koʻkalamzorlashtirilgan ayvonlar} or green roofs in new developments helps. Practical support matters too - free seeds, workshops, and simply making sure new housing has balconies big enough to {be of use|foydali boʻlish}, which a great many do not.

sessions.t2: A sportsperson you know
p1: Where do you live?
I live in Urgench, in a flat in a residential district about ten minutes from the centre. It is not the liveliest part of town, but it is {within easy reach of|yaqin joylashgan} everything I need.
Do you like the place where you live?

I do. It is quiet, the neighbours have been there for years, and everything - market, clinic, bus stop - is {a short walk away|bir necha qadam narida}. It is unremarkable in a way that I have come to appreciate.
Is there anything you would like to change about your home?

The kitchen, mainly. It is {cramped|tor} and badly laid out, so two people cooking {get in each other's way|bir-biriga xalaqit beradi}. I would also replace the windows, because the insulation is poor and the winters here are genuinely cold.
What would you like to change in your home?

If I could do one thing, I would open the kitchen out into the living room. The kitchen is where my family actually {spends time together|birga vaqt oʻtkazadi}, and at the moment its size {puts people off|odamlarni bezdiradi} staying there, so everyone drifts to their own room.
Do you spend a lot of money on clothes?

Not a great deal. I buy a few items a year and I would rather spend more on something that lasts than replace cheap things constantly. It {works out cheaper|arzonroqqa tushadi} in the end and produces considerably less waste.
What kind of clothes do you usually like to wear?

Simple, plain things - jeans, shirts, a jacket in winter. I prefer {neutral colours|betaraf ranglar} because they combine easily, which means I spend almost no time deciding what to wear, and that suits me.
Do you prefer comfortable clothes or stylish clothes?

Comfortable, although I would say the two overlap more than people think. Something that fits properly tends to look better and feel better at the same time. Where they genuinely {conflict|qarama-qarshi keladi}, comfort wins.
Do you usually choose clothes for comfort or style?

Comfort first, and then I ask whether it looks acceptable. I think most people {do it the other way round|teskarisini qiladi} and then spend the day regretting it. For formal occasions I will obviously {make an exception|istisno qilaman}, but those are rare.

p2.task: Describe a sportsperson that you know.
bullets: how they became good at it
and explain why you find them interesting
p2.ans:
The person I want to describe is a wrestler called Sanjar, who is a few years older than me and who trains at the club attached to my old school.

He is from an ordinary family in Urgench and he started wrestling at about nine, which is fairly typical here - it is {deeply embedded|chuqur singib ketgan} in the culture of this region and most boys try it at some point. What is not typical is that he kept going. He is now competing at national level and has won medals at that level twice.

How he became good at it is, frankly, the least glamorous part of the story. He trains six days a week and has done since he was about thirteen. He is at the gym at six in the morning before work, and again in the evening, and he has {kept to|sodiq qolgan} that schedule for close to a decade. He is also extremely careful about weight, which in wrestling means a {permanently restricted|doimiy cheklangan} diet during competition season - something I think people seriously underestimate about combat sports.

What I find interesting about him is not the medals. It is that he is, by his own honest admission, not naturally gifted. He has said more than once that two or three boys in his original group were considerably more {talented|iste'dodli} than him and that every single one of them stopped by eighteen. He simply {outlasted|chidab qoldi} them.

The other thing I find interesting is what he does now. He coaches younger children two afternoons a week, unpaid, because the club cannot afford another coach. Given how little free time he has, that strikes me as genuinely admirable - he is {putting back|qaytarib bermoqda} into the thing that shaped him rather than treating it as something he passed through.

p3: How does sport affect young people?

Physically the benefits are obvious, but I would emphasise the psychological ones. Sport provides {structure|tartib} and a clear link between effort and result, which is rarely so visible elsewhere. It also teaches young people how to lose, how to be part of a team and how to {take instruction|koʻrsatma olish}. And it gives those who struggle academically somewhere to succeed.
How important is sport for young children?

Very, and increasingly so as childhood becomes more {sedentary|harakatsiz}. Physically it develops coordination and bone strength at the age when that matters most. Socially it is one of the few settings where children have to cooperate with people they did not choose. And habits formed young are {remarkably persistent|juda barqaror} - active children tend to become active adults.
Why should children do sports?

For health, obviously, but also because sport teaches things that are hard to teach directly: that improvement requires repetition, that failure is {survivable|chidab boʻladigan}, and that your effort affects other people. It also provides a socially acceptable outlet for energy and competitiveness, which children have in {abundance|mo'l-koʻl}.
What are the benefits of doing sports for young people?

Better physical health and sleep, lower rates of anxiety, and a measurable effect on academic performance - active students generally do better, not worse. Socially, sport {broadens their circle|doirasini kengaytiradi} beyond their class. And it builds a kind of confidence that comes specifically from having been bad at something and then becoming competent.
Do you think children nowadays do enough sport?

Generally not. Screens compete for their time, school days are longer, and parents are understandably {cautious about|ehtiyotkor} unsupervised outdoor play. Organised sport has partly replaced informal play, but it is scheduled and often expensive, so children from lower-income families {lose out|yutqazadi}.
