The decline in simple unstructured activity is the bigger loss.
What can parents do to encourage their children to do sports?

The most effective thing is to be active themselves, because children copy behaviour far more than instruction. Beyond that: letting the child {choose|tanlash} the sport rather than imposing one, emphasising effort rather than results, and making it practically easy - transport and equipment are the real barriers. And crucially, not {over-investing|haddan tashqari berilib ketmaslik} emotionally in whether the child wins.
Is it better for children to do individual sports or team sports?

They teach different things, so ideally both. Team sports develop cooperation and the experience of {shared responsibility|umumiy mas'uliyat}, which is difficult to learn any other way. Individual sports build self-reliance and show very clearly that progress depends on your own work, with nobody to {share the blame|aybni boʻlishish} with. Children who only ever do one miss something.

sessions.t2: A time you got up early
p1: Do you work or are you a student?
I am a student - I am in my third year of a four-year degree, so studying {takes up|egallaydi} the great majority of my week.
What do you study?

I study architecture, which is more {demanding|talabchan} than people assume - it combines design, engineering and a surprising amount of history, and we spend most of our time in the studio rather than in lectures.
Why did you choose this subject?

Because it sits {at the intersection of|kesishmasida} art and science, and I could never choose between the two. I also like that the work is permanent - a building you design might still be standing in a hundred years, which is quite a {sobering thought|jiddiy oʻylantiradigan fikr}.
What do you enjoy most about your studies?

The early stage of a project, when nothing is fixed and you are simply {sketching out|chizib koʻrmoq} possibilities. Once the technical drawings begin it becomes far more {laborious|mashaqqatli}. I also enjoy studying historic buildings and working out why they were built as they were, which in Bukhara is a considerable advantage.
What do you usually buy when you go shopping?

Mostly {everyday essentials|kundalik ehtiyoj mollari} - food and household items. Beyond that, materials for my course, which are not cheap, and occasionally books. I rarely buy anything on {impulse|oʻylamasdan}.
Do you prefer shopping online or in stores?

Online for anything standardised, because the selection is {far wider|ancha keng} and you can compare reviews. For food and clothes I much prefer going in person, since {sizing is unpredictable|oʻlchamlar noaniq} and I like to see what I am buying.
What kind of clothes do you usually wear?
Plain, practical things - jeans, shirts, a jacket. Studio work involves a certain amount of {mess|iflos ish}, so I have essentially given up on wearing anything I would be upset about ruining.
Do you prefer comfortable or fashionable clothes?

Comfortable, decisively. Studio days run for ten or twelve hours, and anything restrictive becomes {intolerable|chidab boʻlmas} by hour six. I am not indifferent to appearance, but it comes a clear second.

p2.task: Describe a time when you got up early.
bullets: and explain how you felt about it
p2.ans:
The occasion I want to describe is a morning last spring when I got up at four in order to photograph the old town of Bukhara before anyone else was awake.

It was for a university project on historic streetscapes, and the reason for the hour was entirely practical. By eight in the morning the main streets are full of people and vehicles, and by ten there are coaches, so if you want photographs of the buildings themselves rather than of crowds, you have to {get there first|birinchi borish kerak}. Sunrise was at about half past five, which meant leaving at four.

I had slept badly out of anxiety about {oversleeping|uxlab qolish}, which is always how it goes, and the first twenty minutes were genuinely unpleasant - it was cold and still completely dark. I walked in, because there was no transport at that hour, and reached the Poi Kalyan complex at around half past four.

What followed is difficult to describe without sounding sentimental. I had the entire square to myself for nearly an hour. I have walked through it a thousand times in my life and I had, honestly, {stopped seeing it|koʻrmay qoʻygandim} - that is what happens with monuments in your own city. In complete silence, with the light changing gradually from grey to a kind of gold, it was effectively a different place. I took about two hundred photographs, perhaps six of which were any good, which is a {perfectly normal ratio|butunlay oddiy nisbat}.

How I felt was a strange mixture of exhaustion and something close to {elation|zavq}. I was useless for the rest of the day and fell asleep early that evening.

But it is one of very few mornings from that entire year that I can recall in any detail, and that has stayed with me: the things worth remembering seem almost always to require some {discomfort|noqulaylik} first.

p3: Do you think people today get up earlier or later than people in the past?

Later, on the whole, and they sleep less overall. Artificial light {decoupled|ajratib yubordi} human routines from daylight, and screens have pushed bedtimes later still. Agricultural work once forced early rising on most of the population; office hours and flexible working have removed that {compulsion|majburiyat} for many.
Why do some people find it difficult to get up early?

Most often because they are simply not sleeping enough - the real problem is at the other end of the night. {Biological variation|biologik farq} is also genuine: true evening types find early mornings physically difficult rather than merely unwelcome. And irregular schedules make it far harder, because the body never {settles into|koʻnikadi} a rhythm.
What are the advantages of getting up early?

Uninterrupted time before any demands begin, which is where a great deal of serious work gets done. Early risers also tend to have more {regular|muntazam} sleep patterns, since an early start naturally pulls bedtime earlier. And there is a psychological benefit - starting the day {ahead of it|undan oldinda} rather than chasing it changes how the whole day feels.
Do you think schools and workplaces should start later in the morning?

For secondary schools, there is a strong case. The evidence that adolescent body clocks {shift later|kechroqqa suriladi} during puberty is now quite solid, and several systems that pushed start times back have reported better attendance and results. For workplaces I would favour {flexibility|moslashuvchanlik} over a fixed later start, since adults vary enormously and a universal rule would suit nobody.
Is it better to work in the morning or in the evening?

It depends entirely on the individual, and I am sceptical of the idea that mornings are {inherently|tabiatan} superior. What is reliable is that most people have a window of a few hours when concentration is at its best, and the useful skill is identifying your own and {protecting|himoya qilish} it for the hardest work rather than spending it on email.
How can people develop the habit of getting up early?

By {moving bedtime first|avval uxlash vaqtini surish}, because forcing yourself up on insufficient sleep fails within a week - I have tried it. Beyond that: consistency, including at weekends, exposure to daylight soon after waking, and having a specific reason to get up. A vague intention to be an early riser almost never {survives|omon qolmaydi} a cold morning.
Do you think modern technology has affected people's sleeping habits?

Substantially, and in several ways at once. Screens emit light that {delays|kechiktiradi} the body's sleep signals, and more importantly the content is engineered to be difficult to stop. Being permanently reachable also means work and social obligations {intrude into|bostirib kiradi} the evening. Technology does offer tools for tracking and improving sleep, but on balance it has clearly made the problem worse rather than better.
